questions.memo: Understanding the audience lets the presenter pitch the language and visuals at the right level so the message is understood.

questions.question: A presenter crams tiny text and ten graphs onto one slide and reads every word aloud. Which evaluation is best?
options: The layout is poor; clear slides with key points and readable visuals would communicate better
The slide is perfect because it has lots of information
More text always means a better presentation
questions.expected: The layout is poor; clear slides with key points and readable visuals would communicate better
questions.memo: Overcrowded slides overwhelm the audience. A clear layout with key points and readable visuals communicates far better.

questions.question: Why is combining verbal and non-verbal formats often the most effective presentation?
options: The spoken words explain, while visuals make the information clearer and more memorable
Two formats always confuse the audience
Words and visuals cannot be used together
questions.expected: The spoken words explain, while visuals make the information clearer and more memorable
questions.memo: Words give the explanation and visuals make patterns clear and memorable, so using both together reaches the audience best.

questions.question: Two presenters share the same data. One opens with the key finding and a clear graph; the other buries it on the last slide. Which is more effective, and why?
options: The first, because leading with the key point and a clear visual makes the message land
The second, because hiding the point builds suspense
They are equally effective regardless of order
questions.expected: The first, because leading with the key point and a clear visual makes the message land
questions.memo: Putting the most important information first, supported by a clear visual, ensures the audience grasps the key message.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about presenting information.

items.text: A graph is a non-verbal presentation
Visual aids support the spoken words
Good presentations hide the main point
A clear layout uses headings and short points
Crowded, tiny text helps the audience

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Verbal = words, non-verbal = visuals; aids support the talk; and good layout leads with the key point in a clear, readable way.

BUS.G10.T3.BUSPLAN.A1.title: The business plan
BUS.G10.T3.BUSPLAN.A1.description: The purpose and components of a business plan — cover page, executive summary, business description, vision/mission, ownership, product/service, legal requirements, SWOT and the marketing plan (market research and the marketing mix, the 4 or 7 Ps) — and the job each part does.
BUS.G10.T3.BUSPLAN.A1.strand: T3 — Creative thinking, opportunity, location, contracts, presentation & the business plan
BUS.G10.T3.BUSPLAN.A1.recovery_strategy: A business plan proves the venture is viable. Know each component's job: executive summary = short overview; marketing plan = how you reach customers (the Ps); financial analysis = does it make money.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a business plan?
options: To show that the venture is viable and plan how it will work
To replace the need for any customers
questions.expected: To show that the venture is viable and plan how it will work
questions.memo: A business plan sets out how the business will work and shows that the venture can succeed (is viable).

questions.question: True or false: The executive summary gives a short overview of the whole business plan.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The executive summary is a short overview of the key points, so a reader grasps the plan quickly.

questions.question: The _________ plan explains how the business will reach and sell to its customers.
questions.expected: marketing
questions.memo: The marketing plan covers market research and the marketing mix — how the business will reach and sell to customers.

questions.question: Which of these is a component of a business plan?
questions.expected: The executive summary
questions.memo: The executive summary is a real component of a business plan. The others have nothing to do with it.

questions.question: True or false: A business plan usually includes a SWOT analysis.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A SWOT analysis is part of a business plan — it weighs the venture's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats.

questions.question: The 4 Ps of the marketing mix are product, price, place and _________.
questions.expected: promotion
questions.memo: The 4 Ps are product, price, place and promotion. (The 7 Ps add people, process and physical evidence.)

questions.question: What does the executive summary of a business plan contain?
options: A short overview of the key points of the whole plan
A list of competitors' phone numbers
questions.expected: A short overview of the key points of the whole plan
questions.memo: The executive summary is a brief overview of the main points — not personal details or raw data.

questions.question: What does the marketing plan section cover?
options: Market research and the marketing mix (the Ps)
questions.expected: Market research and the marketing mix (the Ps)
questions.memo: The marketing plan sets out market research and the marketing mix — how the business will reach customers.

questions.question: Match each component of a business plan to the job it does.

items.text: Gives a short overview of the whole plan
Shows how the business will reach customers
Shows whether the business will make a profit
The key points an investor reads first
Covers product, price, place and promotion
Sets out the expected income and costs

questions.expected: All six matched to the correct component (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Executive summary = short overview; marketing plan = how to reach customers (the Ps); financial plan = does it make money.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the financial section of a business plan?
options: To show whether the business will make enough money to be viable
questions.expected: To show whether the business will make enough money to be viable
questions.memo: The financial section shows expected income, costs and profit — proving the venture can pay its way.

questions.question: The cover page of a business plan shows the business's _________ and contact details.
questions.expected: name
questions.memo: The cover page carries the business's name and contact details — the first thing the reader sees.

questions.question: Which option shows the usual order of the main parts of a business plan?
options: Cover page → executive summary → business description → marketing plan → financial plan
Financial plan → marketing plan → business description → executive summary → cover page
Marketing plan → cover page → financial plan → business description → executive summary
Business description → financial plan → cover page → marketing plan → executive summary
questions.expected: Cover page → executive summary → business description → marketing plan → financial plan
questions.memo: A plan opens with the cover page and executive summary, then describes the business, then the marketing plan, and ends with the financial plan.

questions.question: Why does a business plan include a section on legal requirements?
options: To show the business will operate within the law (licences, registration, regulations)
To list the owner's favourite laws
questions.expected: To show the business will operate within the law (licences, registration, regulations)
questions.memo: The legal section shows the business knows and will meet its legal duties — licences, registration and regulations.

questions.question: True or false: The executive summary should list the owner's personal hobbies.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: False — the executive summary gives a short overview of the plan's key points, not personal hobbies.

questions.question: Which three Ps do the 7 Ps add to the original 4 Ps?
questions.expected: People, process and physical evidence
questions.memo: The 7 Ps add people, process and physical evidence to the original product, price, place and promotion.

questions.question: Sort each item as part of the marketing mix (a 'P') or not part of it.

buckets.label: Not part of the marketing mix

questions.expected: All six items sorted correctly (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: The marketing mix is the Ps: product, price, place, promotion (and more). The owner's food and the weather are not part of it.

questions.question: An entrepreneur shows investors a business plan with no financial section. What is the main risk?
options: Investors cannot see whether the business will make money, so they are unlikely to back it
The plan is automatically perfect without it
It makes no difference to investors
It guarantees the business will succeed
questions.expected: Investors cannot see whether the business will make money, so they are unlikely to back it
questions.memo: Without a financial section, no one can judge whether the venture is viable — so investors will not risk their money.

questions.question: Why is a SWOT analysis useful inside a business plan?
options: It honestly weighs the venture's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats so readers can judge its chances
It replaces the marketing plan entirely
questions.expected: It honestly weighs the venture's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats so readers can judge its chances
questions.memo: A SWOT shows the plan has honestly assessed the venture's internal and external position, helping readers judge whether it is viable.

questions.question: A busy investor has only two minutes and wants the gist of the whole venture. Which component should she read?
options: The executive summary, because it is the short overview of the whole plan
questions.expected: The executive summary, because it is the short overview of the whole plan
questions.memo: The executive summary exists exactly for this: a quick overview so a busy reader gets the key points fast.

questions.question: Match each piece of content to the business-plan component it belongs in.

items.text: A one-page summary for a busy investor
A plan for advertising and pricing
A forecast of profit and cash flow
A quick overview of the whole venture
Details of the target market and the Ps

questions.expected: All six pieces matched to the right component (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Overviews go in the executive summary; reaching customers and the Ps go in the marketing plan; income, costs and profit go in the financial plan.

BUS.G10.T4.SELFMAN.A1.title: Self-management
BUS.G10.T4.SELFMAN.A1.description: The concept of self-management and its place in business — time management, personal goals, a balanced lifestyle, a professional image, self-knowledge, self-confidence, stress management and adaptability — kept apart from being managed by others.
BUS.G10.T4.SELFMAN.A1.recovery_strategy: Self-management = managing yourself: your time, goals, image and stress, without being told. It is the foundation for managing others later.

questions.question: What is self-management?
options: Managing your own time, goals and behaviour without being told
Waiting for a boss to control everything you do
Managing other people's work for them
questions.expected: Managing your own time, goals and behaviour without being told
questions.memo: Self-management means taking charge of yourself — your time, goals and behaviour — without needing to be told.

questions.question: True or false: Time management is part of self-management.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Managing your own time well is a core part of self-management.

questions.question: Managing how you use your hours each day is called _________ management.
questions.expected: time
questions.memo: Time management is planning and using your hours well so you get your work done.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of self-management?
options: Setting your own goals and meeting your deadlines
Waiting to be told to start every task
Letting others plan your whole day
questions.expected: Setting your own goals and meeting your deadlines
questions.memo: Setting goals and meeting deadlines on your own is self-management in action.

questions.question: True or false: Self-management means waiting for your supervisor to tell you what to do.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: False — that is being managed by others. Self-management is taking charge of yourself without being told.

questions.question: Keeping a healthy balance between work, rest and personal life is having a balanced _________.
questions.expected: lifestyle
questions.memo: A balanced lifestyle — mixing work with rest and personal time — is part of managing yourself well.

questions.question: A worker plans her own day, prioritises her tasks and meets deadlines without being reminded. What is she showing?
options: A need to be controlled by others
questions.expected: Good self-management
questions.memo: Planning, prioritising and meeting deadlines on her own is exactly what good self-management looks like.

questions.question: What does developing a professional image mean?
options: Dressing and behaving appropriately so people take you seriously at work
Wearing whatever you like, however untidy
questions.expected: Dressing and behaving appropriately so people take you seriously at work
questions.memo: A professional image is about how you present yourself — dressing and behaving in a way that earns respect at work.

questions.question: Sort each action as self-management or being managed by others.

items.text: Needing a supervisor to check every step

questions.expected: All six actions sorted correctly (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Self-management is acting on your own (planning, goal-setting, meeting deadlines). Being managed by others is waiting to be told at every step.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of stress management?
options: Taking a short break and breathing slowly before a big task
Bottling everything up until you explode
questions.expected: Taking a short break and breathing slowly before a big task
questions.memo: Stress management means using healthy ways — breaks, breathing, exercise — to stay calm and cope with pressure.

questions.question: Build an explanation of why self-management matters in business.
questions.prompt: Pick the best option for each slot to explain why self-management matters.

options.text: Self-management means taking charge of your own time, goals and behaviour
Self-management means waiting for others to manage you
Self-management means avoiding all work
A self-managed person plans their day, meets deadlines and stays professional without being told
A self-managed person only acts when a supervisor gives an instruction
A self-managed person ignores their goals and deadlines
This makes them reliable and productive and prepares them to manage others later
This means they can never work in a team
This is exactly the same as being controlled by others

questions.memo: Claim: self-management is taking charge of yourself. Evidence: planning, meeting deadlines, staying professional without being told. Explanation: it makes you reliable and ready to manage others.

questions.question: Knowing your own strengths and weaknesses honestly is called self-_________.
questions.expected: knowledge
questions.memo: Self-knowledge is understanding your own strengths and weaknesses, so you can build on them and improve.

questions.question: How does adaptability show good self-management?
options: You stay calm and adjust your plans when things change
You refuse to change anything ever
You panic and give up when plans change
You wait for someone else to fix everything
questions.expected: You stay calm and adjust your plans when things change
questions.memo: Adaptability is adjusting calmly to change — a key self-management skill when plans don't go as expected.

questions.question: True or false: Self-confidence helps a person take on tasks and bounce back from setbacks.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Self-confidence — believing in your own ability — helps you take on challenges and recover from setbacks.

questions.question: Which of these shows POOR self-management?
options: Leaving every task to the last minute and missing deadlines
questions.expected: Leaving every task to the last minute and missing deadlines
questions.memo: Procrastinating and missing deadlines is poor self-management. The others are all good self-management habits.

questions.question: Sort each habit as good or poor self-management.

items.text: Leaving everything to the last minute
Ignoring your own health and rest

questions.expected: All six habits sorted good vs poor (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Good self-management: punctual, calm, professional. Poor self-management: procrastinating, neglecting health, blaming others.

questions.question: A learner says: 'Self-management just means doing whatever the supervisor tells me.' How should this be corrected?
options: Self-management is taking charge of yourself without being told; following orders is being managed by others
She is right, it means obeying orders
Self-management means ignoring the supervisor completely
Self-management has nothing to do with work
questions.expected: Self-management is taking charge of yourself without being told; following orders is being managed by others
questions.memo: Don't confuse the two: managing yourself is doing the right things on your own initiative, not simply obeying instructions.

questions.question: Why is self-management often called the foundation for managing other people?
options: If you can reliably manage your own time, goals and behaviour, you can be trusted to manage others
Because managing others requires no skills at all
Because self-management replaces the need for any managers
questions.expected: If you can reliably manage your own time, goals and behaviour, you can be trusted to manage others
questions.memo: You must master managing yourself first; that reliability is what earns the trust and skill to manage other people.

questions.question: How do strong self-management skills help a person succeed at work?
options: They make the person reliable, productive and able to cope with pressure and change
They make the person dependent on constant supervision
They have no effect on the person's work
They guarantee the person never has to learn anything
questions.expected: They make the person reliable, productive and able to cope with pressure and change
questions.memo: Self-management makes someone dependable and productive, and helps them handle stress and change — all of which support success.

questions.question: Match each action to the self-management skill it shows.

items.text: Making a daily schedule and sticking to it
Taking deep breaths before a big presentation
Dressing neatly and speaking politely at work
Prioritising the most urgent tasks first
Going for a walk to clear your head

questions.expected: All six actions matched to the right skill (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Scheduling and prioritising = time management; staying calm = stress management; dressing and behaving well = professional image.

BUS.G10.T4.TEAM.A1.title: Relationships & team performance
BUS.G10.T4.TEAM.A1.description: How people work together to reach business goals, the factors that affect workplace relationships (prejudice, beliefs, values, diversity), and the criteria for successful, collaborative team performance — kept apart from the barriers to it.
BUS.G10.T4.TEAM.A1.recovery_strategy: Good teams share: clear goals, openness, mutual respect and trust, commitment, sound relations. Barriers are the opposite: prejudice, poor communication, distrust. Diversity is a strength when managed well.

questions.question: What is a team in a business?
options: A group of people working together towards a shared goal
A list of the business's customers
questions.expected: A group of people working together towards a shared goal
questions.memo: A team is people working together towards a shared goal, combining their efforts and skills.

questions.question: True or false: Mutual respect and trust help a team perform well.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Respect and trust are key criteria for good teamwork — they reduce conflict and help members work together.

questions.question: Clear, shared _________ are a key criterion for good teamwork.
questions.expected: goals
questions.memo: A good team shares clear goals, so everyone is pulling in the same direction.

questions.question: Which of these is a criterion for successful teamwork?
questions.expected: Open communication between members
questions.memo: Open communication is a criterion for good teamwork. The others are barriers that harm a team.

questions.question: True or false: Prejudice is a criterion for good teamwork.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: False — prejudice is a barrier, not a criterion. Good teamwork needs respect, trust and openness.

questions.question: When team members judge others unfairly because of their background, this is called _________.
questions.expected: prejudice
questions.memo: Prejudice is judging people unfairly because of their background — a barrier to good workplace relationships.

questions.question: Which pair correctly shows one thing that HELPS a team and one that HARMS it?
questions.expected: Mutual respect helps; distrust harms
questions.memo: Respect helps a team; distrust harms it. Keep the helpers (criteria) apart from the harmers (barriers).

questions.question: How can diversity strengthen a team when it is managed well?
options: Different backgrounds bring a wider range of skills, ideas and viewpoints
It guarantees the team will always argue
It makes everyone think exactly alike
It removes the need for any goals
questions.expected: Different backgrounds bring a wider range of skills, ideas and viewpoints
questions.memo: Well-managed diversity is a strength: varied backgrounds add more skills, ideas and perspectives to the team.

questions.question: Sort each factor by whether it helps or harms teamwork.
questions.expected: All six factors sorted helps vs harms (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Communication, trust, respect and commitment help a team. Prejudice, secrecy and distrust harm it.

questions.question: What happens to a team when communication is poor?
options: Misunderstandings, mistakes and conflict become more likely
questions.expected: Misunderstandings, mistakes and conflict become more likely
questions.memo: Poor communication leads to misunderstandings, errors and conflict — it is a barrier to good team performance.

questions.question: Thesis: 'Good teamwork improves a business's performance.' Choose the THREE strongest supporting reasons.
questions.thesis: Good teamwork improves a business's performance.

pool.text: Members share ideas and skills, so problems are solved faster
Trust and respect reduce conflict and wasted time
Clear shared goals keep everyone pulling in the same direction
Teams always work slower than one person alone
The team happens to meet in a room with blue walls
Teamwork only matters at the year-end party

questions.memo: Shared skills, trust and clear goals all lift performance. The 'slower than one person' point is a counter, the blue walls are irrelevant, and 'only at the party' is weak.

questions.question: A team works best when its members are _________ to the shared goal.
questions.expected: committed
questions.memo: Commitment — members genuinely caring about the shared goal — is a key criterion for strong teamwork.

questions.question: Two team members hold different personal beliefs. What is the best way to handle this for good teamwork?
options: Respect each other's differences and focus on the shared goal
Mock the beliefs they disagree with
Exclude one member from the team
Refuse to work with anyone different
questions.expected: Respect each other's differences and focus on the shared goal
questions.memo: Differences in beliefs and values are handled well through respect — keeping the focus on the shared goal.

questions.question: True or false: Diversity in a team is always a weakness.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: False — diversity is a strength when managed well, bringing more skills and ideas. Only poorly handled differences cause problems.

questions.question: Which of these is a BARRIER to good teamwork?
questions.expected: Distrust between members
questions.memo: Distrust is a barrier that harms a team. Clear goals, communication and respect are criteria that help it.

questions.question: Sort each item as a criterion for good teamwork or a barrier to it.
questions.expected: All six items sorted criterion vs barrier (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Criteria are the things good teams share (clear goals, respect, commitment). Barriers are the opposite (poor communication, prejudice, distrust).

questions.question: Thesis: 'A diverse team can be a strength for a business.' Choose the THREE strongest reasons.
questions.thesis: A diverse team can be a strength for a business.

pool.text: Different backgrounds bring a wider range of ideas and skills
Members can understand and serve a wider range of customers
Varied viewpoints help the team avoid blind spots
Differences always cause arguments that ruin teams
The team's logo is green
Diversity only counts on public holidays

questions.memo: Diversity adds ideas and skills, helps the team understand more customers, and reduces blind spots. The 'always argues' point is a counter, the logo is irrelevant, and 'only on holidays' is weak.

questions.question: A learner lists 'prejudice' as a criterion for successful teamwork. How should this be corrected?
options: Prejudice is a barrier, not a criterion; good teamwork needs respect, trust and openness
She is right, prejudice builds strong teams
Prejudice has no effect on teams
Prejudice is the most important criterion
questions.expected: Prejudice is a barrier, not a criterion; good teamwork needs respect, trust and openness
questions.memo: Don't confuse the two: prejudice harms a team (a barrier). The criteria for good teamwork are respect, trust, openness and shared goals.

questions.question: Why is mutual trust so important for collaboration in a team?
options: When members trust each other they share openly, rely on one another and work towards the goal without fear
Trust makes members compete against each other
Trust removes the need for any communication
Trust means no one has to do any work
questions.expected: When members trust each other they share openly, rely on one another and work towards the goal without fear
questions.memo: Trust is the glue of collaboration: it lets members share honestly and depend on one another to reach the goal.

questions.question: Sort each behaviour as good team behaviour or a barrier to teamwork.

items.text: Listening to a teammate's idea respectfully
Excluding someone because of their background

questions.expected: All six behaviours sorted correctly (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Good team behaviour builds trust and shares the load. Barriers exclude people, hide information and refuse to cooperate.

BUS.G11.T1.INFLUENCE.A1.title: Influences and control over the three environments
BUS.G11.T1.INFLUENCE.A1.description: The degree of control a business has over the micro (full control), market (influence only) and macro (no control) environments, and getting involved in the macro environment when it benefits the business.
BUS.G11.T1.INFLUENCE.A1.strand: T1 — Business environments, socio-economic issues, sectors, ownership & acquiring a business
BUS.G11.T1.INFLUENCE.A1.recovery_strategy: Control shrinks as you move out: micro = full control, market = influence only, macro = no control (adapt). A business can still get involved in the macro environment (e.g. lobbying) when it benefits the business.

questions.question: Over which environment does a business have the MOST control?
questions.expected: The micro (internal) environment
questions.memo: A business controls its micro environment fully — its mission, structure, resources and culture. It can only influence the market and must adapt to the macro environment.

questions.question: Over which environment does a business have NO control?
questions.expected: The macro environment
questions.memo: The macro environment — the economy, laws, technology, society — is beyond the business's control. It can only adapt to it.

questions.question: True or false: A business can fully control its market environment.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: A business cannot control the market environment — customers, suppliers and competitors make their own decisions. It can only influence them (e.g. by advertising or negotiating).

questions.question: A business can _________ the market environment, but it cannot control it.
questions.expected: influence
questions.memo: The market environment is close enough to influence — through advertising, negotiating and good service — but not to control.

questions.question: When is it worthwhile for a business to get involved in its macro environment (for example by lobbying)?
options: Never, because the macro environment cannot be changed at all
Only when the business is making a loss
Only when ordered to by the government
questions.expected: When it benefits the business
questions.memo: A business cannot control the macro environment, but it can get involved (e.g. lobby for fair laws) when doing so benefits the business.

questions.question: True or false: Management primarily controls the micro environment — the mission, structure, resources and culture of the business.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The micro environment is inside the business, so management controls it: the mission and objectives, the management structure, the resources and the culture.

questions.question: Customers, suppliers and competitors that create opportunities and threats for a business are part of its _________ environment.
questions.expected: market
questions.memo: The market environment is made up of the close outside parties — customers, suppliers, competitors, regulators — that create opportunities and threats the business cannot control.

questions.question: Sort each factor by how much control the business has over it.

items.text: The wording of the company's mission statement
A new tax law passed by parliament
How staff are trained and managed
Which supplier the business buys stock from
The rand's exchange rate against the dollar

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Micro = inside and controllable (mission, staff). Market = close outside, influence only (competitors, suppliers). Macro = broad outside, no control (laws, exchange rates).

questions.question: A business lobbies the government to change a proposed law. Which environment is it trying to influence?
questions.expected: The macro environment
questions.memo: Laws are part of the macro environment. Lobbying is a way of getting involved in the macro environment even though the business cannot control it.

questions.question: Why can a business NOT control its market environment?
options: Because customers, suppliers and competitors make their own independent decisions
Because the market environment is inside the business
Because the government runs the market environment
Because the market environment does not affect the business
questions.expected: Because customers, suppliers and competitors make their own independent decisions
questions.memo: The parties in the market environment act independently, so the business can only influence them — not control them.

questions.question: Building useful contacts in order to find new customers and partners is called _________.
questions.expected: networking
questions.memo: Networking means building relationships and contacts that benefit the business, such as meeting potential customers or partners.

questions.question: True or false: A business has more control over its market environment than over its macro environment.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Control decreases outward: full control of the micro, some influence over the market, and no control over the macro environment.

questions.question: Which is an example of a business getting involved in its macro environment for its own benefit?
options: Joining an industry body to lobby for better regulations
Training its own staff to work faster
questions.expected: Joining an industry body to lobby for better regulations
questions.memo: Lobbying through an industry body is a way to get involved in the macro environment. The other options are internal (micro) changes.

questions.question: Sort each business action by the environment it works on.

items.text: Changing the company's culture and values
Negotiating a better price with a supplier
Raising prices because inflation pushed up costs
Advertising to win customers away from a rival
Complying with a new environmental law

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Internal changes act on the micro environment; negotiating and advertising influence the market; responding to inflation and laws is adapting to the macro environment.

questions.question: A weakening rand has made imported fabric more expensive. What is the business's best response?
options: Adapt its plans, because it cannot control the exchange rate
Pass a law to fix the exchange rate
Ignore it, because the macro environment never affects business
questions.expected: Adapt its plans, because it cannot control the exchange rate
questions.memo: The exchange rate is a macro factor the business cannot control. The realistic response is to adapt — e.g. find local fabric or adjust prices.

questions.question: Read both views, then decide which business each statement matches.

source_a.text: We only manage what happens inside our own walls. The economy, new laws and our competitors are someone else's concern.

source_b.text: We lobby for fair regulations, network to find new customers, and form alliances to cope with the outside world we cannot control.

statements.text: Tries to influence the macro environment
Focuses only on the micro environment
Operates within a market environment
Claims to fully control the national economy

questions.expected: s1=b_only, s2=a_only, s3=both, s4=neither
questions.memo: Business B gets involved in the macro environment (lobbying, alliances); Business A focuses only on the micro environment. Both have a market environment, and neither controls the economy.

questions.question: A business forms a strategic alliance with a large competitor and persuades big investors to back it. This best illustrates a business that is:
options: using power relationships to cope with an environment it cannot control
questions.expected: using power relationships to cope with an environment it cannot control
questions.memo: Strategic alliances and persuading large investors are power relationships — ways to cope with environments the business cannot control, not ways to control them outright.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement: 'Because a business cannot control the macro environment, there is nothing it can do about it.'
options: Incorrect — it can still adapt and get involved, e.g. by lobbying and networking
Correct — the macro environment must simply be ignored
Correct — only the government can respond to the macro environment
Incorrect — a business can fully control the macro environment if it is large enough
questions.expected: Incorrect — it can still adapt and get involved, e.g. by lobbying and networking
questions.memo: No control does not mean no response. A business adapts to macro change and gets involved (lobbying, networking, alliances) to limit the impact.

questions.question: Read both managers' approaches, then decide which each statement matches.

source_a.text: Interest rates and new laws are not our problem. We will keep our plans exactly the same no matter what happens out there.

source_b.text: We watch interest rates, new laws and technology closely, and we change our internal plans whenever the outside world shifts.

statements.text: Is likely to be caught off-guard by macro change
Adapts internal plans in response to macro change
Runs a business that has a micro environment to manage
Is able to set the country's interest rates

questions.expected: s1=a_only, s2=b_only, s3=both, s4=neither
questions.memo: Manager B adapts to the macro environment and is better prepared; Manager A ignores it and risks being caught off-guard. Both manage a micro environment; neither sets interest rates.

questions.question: Influencing decision-makers or regulators to act in the business's favour is called _________.
questions.expected: lobbying
questions.memo: Lobbying is influencing those who make the rules — government or regulators — to act in ways that benefit the business.

BUS.G11.T1.CHALLENGES.A1.title: Challenges of the micro, market and macro environments
BUS.G11.T1.CHALLENGES.A1.description: Identifying the challenges of each environment: micro (difficult employees, weak vision, poor management, strikes), market (competition, supply shortages, changing consumer behaviour) and macro (legislation, income changes, globalisation, socio-economic issues).
BUS.G11.T1.CHALLENGES.A1.strand: T1 — Business environments, socio-economic issues, sectors, ownership & acquiring a business
BUS.G11.T1.CHALLENGES.A1.recovery_strategy: Sort a challenge by where it comes from: inside the business = micro (staff, vision, management); close outside = market (competitors, suppliers, customers); broad outside = macro (laws, economy, globalisation).

questions.question: A lack of vision and difficult employees are challenges of which environment?
questions.expected: The micro (internal) environment
questions.memo: Vision and employees are inside the business, so problems with them are micro-environment challenges.

questions.question: Strong competition and supply shortages are challenges of which environment?
questions.expected: The market environment
questions.memo: Competitors and suppliers are part of the market environment, so problems with them are market-environment challenges.

questions.question: True or false: New legislation and globalisation are challenges of the macro environment.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Laws and globalisation are broad outside forces, which makes them macro-environment challenges.

questions.question: A strike by the business's own workers is a challenge of the _________ environment.
questions.expected: micro
questions.memo: The workers are inside the business, so a strike by them is a micro-environment challenge.

questions.question: Which of these is a market-environment challenge?
options: A change in consumer buying behaviour
A rise in the national inflation rate
questions.expected: A change in consumer buying behaviour
questions.memo: Consumers are part of the market environment. A demotivated workforce and weak mission are micro; inflation is macro.

questions.question: True or false: A supplier running out of stock is a micro-environment challenge.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: A supplier is part of the market environment, so a supply shortage is a market-environment challenge, not a micro one.

questions.question: Sort each challenge into the environment it belongs to.

items.text: Managers who lack the right skills
A supplier who cannot deliver stock

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Inside the business = micro (staff, managers). Close outside = market (competitors, suppliers). Broad outside = macro (interest rates, laws).

questions.question: Read the case and select the MACRO-environment challenges it mentions.
questions.source_text: A furniture maker is under pressure. A new import tax has raised the price of its timber. The economy has slowed and customers are spending less. On top of this, two of its machine operators have resigned and its main competitor has dropped its prices.
questions.task: Tap the parts that describe macro-environment challenges (broad outside forces the business cannot control).

targets.phrase: A new import tax has raised the price of its timber
targets.reason: Taxes and laws are a legal/economic macro force.

targets.phrase: The economy has slowed and customers are spending less
targets.reason: A slowing economy is an economic macro force.

questions.expected: A new import tax has raised the price of its timber; The economy has slowed and customers are spending less
questions.memo: The import tax and the slowing economy are macro forces. The resigning operators are a micro challenge; the competitor's price drop is a market challenge.

questions.question: Why is competition treated as a MARKET challenge rather than a macro one?
options: Competitors are specific firms close to the business, not a broad force affecting everyone
Competition only ever affects large businesses
Competition is controlled by the government
Competition has no effect on a business
questions.expected: Competitors are specific firms close to the business, not a broad force affecting everyone
questions.memo: Market challenges come from specific close parties (competitors, suppliers, customers). Macro challenges are broad forces like the economy or laws.

questions.question: Changes in income levels, political changes and globalisation are challenges of the _________ environment.
questions.expected: macro
questions.memo: Income levels, politics and globalisation are broad outside forces — macro-environment challenges.

questions.question: A business is struggling because its managers lack skills and its staff are demotivated. These are challenges of the _________ environment.
questions.expected: micro
questions.memo: Managers and staff are inside the business, so these are micro-environment challenges that management can act on directly.

questions.question: True or false: Changes in demographics and socio-cultural values can challenge a business through both its market and its macro environment.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Shifts in what specific customers want show up in the market environment, while broad social and demographic change is a macro force — both are challenges.

questions.question: Which best describes a macro-environment challenge?
options: A broad force, like the economy or new laws, that affects all businesses
The business choosing a new logo
questions.expected: A broad force, like the economy or new laws, that affects all businesses
questions.memo: Macro challenges are broad, society-wide forces. A single employee is micro; one supplier is market; a logo is an internal choice.

questions.question: Sort each challenge into the environment it belongs to.

items.text: Customers switching to a rival brand
A key supplier raising its prices

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Go-slows and a weak vision are inside (micro); customers and suppliers are close outside (market); a recession and import rules are broad outside (macro).

questions.question: A new minimum-wage law raises a factory's labour costs. This is a challenge of which environment?
questions.expected: The macro environment
questions.memo: Laws are part of the macro environment. The factory must adapt because it cannot control legislation.

questions.question: Read the case and select the MARKET-environment challenges it mentions.
questions.source_text: A bakery is battling on several fronts. Its head baker keeps arriving late. A bigger bakery has opened across the road and is undercutting its prices. Its flour supplier has run short and cannot deliver, while a new health regulation has forced it to upgrade its kitchen.
questions.task: Tap the parts that describe market-environment challenges (close outside parties the business deals with).

targets.phrase: A bigger bakery has opened across the road and is undercutting its prices
targets.reason: A competitor is part of the market environment.

targets.phrase: Its flour supplier has run short and cannot deliver
targets.reason: A supplier is part of the market environment.

questions.expected: A bigger bakery has opened across the road and is undercutting its prices; Its flour supplier has run short and cannot deliver
questions.memo: The rival bakery and the flour supplier are market challenges. The late head baker is micro; the new health regulation is macro.

questions.question: A company faces difficult unions inside the business and fierce competition outside it. How are these two challenges best classified?
options: The union issue is micro; the competition is market
The union issue is market; the competition is micro
questions.expected: The union issue is micro; the competition is market
questions.memo: Unions and staff sit inside the business (micro); competitors sit close outside (market). Classifying them correctly shapes how the business responds.

questions.question: Why does it matter whether a challenge is micro, market or macro?
options: Because the business has different levels of control over each, so its response must differ
Because only macro challenges are real
Because micro challenges can always be ignored
Because the classification changes the law
questions.expected: Because the business has different levels of control over each, so its response must differ
questions.memo: A micro challenge can be fixed directly, a market challenge influenced, and a macro challenge only adapted to. Knowing the type guides the response.

questions.question: Read the case and select ONLY the macro-environment challenges.
questions.source_text: A clothing factory reports its problems. Load-shedding from the national grid keeps halting production. A weaker rand has raised the cost of imported zips. Meanwhile, two sewing machines have broken down and a long-standing customer has placed a smaller order than usual.
questions.task: Tap only the macro-environment challenges (broad forces beyond the factory's control).

targets.phrase: Load-shedding from the national grid keeps halting production
targets.reason: The national power supply is a macro (institutional/economic) force.

targets.phrase: A weaker rand has raised the cost of imported zips
targets.reason: The exchange rate is an economic/international macro force.

questions.expected: Load-shedding from the national grid keeps halting production; A weaker rand has raised the cost of imported zips
questions.memo: Load-shedding and the weaker rand are macro forces. The broken machines are micro; the smaller customer order is a market challenge.

questions.question: A business lists 'go-slows by staff' as a market-environment challenge. Why is this wrong?
options: Staff are inside the business, so a go-slow is a micro challenge
Go-slows are not challenges at all
Staff are part of the macro environment
questions.expected: Staff are inside the business, so a go-slow is a micro challenge
questions.memo: A go-slow comes from the business's own workers, who are inside the business — that makes it a micro-environment challenge.

BUS.G11.T1.ADAPT.A1.title: Adapting to environmental challenges
BUS.G11.T1.ADAPT.A1.description: How a business adapts to challenges of the three environments: information management, strategic responses, mergers/takeovers/alliances, organisation design and flexibility, social responsibility, and lobbying, networking and power relationships.
BUS.G11.T1.ADAPT.A1.strand: T1 — Business environments, socio-economic issues, sectors, ownership & acquiring a business
BUS.G11.T1.ADAPT.A1.recovery_strategy: Lobbying = influencing decision-makers. Networking = building useful contacts. Power relationships = strategic alliances and persuading big investors. Mergers/takeovers combine firms; flexibility and information management prepare the business for change it cannot control.

questions.question: When a business cannot control an environment, what is the realistic response?
questions.expected: Adapt to it
questions.memo: A business cannot control the market or macro environment, so it must adapt — change its own plans to fit the new situation.

questions.question: When two businesses combine to form one, it is called a _________.
questions.expected: merger
questions.memo: A merger is when two businesses join together to become a single, larger business.

questions.question: True or false: Lobbying is one way a business can respond to its macro environment.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Lobbying — influencing decision-makers and regulators — is a recognised way of getting involved in the macro environment.

questions.question: Building useful contacts and relationships to help cope with the business environment is called _________.
questions.expected: networking
questions.memo: Networking is building contacts and relationships — for example to find new customers or partners.

questions.question: True or false: A takeover (acquisition) is when one business buys another business.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: In a takeover or acquisition, one business buys another and takes control of it.

questions.question: Cooperating with another business while each stays separate is called forming a _________ alliance.
questions.expected: strategic
questions.memo: A strategic alliance is an agreement where two businesses cooperate for mutual benefit while remaining separate companies.

questions.question: Sort each way of adapting into the right group.

items.text: Lobbying the government for fair rules
Cross-training staff so they can switch roles

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Mergers and takeovers combine firms; lobbying and networking influence outsiders; reorganising and cross-training build internal flexibility.

questions.question: A business merges with a competitor to cope with tough competition. This adaptation is best described as a:
questions.expected: strategic response (a merger)
questions.memo: Merging with a competitor is a strategic response to market pressure — combining strengths to compete better.

questions.question: _________ management means gathering and using information about the environment so the business can make better decisions.
questions.expected: Information
questions.memo: Information management is collecting and using reliable information about the environment to respond well to change.

questions.question: Why might a business form a strategic alliance with another firm?
options: To gain strength to cope with an environment it cannot control
questions.expected: To gain strength to cope with an environment it cannot control
questions.memo: Alliances pool strengths and contacts so each business is better able to cope with pressures it cannot face alone.

questions.question: True or false: Acting with social responsibility can be a way for a business to respond positively to its environment.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Social responsibility — giving back to the community and protecting the environment — is one recognised way a business responds to its environment and builds goodwill.

questions.question: Thesis: 'A small business should network actively to help it cope with its business environment.' Choose the THREE strongest supporting reasons.
questions.thesis: A small business should network actively to help it cope with its business environment.

pool.text: Networking can bring in new customers and suppliers
Contacts can share useful information about coming changes
Partnerships built through networking can open new opportunities
Networking lets the business control the whole economy
The owner enjoys free snacks at networking events
Networking is only worth doing once the business is already huge

questions.memo: The strong reasons are new customers/suppliers, early information, and new opportunities. The others overclaim, are irrelevant, or wrongly limit networking to big businesses.

questions.question: A firm redesigns its structure so it can react faster when the market changes. This is an example of:
questions.expected: organisation design and flexibility
questions.memo: Changing the structure to respond quickly is organisation design and flexibility — building the ability to adapt into the business itself.

questions.question: Sort each action into the type of involvement it shows.

items.text: Petitioning regulators to change a proposed rule
Meeting potential clients at a trade fair
Forming a strategic alliance with a major firm
Bargaining with government over an industry law
Swapping contacts with other small business owners
Persuading large investors to back the business

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Lobbying influences rule-makers; networking builds contacts; power relationships use alliances and big investors to gain strength.

questions.question: What is the difference between a merger and a takeover?
options: A merger combines two firms into one; a takeover is one firm buying another
A merger is illegal; a takeover is legal
A merger only happens between small firms
There is no difference between them
questions.expected: A merger combines two firms into one; a takeover is one firm buying another
questions.memo: In a merger both firms join as equals into one business; in a takeover one firm buys and controls the other.

questions.question: Persuading large investors to back the business and forming alliances are examples of using _________ relationships.
questions.expected: power
questions.memo: Power relationships use strategic alliances and the influence of large investors to give the business more strength in its environment.

questions.question: A rise in fuel prices (a macro factor) has pushed up a delivery firm's costs. Which response shows it adapting sensibly?
options: Planning more efficient routes and reviewing its prices
Demanding that fuel prices be lowered for it alone
questions.expected: Planning more efficient routes and reviewing its prices
questions.memo: It cannot control fuel prices, so it adapts — cutting fuel use through better routes and adjusting prices to stay viable.

questions.question: Two firms agree to share a distribution network while staying fully independent companies. This is best described as:
questions.expected: a strategic alliance
questions.memo: Cooperating for mutual benefit while remaining separate companies is a strategic alliance — not a merger (one firm) or takeover (one buys the other).

questions.question: Evaluate: 'A business facing a macro challenge can only sit back and suffer.' Which response is best?
options: Incorrect — it can adapt, manage information, build flexibility, and lobby or network
Correct — there is nothing any business can ever do
Incorrect — it can simply control the macro environment
questions.expected: Incorrect — it can adapt, manage information, build flexibility, and lobby or network
questions.memo: A business cannot control the macro environment but has many active responses: adapting, gathering information, staying flexible, and lobbying or networking.

questions.question: A struggling business buys out the supplier it depends on so it can secure its raw materials. This adaptation is a:
questions.expected: takeover (acquisition)
questions.memo: Buying out another business — here a supplier — is a takeover or acquisition, used as a strategic response to secure supply.

BUS.G11.T1.SOCIOECON.A1.title: Socio-economic issues & industrial relations
BUS.G11.T1.SOCIOECON.A1.description: The impact of contemporary socio-economic issues (inflation, economic crime, ethical misconduct, illiteracy, skills shortages, piracy, strikes) on business, possible business solutions, the intellectual property rights, and industrial relations: strikes, go-slows, lockouts, the Labour Relations Act and trade unions.
BUS.G11.T1.SOCIOECON.A1.strand: T1 — Business environments, socio-economic issues, sectors, ownership & acquiring a business
BUS.G11.T1.SOCIOECON.A1.recovery_strategy: Socio-economic issues hit business through cost, productivity or lost sales. Copyright protects creative work, a patent protects an invention, a trademark protects a brand. A trade union represents workers; a go-slow is working slowly, a lockout is the employer shutting workers out.

questions.question: Illegally copying or reproducing someone else's product is called _________.
questions.expected: piracy
questions.memo: Piracy is the illegal copying or reproduction of someone's product, which steals sales from the original business.

questions.question: Which intellectual property right protects a new invention?
questions.expected: A patent
questions.memo: A patent protects a new invention, giving the inventor the sole right to use it for a period.

questions.question: Which intellectual property right protects a brand name or logo?
questions.expected: A trademark
questions.memo: A trademark protects a brand name, logo or symbol that identifies a business's products.

questions.question: True or false: A trade union represents workers in negotiations with employers.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A trade union is an organisation that represents workers, negotiating wages and conditions on their behalf.

questions.question: _________ protects original creative work such as books, music and films.
questions.expected: Copyright
questions.memo: Copyright protects original creative works — writing, music, art and film — from being copied without permission.

questions.question: True or false: High inflation raises a business's costs.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Inflation pushes up the prices a business pays for stock, wages and services, raising its costs.

questions.question: Sort each item under the intellectual property right that protects it.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Copyright = creative works (novels, songs); patent = inventions (machines, formulas); trademark = brand identity (logos, names).

questions.question: How does a high crime rate most directly affect a business?
options: It raises security costs and causes losses from theft
It has no effect on business
It lowers the business's electricity bill
questions.expected: It raises security costs and causes losses from theft
questions.memo: Crime forces a business to spend more on security and causes losses through theft and damage, cutting into profit.

questions.question: Read the case and select the socio-economic issues that are hurting this business.
questions.source_text: A small manufacturer is battling. Cheap counterfeit copies of its product are flooding the market. Many job applicants cannot read instructions because of low literacy. Its delivery vans were recently broken into. Its newest machine, however, is running perfectly.
questions.task: Tap the parts that describe socio-economic issues affecting the business.

targets.phrase: Cheap counterfeit copies of its product are flooding the market
targets.reason: Counterfeiting/piracy steals the business's sales.

targets.phrase: Many job applicants cannot read instructions because of low literacy
targets.reason: Illiteracy is a socio-economic issue that limits the available workforce.

targets.phrase: Its delivery vans were recently broken into
targets.reason: Crime causes losses and raises security costs.

questions.expected: Cheap counterfeit copies of its product are flooding the market; Many job applicants cannot read instructions because of low literacy; Its delivery vans were recently broken into
questions.memo: Counterfeiting, illiteracy and crime are socio-economic issues hurting the business. The machine running perfectly is not a problem.

questions.question: When workers collectively stop working to demand better pay or conditions, it is called a _________.
questions.expected: strike
questions.memo: A strike is when workers stop working together to press for better pay or conditions.

questions.question: What is the difference between a go-slow and a lockout?
options: A go-slow is workers working slowly on purpose; a lockout is the employer shutting workers out
A go-slow is the employer closing the gates; a lockout is workers resigning
A go-slow is a type of patent; a lockout is a type of trademark
questions.expected: A go-slow is workers working slowly on purpose; a lockout is the employer shutting workers out
questions.memo: In a go-slow workers deliberately work slowly; in a lockout the employer prevents workers from coming in to work.

questions.question: True or false: The Labour Relations Act governs the relationship between employers, employees and trade unions.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The Labour Relations Act (LRA) sets the rules for fair dealings between employers, employees and unions, including strikes and bargaining.

questions.question: Which of these is a role of a trade union?
options: Negotiating wages and protecting the interests of its members
questions.expected: Negotiating wages and protecting the interests of its members
questions.memo: Trade unions represent workers — negotiating pay and conditions and protecting members' rights.

questions.question: Sort each item into whether it is a problem for the business or a business response to a problem.

items.text: Running training programmes to fix a skills shortage
Funding a community project to reduce local poverty

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Crime, piracy and strikes are problems. Training, community projects and registering trademarks are responses the business chooses to deal with socio-economic issues.

questions.question: How do a skills shortage and illiteracy affect a business?
options: They make it hard to find capable workers and lower productivity
They raise the business's share price
They reduce the need for training
They have no effect on the business
questions.expected: They make it hard to find capable workers and lower productivity
questions.memo: When workers lack skills or cannot read well, the business struggles to fill roles and productivity falls.

questions.question: Read the case and select the examples of ETHICAL MISCONDUCT inside the business.
questions.source_text: An investigation at a company uncovers several issues. A manager has been taking bribes from suppliers. A senior employee has been sexually harassing junior staff. The company's profits have also fallen because of a national recession, and one of its delivery trucks is old and unreliable.
questions.task: Tap the parts that describe ethical misconduct within the business.

targets.phrase: A manager has been taking bribes from suppliers
targets.reason: Bribery and corruption are ethical misconduct.

targets.phrase: A senior employee has been sexually harassing junior staff
targets.reason: Sexual harassment is ethical misconduct.

questions.expected: A manager has been taking bribes from suppliers; A senior employee has been sexually harassing junior staff
questions.memo: Bribery and sexual harassment are ethical misconduct. The recession is a macro issue and the old truck is an operational (micro) problem, not misconduct.

questions.question: Why is it worthwhile for a business to register patents and trademarks for its products?
options: They give legal protection against piracy and counterfeiting, protecting its sales
They make the product cheaper to produce
They remove the need to pay any tax
They guarantee the business will never face competition
questions.expected: They give legal protection against piracy and counterfeiting, protecting its sales
questions.memo: Registered patents and trademarks let a business take legal action against copies, protecting the sales and reputation those copies would steal.

questions.question: A business in an area of high unemployment wants to respond constructively. Which action is the best business solution?
options: Creating jobs and offering skills training to local people
Closing down to avoid the problem
questions.expected: Creating jobs and offering skills training to local people
questions.memo: A constructive response to unemployment and skills shortages is to create jobs and train people, helping both the community and the business's labour supply.

questions.question: Apart from negotiating wages, which is a function of a trade union?
options: Representing members in disputes and improving working conditions
questions.expected: Representing members in disputes and improving working conditions
questions.memo: Beyond wage talks, unions represent members in disputes and push for better, safer working conditions.

questions.question: A long strike has halted production for weeks. Which statement best evaluates the situation for the business?
options: Lost production and income hurt the business, so resolving the dispute fairly is in its interest
A strike always benefits the business financially
Strikes have no effect on production
The business should simply ignore the strike forever
questions.expected: Lost production and income hurt the business, so resolving the dispute fairly is in its interest
questions.memo: Strikes stop production and lose income, so it is in the business's interest to deal with workers fairly through the proper industrial-relations channels.

BUS.G11.T1.SECTORS.A1.title: Links between the business sectors
BUS.G11.T1.SECTORS.A1.description: Investigating the links between primary, secondary and tertiary enterprises — how raw materials from primary enterprises flow to secondary enterprises that process them and to tertiary enterprises that distribute and service them.
BUS.G11.T1.SECTORS.A1.strand: T1 — Business environments, socio-economic issues, sectors, ownership & acquiring a business
BUS.G11.T1.SECTORS.A1.recovery_strategy: Follow the chain: primary extracts raw materials (farm, mine) → secondary processes them (factory, bakery) → tertiary sells and services (shop, bank, transport). Each sector depends on the one before it.

questions.question: What do primary enterprises do?
options: Turn raw materials into finished goods
questions.expected: Extract or grow raw materials
questions.memo: Primary enterprises extract or grow raw materials — for example mining, farming, fishing and forestry.

questions.question: What do secondary enterprises do?
options: Process raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods
Dig minerals out of the ground
questions.expected: Process raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods
questions.memo: Secondary enterprises process raw materials — factories, mills and bakeries that make products.

questions.question: What do tertiary enterprises do?
questions.expected: Provide services and distribute goods
questions.memo: Tertiary enterprises provide services and distribute goods — shops, banks, transport and insurance.

questions.question: True or false: A bakery is a secondary enterprise.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A bakery turns flour (a raw material) into bread, so it processes materials — making it a secondary enterprise.

questions.question: Mining is an example of a _________ enterprise.
questions.expected: primary
questions.memo: Mining extracts raw materials from the earth, so it is a primary enterprise.

questions.question: True or false: The three business sectors depend on each other.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The sectors are linked: secondary needs raw materials from primary, and tertiary distributes and services what secondary makes.

questions.question: Sort each enterprise into the correct sector.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Farms and mines extract (primary); mills and factories process (secondary); supermarkets and banks serve and distribute (tertiary).

questions.question: Put the bread supply chain in the correct order, from raw material to customer.

items.text: A mill grinds the wheat into flour
A bakery bakes the flour into bread
A shop sells the bread to customers

questions.expected: farm, mill, bakery, shop
questions.memo: The chain runs primary (farm) → secondary (mill, bakery) → tertiary (shop). Each step depends on the one before it.

questions.question: How does a secondary enterprise depend on a primary enterprise?
options: It needs the raw materials the primary enterprise produces
It lends money to the primary enterprise
It sells services to the public
questions.expected: It needs the raw materials the primary enterprise produces
questions.memo: Secondary enterprises process raw materials, so they rely on primary enterprises to supply those materials.

questions.question: A clothing factory buys raw cotton. It buys this from a _________ enterprise.
questions.expected: primary
questions.memo: Raw cotton is grown on a farm — a primary enterprise — which supplies the secondary clothing factory.

questions.question: Which statement shows the correct links between the sectors?
options: Primary supplies secondary, and secondary supplies tertiary
Tertiary supplies primary, and primary supplies secondary
Secondary supplies primary, and primary supplies tertiary
The sectors never supply each other
questions.expected: Primary supplies secondary, and secondary supplies tertiary
questions.memo: Materials flow primary → secondary → tertiary: extracted, then processed, then distributed and serviced.

questions.question: True or false: Tertiary enterprises distribute and sell the goods that secondary enterprises make.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Tertiary enterprises such as shops and transport firms move and sell the goods that secondary enterprises produce.

questions.question: Sort each enterprise into the correct sector.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Trawlers and farms extract (primary); canning and assembly plants process (secondary); couriers and insurers provide services (tertiary).

questions.question: Which tertiary service most directly helps link the sectors together?
options: Transport that carries goods between farms, factories and shops
questions.expected: Transport that carries goods between farms, factories and shops
questions.memo: Transport is a tertiary service that physically moves goods between the sectors, keeping the chain connected.

questions.question: Put the leather-shoe supply chain in the correct order, from raw material to customer.

items.text: A tannery turns the hides into leather
A factory makes the leather into shoes
A store sells the shoes to customers

questions.expected: farm, tannery, factory, store
questions.memo: Primary (farm) supplies hides; secondary (tannery, factory) processes them into shoes; tertiary (store) sells them.

questions.question: If a drought sharply reduces a region's farm output, what is the likely knock-on effect?
options: Secondary and tertiary enterprises also suffer because their supply is disrupted
Only the farms are affected and nothing else changes
Factories and shops benefit from the drought
The drought lowers the businesses' electricity bills
questions.expected: Secondary and tertiary enterprises also suffer because their supply is disrupted
questions.memo: Because the sectors are linked, a fall in primary output starves secondary enterprises of materials and reduces what tertiary enterprises have to sell.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to say the three sectors operate independently of each other?
options: Because each sector relies on the others for materials, processing or distribution
Because all three sectors are actually the same enterprise
Because only the primary sector matters
Because the sectors never trade with one another
questions.expected: Because each sector relies on the others for materials, processing or distribution
questions.memo: The sectors are interdependent — primary supplies, secondary processes, tertiary distributes — so none works in isolation.

questions.question: A butchery slaughters cattle and also sells the meat directly to the public over a counter. Which best describes it?
options: It combines secondary activity (processing) with tertiary activity (selling)
It is purely a primary enterprise
It is purely a tertiary enterprise
It belongs to no sector at all
questions.expected: It combines secondary activity (processing) with tertiary activity (selling)
questions.memo: Processing the meat is secondary; selling it directly to the public is tertiary, so the butchery spans both sectors.

questions.question: A secondary manufacturer wants to secure its raw-material supply. Which strategy uses the sector links to do this?
options: Buying or partnering with a primary enterprise that supplies its materials
Refusing to deal with any primary enterprise
questions.expected: Buying or partnering with a primary enterprise that supplies its materials
questions.memo: By linking up the chain to its primary supplier, the manufacturer secures the raw materials its secondary processing depends on.

questions.question: Put the stages of a wooden-furniture chain in the correct order, from raw material to customer.

items.text: A sawmill cuts the timber into planks
A factory builds the planks into furniture
A showroom sells the furniture to customers

questions.expected: forest, sawmill, factory, showroom
questions.memo: Forestry (primary) supplies timber; the sawmill and factory (secondary) process it into furniture; the showroom (tertiary) sells it.

BUS.G11.T1.COMPANY.A1.title: A company vs other forms of ownership
BUS.G11.T1.COMPANY.A1.description: The benefits and challenges of establishing a company versus a sole trader, partnership, close corporation or co-operative (including taxation), and the formation of companies — the Memorandum of Incorporation, the company name, incorporation and the prospectus.
BUS.G11.T1.COMPANY.A1.strand: T1 — Business environments, socio-economic issues, sectors, ownership & acquiring a business
BUS.G11.T1.COMPANY.A1.recovery_strategy: A company is a separate legal person with limited liability and continuity, but more paperwork and tax. A sole trader or partnership is simpler but has unlimited liability. Weigh capital, liability, tax and continuity.

questions.question: A company is regarded in law as a separate _________ person.
questions.expected: legal
questions.memo: A company has its own separate legal personality — it can own property, sign contracts and be sued in its own name, apart from its owners.

questions.question: True or false: A company offers its shareholders limited liability.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Shareholders of a company have limited liability — they can lose only what they invested, not their personal assets.

questions.question: A sole trader has _________ liability for the debts of the business.
questions.expected: unlimited
questions.memo: A sole trader has unlimited liability — personal assets like a house or car can be taken to pay business debts.

questions.question: The founding document of a company is the Memorandum of _________.
questions.expected: Incorporation
questions.memo: The Memorandum of Incorporation (MOI) is the founding document that sets out how a company is run, under the Companies Act 71 of 2008.

questions.question: True or false: A company can continue to exist even if one of its owners dies.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A company has continuity of existence — it carries on regardless of changes in its shareholders, unlike a sole trader.

questions.question: Which form of ownership can raise capital by selling shares to the general public?
questions.expected: A public company
questions.memo: Only a public company (Ltd) may offer its shares to the public; a private company (Pty Ltd) may not.

questions.question: Sort each feature into whether it is a benefit or a challenge of forming a company.

items.text: More legal paperwork to set up and run
Continuity if an owner leaves or dies
Easier to raise large amounts of capital

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Benefits: limited liability, continuity, easier capital. Challenges: more paperwork, higher costs, more regulation and disclosure.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of a company compared with a sole trader?
options: Limited liability protects the owners' personal assets
It needs no registration at all
It pays no tax of any kind
questions.expected: Limited liability protects the owners' personal assets
questions.memo: Because a company is a separate legal person with limited liability, owners risk only their investment, not their personal possessions.

questions.question: A document that invites the public to buy shares in a company is called a _________.
questions.expected: prospectus
questions.memo: A prospectus is the document a public company issues to invite the public to buy its shares.

questions.question: True or false: A private company (Pty) Ltd may not sell its shares to the general public.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A private company cannot offer shares to the public — that is reserved for public companies.

questions.question: How does the taxation of a company differ from that of a sole trader?
options: A company is taxed at a company tax rate; a sole trader's profit is taxed as the owner's personal income
A company pays no tax, but a sole trader does
A sole trader pays company tax; a company pays personal tax
Neither a company nor a sole trader pays any tax
questions.expected: A company is taxed at a company tax rate; a sole trader's profit is taxed as the owner's personal income
questions.memo: A company pays tax in its own name at the company rate; a sole trader is not separate from the owner, so the profit is taxed as the owner's personal income.

questions.question: Read both entrepreneurs' choices, then decide which each statement matches.

source_a.text: I started as a sole trader because it was quick and cheap to set up and I wanted full control. I accept that I am personally liable for the debts.

source_b.text: I registered a company so that my personal assets are protected and the business can continue and raise capital, even though it costs more to run.

statements.text: Has chosen limited liability
Accepts unlimited personal liability
Is running a business that aims to make a profit
Pays no tax at all

questions.expected: s1=b_only, s2=a_only, s3=both, s4=neither
questions.memo: Entrepreneur B chose a company (limited liability); A chose a sole trader (unlimited liability). Both seek profit, and neither escapes tax.

questions.question: Why might an entrepreneur still choose a sole trader rather than a company?
options: It is simpler and cheaper to set up and gives full control
It always pays less tax than any company
It can list on the stock exchange
questions.expected: It is simpler and cheaper to set up and gives full control
questions.memo: A sole trader is quick and cheap to start and the owner keeps full control — the trade-off is unlimited liability.

questions.question: Sort each form of ownership by the liability of its owners.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Companies, close corporations and co-operatives give limited liability. Sole traders and partnerships have unlimited liability.

questions.question: Which of these is a step in forming a company?
options: Reserving the company name and lodging the Memorandum of Incorporation
Opening a savings account for a child
questions.expected: Reserving the company name and lodging the Memorandum of Incorporation
