questions.memo: Forming a company involves reserving the name and registering the Memorandum of Incorporation so the company can be incorporated.

questions.question: A company legally comes into existence when it is _________ — registered and issued with its registration.
questions.expected: incorporated
questions.memo: Incorporation is the act of registering a company so that it becomes a separate legal person.

questions.question: Read both views on raising capital, then decide which each statement matches.

source_a.text: Our partnership relies on the partners' own savings and a bank loan. We cannot sell shares, so our capital is limited to what we and the bank can put in.

source_b.text: As a public company we can issue shares to thousands of investors, which lets us raise large amounts of capital for expansion.

statements.text: Can raise capital by issuing shares to the public
Is limited to owners' funds and loans for capital
Needs capital to operate and grow
Can raise capital without anyone investing anything

questions.expected: s1=b_only, s2=a_only, s3=both, s4=neither
questions.memo: The public company can raise large capital through shares; the partnership is limited to partners' funds and loans. Both need capital, and neither raises it from nothing.

questions.question: When is forming a company clearly the better choice over a sole trader?
options: When the owners want limited liability, continuity and to raise large capital
When the owner wants the very cheapest, simplest possible start
When the owner wants to avoid all registration
When the business will never grow or take on risk
questions.expected: When the owners want limited liability, continuity and to raise large capital
questions.memo: A company suits owners who value protection of personal assets, an ongoing business and access to larger capital, and who accept the extra cost and paperwork.

questions.question: Why can the extra paperwork and tax of a company be a worthwhile trade-off?
options: Because limited liability and continuity reduce the owners' risk and support growth
Because companies are exempt from all regulation
Because it removes the need for any capital
questions.expected: Because limited liability and continuity reduce the owners' risk and support growth
questions.memo: The cost of compliance buys real advantages — protection of personal assets, an ongoing business and easier access to capital — which can be worth it for a growing venture.

questions.question: A growing partnership wants limited liability and the ability to bring in outside investors. What should it consider doing?
questions.expected: Converting into a company
questions.memo: To gain limited liability and raise capital from outside investors, the partnership would convert to a company, accepting the added regulation in return.

BUS.G11.T1.ACQUIRE.A1.title: Avenues of acquiring a business
BUS.G11.T1.ACQUIRE.A1.description: Ways of acquiring a business — franchising, outsourcing and leasing — with their advantages, disadvantages and contractual implications such as royalties and legalities.
BUS.G11.T1.ACQUIRE.A1.strand: T1 — Business environments, socio-economic issues, sectors, ownership & acquiring a business
BUS.G11.T1.ACQUIRE.A1.recovery_strategy: Franchising = buy the right to trade under a proven brand and pay royalties. Outsourcing = pay another firm to do a task for you. Leasing = rent an asset instead of buying it.

questions.question: Buying the right to trade under an established brand, using its name and system, is called _________.
questions.expected: franchising
questions.memo: Franchising means buying the right to run a business under a proven brand's name and system, usually in return for fees and royalties.

questions.question: Paying another company to handle a task or function for you, such as cleaning or payroll, is called _________.
questions.expected: outsourcing
questions.memo: Outsourcing is paying an outside firm to perform a task instead of doing it in-house.

questions.question: Renting an asset such as equipment or premises instead of buying it is called _________.
questions.expected: leasing
questions.memo: Leasing is paying to use an asset for a period without owning it — for example renting machines or a shop.

questions.question: True or false: A franchisee usually pays the franchisor royalties.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A franchisee typically pays ongoing royalties (and often an initial fee) to the franchisor for the right to use the brand and system.

questions.question: In franchising, the person who buys the right to run the branded business is called the _________.
questions.expected: franchisee
questions.memo: The franchisor owns the brand and sells the rights; the franchisee buys those rights and runs the outlet.

questions.question: True or false: When you lease an asset, you become its legal owner immediately.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Leasing gives you the use of an asset but not ownership — the lessor still owns it.

questions.question: Sort each example under the avenue of acquiring a business it illustrates.

items.text: Opening a branch of a national fast-food brand and paying royalties
Hiring an outside firm to run the company's payroll
Renting delivery vehicles instead of buying them
Running a branded coffee shop under licence from the brand owner
Paying a security company to guard the premises
Renting the shop premises from a landlord

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Trading under a brand for royalties is franchising; paying an outside firm to do a task is outsourcing; renting assets is leasing.

questions.question: What is an advantage of buying a franchise rather than starting a business from scratch?
options: You trade under a proven brand with an established system and support
You never have to pay any fees
You can ignore the franchisor's rules
questions.expected: You trade under a proven brand with an established system and support
questions.memo: A franchise comes with a known brand, a tested business model and franchisor support, which lowers the risk of starting alone.

questions.question: What is a disadvantage of franchising for the franchisee?
options: You must pay royalties and follow the franchisor's rules, limiting your freedom
You get no brand recognition at all
You can never make a profit
You are forced to invent your own product
questions.expected: You must pay royalties and follow the franchisor's rules, limiting your freedom
questions.memo: Franchisees pay ongoing royalties and must stick to the franchisor's system, so they have less independence than an owner starting fresh.

questions.question: An advantage of outsourcing a task such as IT support is that the business can _________.
options: focus on what it does best while experts handle the task
stop paying any staff ever again
ignore the quality of the work
questions.expected: focus on what it does best while experts handle the task
questions.memo: Outsourcing lets a business concentrate on its core work and hand specialist tasks to firms that do them well, often at lower cost.

questions.question: True or false: Leasing equipment instead of buying it helps a new business preserve its cash.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Leasing spreads the cost over time rather than requiring a large upfront purchase, which helps a new business keep cash for other needs.

questions.question: Thesis: 'A first-time owner should buy a franchise rather than start a brand-new business.' Choose the THREE strongest supporting reasons.
questions.thesis: A first-time owner should buy a franchise rather than start a brand-new business.

pool.text: The brand is already known, so customers come more easily
The franchisor provides a proven system and training
There is a lower risk of failure than starting from nothing
A franchisee never has to pay any royalties
The franchise sign is a nice colour
A franchise lets you ignore the franchisor's rules

questions.memo: The strong reasons are brand recognition, a proven system with training, and lower risk. The others are false (royalties are paid, rules must be followed) or irrelevant.

questions.question: A business pays a specialist firm to manage its cleaning so its own staff can focus on production. This is an example of:
questions.expected: outsourcing
questions.memo: Handing a non-core task (cleaning) to an outside firm is outsourcing.

questions.question: Sort each item into whether it is an advantage or a disadvantage of franchising for the franchisee.

items.text: Ongoing royalty payments to the franchisor
Training and support from the franchisor
Strict rules that limit the owner's freedom

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Advantages: brand recognition, support, a proven model. Disadvantages: royalties, strict rules and a high initial fee.

questions.question: What is a contractual implication a franchisee must accept?
options: A legal agreement to pay royalties and follow the franchisor's standards
Complete freedom to change the brand's products
Ownership of the franchisor's entire brand
questions.expected: A legal agreement to pay royalties and follow the franchisor's standards
questions.memo: The franchise contract legally binds the franchisee to pay royalties and uphold the franchisor's standards and rules.

questions.question: A start-up rents its machinery rather than buying it outright. Which avenue of acquiring resources is this, and why might it suit a start-up?
options: Leasing — it avoids a large upfront cost and preserves cash
Franchising — it gives the start-up a famous brand
Outsourcing — it hands production to another firm
A merger — it combines two businesses
questions.expected: Leasing — it avoids a large upfront cost and preserves cash
questions.memo: Renting machinery is leasing, which spreads cost and keeps cash free — useful for a start-up with limited capital.

questions.question: A franchisee wants to sell a completely new product the franchisor does not allow. What does the franchise agreement most likely mean for this plan?
options: The franchisee is bound by the contract to follow the franchisor's product range
The franchisee can ignore the contract freely
The contract has no effect on products
The franchisee automatically owns the brand
questions.expected: The franchisee is bound by the contract to follow the franchisor's product range
questions.memo: Franchise contracts require franchisees to stick to the approved system and product range, so the franchisee cannot simply add an unapproved product.

questions.question: A business is deciding between outsourcing its deliveries and buying its own fleet. Which best evaluates outsourcing here?
options: It avoids the cost and management of a fleet but means relying on another firm's reliability
It is always cheaper and carries no risks at all
It forces the business to buy vehicles anyway
It has no effect on cost or control
questions.expected: It avoids the cost and management of a fleet but means relying on another firm's reliability
questions.memo: Outsourcing deliveries saves the cost and effort of owning a fleet, but the business becomes dependent on the outside firm's reliability and quality.

questions.question: Why might an established franchisor benefit from selling franchises rather than opening all the outlets itself?
options: It expands faster using franchisees' capital and effort while earning fees and royalties
It gives away its brand for free
It loses all income from the outlets
It must run every outlet personally
questions.expected: It expands faster using franchisees' capital and effort while earning fees and royalties
questions.memo: Franchising lets the franchisor grow quickly using franchisees' money and management, while collecting fees and royalties — a benefit to both sides.

questions.question: Which situation best calls for outsourcing rather than franchising or leasing?
options: A firm wants a specialist to handle its accounting so it can focus on its core work
A person wants to run a branded outlet of a national chain
A business wants to use machines without buying them
A business wants to combine fully with a competitor
questions.expected: A firm wants a specialist to handle its accounting so it can focus on its core work
questions.memo: Handing a specialist task like accounting to an outside expert is outsourcing. The other situations describe franchising, leasing and a merger.

BUS.G11.T2.CREATIVE.A1.title: Creative thinking & problem-solving (advanced)
BUS.G11.T2.CREATIVE.A1.description: Applying creative thinking to business problems: routine vs creative thinking, mental blocks, techniques (brainstorming, mind-mapping, Delphi, force-field analysis), working with others, and conventional vs non-conventional (including indigenous) solutions checked against reality.
BUS.G11.T2.CREATIVE.A1.strand: T2 — Creative thinking, stress & change, action plans, setting up, ethics & presentation
BUS.G11.T2.CREATIVE.A1.recovery_strategy: Routine thinking follows known steps; creative thinking breaks the pattern to find new ideas. Mental blocks (fear of failure, assuming one right answer) stop creativity. Techniques such as brainstorming, mind-mapping, Delphi and force-field analysis help generate and weigh options.

questions.question: What best describes creative thinking, compared with routine thinking?
options: Generating new ideas by breaking away from the usual pattern
Repeating the same fixed steps every time
Doing exactly what a manual says
questions.expected: Generating new ideas by breaking away from the usual pattern
questions.memo: Creative thinking produces fresh ideas by departing from habit; routine thinking simply follows familiar, fixed steps.

questions.question: Something that stops a person from thinking creatively is called a _________ block.
questions.expected: mental
questions.memo: A mental block — such as fear of failure or assuming there is only one right answer — prevents creative thinking.

questions.question: True or false: In brainstorming, ideas are generated freely at first without being judged.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Brainstorming encourages many ideas without early judgement, so people feel free to contribute; evaluation comes later.

questions.question: Which of these is a creative-thinking technique?
questions.expected: Mind-mapping
questions.memo: Mind-mapping is a creative-thinking technique that visually links ideas around a central topic.

questions.question: The _________ technique gathers expert opinions in rounds, without the experts meeting face to face.
questions.expected: Delphi
questions.memo: The Delphi technique collects and refines expert views over several rounds without the experts meeting, reducing the influence of dominant personalities.

questions.question: True or false: Creative thinking can help a business improve the way it works.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Creative thinking generates new solutions and improvements, helping a business solve problems and work better.

questions.question: Sort each example into routine thinking or creative thinking.

items.text: Following the same daily checklist without change
Combining two unrelated ideas to invent a new product
Brainstorming fresh ways to reach customers
Finding an unconventional use for a waste material

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Following fixed steps is routine; generating new ideas, combinations and unconventional uses is creative thinking.

questions.question: Which of these is a mental block to creativity?
options: Assuming there is only one right answer to a problem
Asking 'what if we tried something different?'
Listening to many points of view
questions.expected: Assuming there is only one right answer to a problem
questions.memo: Assuming a single right answer shuts down new ideas — a classic mental block. The other options open up creative thinking.

questions.question: Put the steps of generating and using a creative solution in the correct order.

items.text: Evaluate the ideas against the real situation
Choose and implement the best idea

questions.expected: define, generate, evaluate, implement
questions.memo: First understand the problem, then generate ideas freely, then judge them against reality, and finally implement the best one.

questions.question: _________-field analysis weighs the forces pushing for a change against the forces resisting it.
questions.expected: Force
questions.memo: Force-field analysis lists the driving forces for a change and the restraining forces against it, to decide whether and how to proceed.

questions.question: What is a benefit of working with others to generate ideas?
options: A wider range of ideas and perspectives is produced
Only one person's view is ever heard
It removes the need to evaluate ideas
questions.expected: A wider range of ideas and perspectives is produced
questions.memo: Different people bring different experiences, so working together produces more varied ideas than thinking alone.

questions.question: What is the difference between a conventional and a non-conventional solution?
options: A conventional solution is the usual, expected one; a non-conventional solution is new or unusual
A conventional solution is always wrong
A non-conventional solution is the one in the textbook
There is no difference between them
questions.expected: A conventional solution is the usual, expected one; a non-conventional solution is new or unusual
questions.memo: Conventional solutions follow the normal approach; non-conventional (including indigenous) solutions take a fresh, less obvious route.

questions.question: Sort each item into whether it is a creative-thinking technique or not.

items.text: Ignoring the problem and hoping it goes away

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Brainstorming, mind-mapping, Delphi and force-field analysis are techniques. Ignoring a problem or copying others is not creative thinking.

questions.question: How can indigenous knowledge help a business solve a problem?
options: It offers local, traditional knowledge that can suggest practical solutions
It must never be used in business
It only works for very large companies
It always costs more than other methods
questions.expected: It offers local, traditional knowledge that can suggest practical solutions
questions.memo: Indigenous knowledge draws on local, traditional experience and can provide creative, context-appropriate solutions.

questions.question: True or false: Even a clever creative idea should be checked against the reality of the business before it is used.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Creative ideas must be tested against the business's real resources, costs and conditions to make sure they can actually work.

questions.question: A manager says, 'We have always done it this way, so there is no other option.' Which mental block is this?
options: Sticking to habit and assuming only one right answer
Being too open to new ideas
questions.expected: Sticking to habit and assuming only one right answer
questions.memo: Relying on 'how it has always been done' is a mental block that blocks new ideas.

questions.question: Faced with a brand-new problem no procedure covers, why is creative thinking more useful than routine thinking?
options: A new problem has no ready-made answer, so fresh ideas are needed
Routine thinking always solves new problems instantly
Creative thinking avoids solving the problem
New problems never need any thinking
questions.expected: A new problem has no ready-made answer, so fresh ideas are needed
questions.memo: Routine thinking only repeats known steps. A genuinely new problem needs creative thinking to generate solutions that do not yet exist.

questions.question: Put the steps of running a force-field analysis in a sensible order.

items.text: List the forces driving the change
List the forces resisting the change
Weigh the forces and decide how to proceed

questions.expected: change, driving, restraining, decide
questions.memo: Name the change, list the forces for it, list the forces against it, then weigh them up to decide.

questions.question: Why is it important to assess a creative solution against the reality of the business environment?
options: So that the idea actually fits the business's resources, costs and conditions
So that the idea can be as expensive as possible
So that no idea is ever used
So that only the oldest idea wins
questions.expected: So that the idea actually fits the business's resources, costs and conditions
questions.memo: An idea is only useful if the business can realistically afford and implement it, so creative solutions are checked against the real situation.

questions.question: A bakery has surplus bread it cannot sell by closing time. Which response shows the most creative thinking?
options: Partnering with a shelter to turn surplus bread into a low-cost evening meal range
Throwing all the surplus away as usual
Refusing to consider any new idea
questions.expected: Partnering with a shelter to turn surplus bread into a low-cost evening meal range
questions.memo: Turning a waste problem into a new offering through a partnership is a creative, non-conventional solution that also adds value.

BUS.G11.T2.STRESS.A1.title: Stress, crisis & change management
BUS.G11.T2.STRESS.A1.description: Concepts relating to stress and how to manage it, the importance of stress management in pressurised workplaces, crisis management (deadlines, loss, illness), and theories of change management — dealing with and adapting to change such as retrenchment, globalisation and affirmative action.
BUS.G11.T2.STRESS.A1.strand: T2 — Creative thinking, stress & change, action plans, setting up, ethics & presentation
BUS.G11.T2.STRESS.A1.caps_topic: Stress, crisis, change and conflict management
BUS.G11.T2.STRESS.A1.recovery_strategy: Stress = pressure on a person (manage with time management, exercise, support). Crisis = a sudden serious threat to the business. Change management = leading people through change so they adapt rather than resist.

questions.question: _________ is the body's reaction to pressure or excessive demands.
questions.expected: Stress
questions.memo: Stress is the physical and emotional reaction to pressure or demands that feel hard to cope with.

questions.question: Which of these is a healthy way to manage stress?
options: Good time management, exercise and asking for support
Ignoring it until you burn out
questions.expected: Good time management, exercise and asking for support
questions.memo: Healthy stress management includes planning your time, exercising and seeking support — not piling on more pressure.

questions.question: True or false: A crisis is a sudden, serious threat to the business.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A crisis is a sudden, serious event — such as a fire or major loss — that threatens the business and needs a fast response.

questions.question: _________ management helps people accept and adjust to new ways of working.
questions.expected: Change
questions.memo: Change management is the process of helping people move through and adapt to change with less resistance.

questions.question: True or false: Good stress management can improve productivity in a pressurised workplace.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: When stress is managed well, staff stay healthier and more focused, which keeps productivity up under pressure.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a business crisis?
options: A fire destroying the factory overnight
Choosing a new font for a poster
questions.expected: A fire destroying the factory overnight
questions.memo: A fire is a sudden, serious threat — a crisis. The other options are ordinary day-to-day activities.

questions.question: Sort each situation into the type of management it mainly calls for.

items.text: A worker is overwhelmed by tight daily deadlines
A burst pipe floods the warehouse overnight
Staff must learn a brand-new computer system
An employee feels constant pressure and cannot switch off
A key supplier suddenly goes bankrupt
The company is restructuring all its departments

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Personal pressure = stress; a sudden serious threat = crisis; helping people adjust to something new = change management.

questions.question: Why is stress management important in a pressurised workplace?
options: It reduces burnout and keeps staff healthy and productive
It guarantees the business never makes a loss
It removes the need to pay staff
questions.expected: It reduces burnout and keeps staff healthy and productive
questions.memo: Managing stress protects employees' health and prevents burnout, which keeps the workforce productive under pressure.

questions.question: Build a 3-part explanation of why a business should manage change well.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-part explanation of why a business should manage change well.

options.text: A business should manage change well because people often resist change
A business should manage change well because change never affects staff
A business should manage change well because change is always harmful
Without support, employees may feel anxious, resist and become less productive
Employees are completely unaffected by new systems or restructuring
Change can be hidden from staff forever
Good change management communicates, involves and supports staff so they adapt rather than resist
Good change management means forcing change with no explanation
Good change management means never changing anything

questions.memo: Claim: change must be managed because people resist it. Evidence: unsupported change breeds anxiety and lower productivity. Explanation: communicating and involving staff helps them adapt.

questions.question: Retrenchment, globalisation and affirmative action are examples of _________ that a business and its staff must adapt to.
questions.expected: change
questions.memo: These are all forms of change that affect the workplace and must be managed so staff can adapt.

questions.question: Which is a sound crisis-management step?
options: Acting quickly with a clear plan to limit the damage
Pretending the crisis is not happening
questions.expected: Acting quickly with a clear plan to limit the damage
questions.memo: Good crisis management means responding fast with a clear plan to contain the damage and protect the business.

questions.question: True or false: Ignoring high stress levels among staff has no cost to the business.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Unmanaged stress leads to burnout, absenteeism and lower productivity — all of which cost the business.

questions.question: Sort each response into a healthy or an unhealthy way of dealing with stress.

items.text: Planning the day and prioritising tasks
Skipping meals and sleep to keep working
Bottling everything up and never asking for help
Talking to a manager about an unrealistic workload
Taking on even more tasks to avoid the problem

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Healthy: planning, breaks, exercise, asking for help. Unhealthy: skipping rest, bottling up stress and overloading yourself further.

questions.question: What is the aim of change management theories?
options: To help people move through change with less resistance
To stop any change from ever happening
To make change as confusing as possible
questions.expected: To help people move through change with less resistance
questions.memo: Change management theories guide how to lead people through change so they accept and adapt to it rather than resist.

questions.question: Which of these is a warning sign of too much stress in an employee?
questions.expected: Constant exhaustion and poor concentration
questions.memo: Ongoing exhaustion and difficulty concentrating are common signs that stress levels are too high.

questions.question: A plan that prepares a business in advance to respond to emergencies is a _________ plan.
questions.expected: crisis
questions.memo: A crisis (or contingency) plan sets out in advance how the business will respond to an emergency so it can act fast.

questions.question: A data centre suffers a sudden power failure during peak trading. Which response shows the best crisis management?
options: Switch to a backup plan immediately and communicate clearly with customers
Wait to see if the power returns on its own
Send all staff home and lock the doors
Deny that anything has gone wrong
questions.expected: Switch to a backup plan immediately and communicate clearly with customers
questions.memo: Good crisis management responds at once using a prepared plan and keeps customers informed to limit the damage.

questions.question: Why is it worth a business spending time and money on staff stress management?
options: Healthier, less stressed staff are more productive and take less sick leave
It removes the need to manage the business at all
It has no effect on the business
questions.expected: Healthier, less stressed staff are more productive and take less sick leave
questions.memo: Investing in stress management pays off through higher productivity, lower absenteeism and better staff retention.

questions.question: A company is introducing automation that worries staff about their jobs. Which approach reflects good change management?
options: Explain the reasons, retrain affected staff and involve them in the rollout
Spring the change on staff with no warning
Refuse to answer any questions about it
questions.expected: Explain the reasons, retrain affected staff and involve them in the rollout
questions.memo: Good change management communicates the reasons, supports staff with retraining and involves them, reducing resistance and anxiety.

questions.question: How are stress, crisis and change management related in a business?
options: A crisis or major change can raise stress, so all three often need managing together
They have nothing to do with one another
Only stress ever affects a business
Managing one makes the others impossible
questions.expected: A crisis or major change can raise stress, so all three often need managing together
questions.memo: Crises and big changes create pressure on people, so handling stress, crisis and change well often go hand in hand.

BUS.G11.T2.ACTIONPLAN.A1.title: From business plan to action plan
BUS.G11.T2.ACTIONPLAN.A1.description: Transforming a business plan into an action plan using planning tools — Gantt charts and a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) with timelines and responsibilities — so that the plan becomes a sequence of dated, assigned tasks.
BUS.G11.T2.ACTIONPLAN.A1.strand: T2 — Creative thinking, stress & change, action plans, setting up, ethics & presentation
BUS.G11.T2.ACTIONPLAN.A1.recovery_strategy: A business plan says WHAT and WHY; an action plan says WHO does WHICH task by WHEN. A Gantt chart shows tasks against a timeline; a WBS breaks the work into smaller tasks.

questions.question: What does an action plan mainly show?
options: Who does which task, and by when
Only the company's profit for last year
questions.expected: Who does which task, and by when
questions.memo: An action plan turns goals into concrete tasks, each with a person responsible and a deadline.

questions.question: A _________ chart shows tasks plotted against a timeline.
questions.expected: Gantt
questions.memo: A Gantt chart lists tasks down the side and time along the top, showing when each task starts, ends and overlaps.

questions.question: True or false: A Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) splits a big project into smaller tasks.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A WBS breaks a large project into smaller, manageable tasks so the work can be planned and assigned.

questions.question: What is the difference between a business plan and an action plan?
options: A business plan says what and why; an action plan says who does what by when
A business plan is illegal; an action plan is legal
They are exactly the same document
An action plan is only about marketing
questions.expected: A business plan says what and why; an action plan says who does what by when
questions.memo: The business plan sets out the idea and the reasons; the action plan turns it into dated, assigned tasks.

questions.question: In the planning tool 'WBS', the letters stand for Work _________ Structure.
questions.expected: Breakdown
questions.memo: WBS stands for Work Breakdown Structure — a tool that breaks a project down into smaller tasks.

questions.question: True or false: An action plan assigns responsibilities to specific people.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: An action plan names who is responsible for each task, so everyone knows what they must do.

questions.question: Sort each item into whether it belongs in the business plan or the action plan.

items.text: A Gantt chart of tasks and dates
A list of who is responsible for each task

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Big-picture items (summary, vision, SWOT) belong in the business plan; dated, assigned tasks (Gantt, responsibilities, timeline) belong in the action plan.

questions.question: What does a Gantt chart help a manager to see at a glance?
options: Which tasks happen when, and which overlap
How much profit was made last year
The history of the company logo
questions.expected: Which tasks happen when, and which overlap
questions.memo: A Gantt chart shows the timing of tasks, including which run in parallel, helping a manager track progress.

questions.question: Put the steps of turning a business plan into an action plan in order.

items.text: Break the goals into smaller tasks (WBS)
Schedule the tasks on a timeline (Gantt chart)
Assign each task to a responsible person

questions.expected: plan, wbs, schedule, assign
questions.memo: Start from the plan's goals, break them into tasks, schedule those tasks, and assign each one to someone.

questions.question: Each task on an action plan should have a deadline and a person _________ for it.
questions.expected: responsible
questions.memo: Naming a responsible person for each task creates accountability, so tasks actually get done.

questions.question: Why does an action plan include timelines?
options: To keep the project on schedule and track progress
To hide the deadlines from staff
questions.expected: To keep the project on schedule and track progress
questions.memo: Timelines set deadlines so the team can stay on track and see whether the project is progressing as planned.

questions.question: True or false: A Gantt chart can show two or more tasks running at the same time.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Because a Gantt chart plots tasks against time, overlapping bars show tasks that run in parallel.

questions.question: Sort each item into whether it is a planning tool or not.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Gantt charts, a WBS, timelines and responsibility lists help plan and manage tasks; a mug or a parking sign do not.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of a Work Breakdown Structure?
options: It makes a big project manageable by splitting it into smaller tasks
It hides the size of the project
It removes the need for any deadlines
It guarantees the project costs nothing
questions.expected: It makes a big project manageable by splitting it into smaller tasks
questions.memo: Breaking a project into smaller tasks makes it easier to plan, schedule, assign and track.

questions.question: Why is an action plan so useful once a business plan is written?
options: It turns intentions into concrete, dated steps people can act on
It replaces the need to do any work
It keeps the goals secret from the team
It only repeats the executive summary
questions.expected: It turns intentions into concrete, dated steps people can act on
questions.memo: An action plan converts the broad intentions of the business plan into specific tasks, deadlines and responsibilities.

questions.question: A _________ shows the start and end dates of each task in a project.
questions.expected: timeline
questions.memo: A timeline lays out when each task starts and finishes, helping the team see the schedule.

questions.question: Put the actions in order when launching a new product from a business plan.

items.text: Set the goal: launch the new product
List all the tasks needed (design, produce, market)
Give each task a deadline on a Gantt chart
Assign each task to a team member

questions.expected: goal, tasks, dates, owners
questions.memo: Define the goal, break it into tasks, schedule them with deadlines, then assign each to someone — that is the plan-to-action sequence.

questions.question: An action plan lists tasks but gives no deadlines and names no one responsible. Why is this likely to fail?
options: With no deadlines or owners, no one is accountable and tasks slip
Because action plans should never list tasks
Because deadlines always slow a project down
questions.expected: With no deadlines or owners, no one is accountable and tasks slip
questions.memo: An action plan only works if each task has a deadline and a responsible person; without these, accountability disappears and work stalls.

questions.question: Why might a project manager use both a WBS and a Gantt chart together?
options: The WBS lists all the tasks; the Gantt chart schedules them over time
They are identical, so using both is a mistake
The WBS hides tasks the Gantt chart shows
questions.expected: The WBS lists all the tasks; the Gantt chart schedules them over time
questions.memo: A WBS first identifies every task; a Gantt chart then places those tasks on a timeline — the two tools complement each other.

questions.question: Two team members both think the other is doing a key task, so it never gets done. Which action-plan feature would have prevented this?
options: Clearly assigning each task to one responsible person
Removing all deadlines from the plan
Hiding the task list from the team
questions.expected: Clearly assigning each task to one responsible person
questions.memo: Assigning each task to a named owner prevents confusion about who is responsible, so nothing falls through the cracks.

BUS.G11.T2.SETUP.A1.title: Setting up a business venture
BUS.G11.T2.SETUP.A1.description: Initiating and setting up a business venture based on an action plan to generate income, and acquiring funding where needed — equity capital, loans/debt capital and other sources of capital.
BUS.G11.T2.SETUP.A1.strand: T2 — Creative thinking, stress & change, action plans, setting up, ethics & presentation
BUS.G11.T2.SETUP.A1.recovery_strategy: Equity capital = the owner's own money or money from investors (no repayment, but shared ownership). Loan/debt capital = borrowed money that must be repaid with interest. A new venture is set up by working through its action plan and securing funding.

questions.question: Money the owner or investors put into a business, which need not be repaid like a loan, is called _________ capital.
questions.expected: equity
questions.memo: Equity capital is the owners' or investors' own money. It is not repaid like a loan, but it gives investors a share of ownership.

questions.question: A bank loan is an example of _________ capital.
questions.expected: loan (debt)
questions.memo: Borrowed money such as a bank loan is loan or debt capital, which must be repaid with interest.

questions.question: True or false: Loan capital must be repaid, usually with interest.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Loan (debt) capital is borrowed, so it must be paid back over time, normally with interest added.

questions.question: Setting up a new venture should be based on the business's _________ plan.
questions.expected: action
questions.memo: A venture is set up by working through the action plan — the list of dated, assigned tasks that turn the idea into a real business.

questions.question: True or false: Equity capital does not have to be repaid in the way a loan does.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Equity is not a loan, so there are no fixed repayments — but investors expect a share of ownership and profit in return.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of setting up a business venture?
options: To keep the idea secret forever
questions.expected: To generate income
questions.memo: A venture is set up to trade and generate income for its owners.

questions.question: Sort each source of funding into equity capital or loan/debt capital.

items.text: Money from investors in exchange for shares
Profit kept in the business (retained profit)
Credit from a supplier that must be repaid

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Owners' savings, investor share money and retained profit are equity. Bank loans, overdrafts and supplier credit are debt that must be repaid.

questions.question: What is an advantage of equity capital over loan capital?
options: There are no fixed repayments or interest
It always comes from a bank
It must be repaid within a month
questions.expected: There are no fixed repayments or interest
questions.memo: Equity has no compulsory repayments or interest, which eases pressure on a new business's cash flow.

questions.question: What is a disadvantage of raising equity capital from investors?
options: The owner has to share ownership and profit
The money must be repaid with high interest
It can never be used to grow the business
questions.expected: The owner has to share ownership and profit
questions.memo: Investors who provide equity take a share of the business and its profits, so the original owner gives up some control and reward.

questions.question: A _________ is borrowed money that a business must repay over time.
questions.expected: loan
questions.memo: A loan is borrowed money that must be repaid, usually in instalments with interest.

questions.question: True or false: The business plan and action plan guide how a venture is set up.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The business plan sets out the idea and the action plan turns it into tasks, together guiding the setting up of the venture.

questions.question: Thesis: 'A new venture should fund itself with a mix of the owner's own equity and not only loans.' Choose the THREE strongest supporting reasons.
questions.thesis: A new venture should fund itself with a mix of the owner's own equity and not only loans.

pool.text: Equity has no fixed repayments, easing cash-flow pressure early on
Investing own money shows commitment and reassures lenders
Too much debt means heavy repayments that can sink a young business
Equity must always be repaid faster than any loan
The owner likes the look of the bank's logo
Loans are never useful for any business

questions.memo: The strong reasons are easier cash flow, showing commitment, and avoiding crippling debt. The others are false or irrelevant.

questions.question: Why might a founder prefer a loan rather than bringing in equity investors?
options: A loan lets the founder keep full ownership of the business
A loan never has to be repaid
A loan gives investors control of the business
A loan charges no interest at all
questions.expected: A loan lets the founder keep full ownership of the business
questions.memo: With a loan the founder keeps full ownership; equity investors would take a share of the business in return for their money.

questions.question: Sort each statement under the funding choice it best supports.

items.text: You want to avoid fixed monthly repayments
You are willing to share profit with investors
You can comfortably afford regular repayments
Cash flow is uncertain in the early months
You do not want to give away any control

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Equity suits those who want no repayments and will share ownership; a loan suits those who can afford repayments and want to keep full control.

questions.question: What is a sensible first step when actually setting up a venture from an action plan?
options: Work through the action-plan tasks and secure the funding needed
Spend all the money before any plan is made
questions.expected: Work through the action-plan tasks and secure the funding needed
questions.memo: Setting up means following the action plan and arranging the capital required so the tasks can be carried out.

questions.question: Interest is best described as the _________ of borrowing money.
questions.expected: cost
questions.memo: Interest is the cost a borrower pays a lender for the use of money over time.

questions.question: An early-stage venture has very uncertain income. Which funding choice usually puts less pressure on it, and why?
options: Equity, because there are no fixed repayments while income is uncertain
A large loan, because the repayments are comforting
A loan, because interest reduces risk
Neither, because funding is never needed
questions.expected: Equity, because there are no fixed repayments while income is uncertain
questions.memo: When income is unpredictable, equity is safer because the business is not forced to make fixed loan repayments it may not be able to afford.

questions.question: Why can relying too heavily on loans be risky for a brand-new business?
options: High repayments and interest can sink the business before it becomes profitable
Loans make a business impossible to register
Loans remove the owner's need to work
questions.expected: High repayments and interest can sink the business before it becomes profitable
questions.memo: Heavy debt means large fixed repayments that a young, not-yet-profitable business may struggle to meet, threatening its survival.

questions.question: Why do many ventures use a mix of equity and loan capital rather than only one?
options: It balances keeping control with limiting repayment pressure
It is required by law to use both
It doubles the amount that must be repaid for no reason
It guarantees the business cannot fail
questions.expected: It balances keeping control with limiting repayment pressure
questions.memo: A blend lets the owner keep some control (loans) while easing cash-flow pressure (equity), spreading the risks of each.

questions.question: A founder launches following the action plan but has not arranged any funding. What is the likely result?
options: The venture stalls, because tasks cannot be paid for without capital
The venture runs perfectly without any money
Funding appears automatically once trading starts
Capital is never needed to set up a business
questions.expected: The venture stalls, because tasks cannot be paid for without capital
questions.memo: Even a good action plan needs capital to fund its tasks; without securing funding, the setup quickly stalls.

BUS.G11.T2.PROFETHICS.A1.title: Professionalism & ethics
BUS.G11.T2.PROFETHICS.A1.description: The theories and principles of professionalism and ethics and how they relate to business: the definitions and differences between them, good vs bad decisions, the concept of ethics and different perspectives, and the skills of professional, responsible, ethical and effective business practice.
BUS.G11.T2.PROFETHICS.A1.strand: T2 — Creative thinking, stress & change, action plans, setting up, ethics & presentation
BUS.G11.T2.PROFETHICS.A1.recovery_strategy: Ethics = doing what is morally right (honest, fair). Professionalism = the standard of conduct in your work (reliable, respectful, competent). You can be professional and still face an ethical choice; the two support each other.

questions.question: What is ethics mainly about?
options: Doing what is morally right and fair
Making the most profit by any means
questions.expected: Doing what is morally right and fair
questions.memo: Ethics is about choosing what is morally right and fair, even when another choice might be easier or more profitable.

questions.question: What is professionalism mainly about?
options: The standard of conduct and competence in your work
questions.expected: The standard of conduct and competence in your work
questions.memo: Professionalism is the standard of behaviour and skill in your work — being reliable, respectful and competent.

questions.question: Honesty and fairness in business are part of business _________.
questions.expected: ethics
questions.memo: Honesty and fairness are core to business ethics — acting in morally right ways.

questions.question: True or false: Professionalism and ethics mean exactly the same thing.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: They are related but different: ethics is about right and wrong; professionalism is about the standard of conduct in your work.

questions.question: True or false: Paying workers a fair wage is an example of ethical business practice.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Paying fair wages treats employees justly, which is ethical business behaviour.

questions.question: Arriving on time, prepared and reliable mainly shows _________.
questions.expected: professionalism
questions.memo: Being punctual, prepared and dependable is professional conduct.

questions.question: Sort each example into whether it mainly shows professionalism or ethics.

items.text: Arriving on time and dressing appropriately
Replying to emails promptly and politely
Telling a customer the truth about a faulty product
Paying suppliers fairly and on time

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Conduct and competence (punctuality, preparation, politeness) is professionalism; doing what is morally right (honesty, fairness, refusing bribes) is ethics.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of UNETHICAL business practice?
options: Paying a bribe to win a contract
questions.expected: Paying a bribe to win a contract
questions.memo: Bribery is dishonest and unfair — clearly unethical. The other options are ethical practices.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of UNPROFESSIONAL behaviour?
options: Arriving late and unprepared for a client meeting
questions.expected: Arriving late and unprepared for a client meeting
questions.memo: Turning up late and unprepared falls below the expected standard of conduct, so it is unprofessional.

questions.question: Build a 3-part explanation of why ethical behaviour matters for a business.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-part explanation of why ethical behaviour matters for a business.

options.text: Ethical behaviour matters because it builds trust with customers and staff
Ethical behaviour matters because it lets a business break the law safely
Ethical behaviour matters only when no one is watching
Customers return to and recommend businesses they believe are honest and fair
Customers prefer businesses that cheat them
Staff work harder for employers who treat them unfairly
A trusted reputation attracts loyal customers and good staff, supporting long-term success
A bad reputation has no effect on a business
Ethics only matters to charities, not businesses

questions.memo: Claim: ethics builds trust. Evidence: people support honest, fair businesses. Explanation: a trusted reputation brings loyal customers and good staff, helping long-term success.

questions.question: An _________ decision weighs what is right and fair, not only what is most profitable.
questions.expected: ethical
questions.memo: An ethical decision considers fairness and the effect on others, not just the profit it brings.

questions.question: True or false: Acting ethically can build customer trust and a good reputation.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: When a business is consistently honest and fair, customers trust it and its reputation grows, which supports success.

questions.question: Sort each practice into ethical or unethical.

items.text: Paying all taxes that are due

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Honest advertising, paying tax and safe conditions are ethical; selling expired goods, taking kickbacks and misleading on price are unethical.

questions.question: What makes a 'good' business decision different from a 'bad' one?
options: A good decision considers the consequences and fairness, not just short-term gain
A good decision always ignores other people
A good decision is simply the fastest one
A good decision is whatever makes the most money today
questions.expected: A good decision considers the consequences and fairness, not just short-term gain
questions.memo: Good decisions weigh the effects on others and fairness, while bad decisions chase short-term gain regardless of the harm caused.

questions.question: Which is a skill of ethical, responsible business practice?
options: Being honest and transparent in dealings
questions.expected: Being honest and transparent in dealings
questions.memo: Honesty and transparency are key skills of ethical, responsible business practice.

questions.question: Different _________ on ethics means people may judge what is right or wrong differently.
questions.expected: perspectives
questions.memo: People hold different perspectives on ethics, so the same action may be judged differently depending on values and context.

questions.question: A manager can win a contract by lying about the product's quality. What does ethical business practice require?
options: Telling the truth, even if it means losing the contract
Lying, because winning is all that matters
Hiding the truth and hoping no one finds out
Blaming a junior employee for any complaints
questions.expected: Telling the truth, even if it means losing the contract
questions.memo: Ethical practice means being honest even when it costs the business, because trust and integrity matter more than one contract.

questions.question: Why does professionalism support ethical behaviour at work?
options: Professional standards like honesty, respect and accountability make ethical conduct part of daily work
Professionalism replaces the need for any ethics
questions.expected: Professional standards like honesty, respect and accountability make ethical conduct part of daily work
questions.memo: A professional standard built on honesty, respect and accountability naturally encourages and supports ethical behaviour.

questions.question: Why might two people disagree about whether a business decision is ethical?
options: They hold different values and perspectives on what is right
Ethics is a fixed mathematical formula
One of them must be lying
questions.expected: They hold different values and perspectives on what is right
questions.memo: Because people bring different values and perspectives, they can reach different conclusions about the same ethical question.

questions.question: An employee notices the company is overcharging vulnerable customers. What is the most ethical and professional response?
options: Raise the concern through the proper channels so it can be corrected
Say nothing because it boosts profit
Quietly overcharge a few more customers
Tell customers to complain on social media anonymously first
questions.expected: Raise the concern through the proper channels so it can be corrected
questions.memo: The ethical and professional path is to raise the issue responsibly through the right channels so the unfair practice is stopped.

BUS.G11.T2.PRESENT.A1.title: Presentation & responding to feedback
BUS.G11.T2.PRESENT.A1.description: Accurate, succinct verbal and non-verbal presentation of business information (tables, graphs, diagrams, posters, handouts), written information such as reports and flyers, and responding to questions and feedback in a non-aggressive, professional manner.
BUS.G11.T2.PRESENT.A1.strand: T2 — Creative thinking, stress & change, action plans, setting up, ethics & presentation
BUS.G11.T2.PRESENT.A1.recovery_strategy: Verbal = spoken/words; non-verbal = visuals (tables, graphs, diagrams). When questioned: answer all questions, make notes, do not argue, and apologise for any errors. Put the most important information first and keep visuals clear.

questions.question: Which of these is a NON-VERBAL way of presenting business information?
questions.expected: A bar graph
questions.memo: Non-verbal presentation uses visuals such as graphs, tables and diagrams; the other options are spoken (verbal).

questions.question: Tables, graphs and diagrams are examples of _________ presentation.
questions.expected: non-verbal
questions.memo: Visual formats such as tables, graphs and diagrams are non-verbal presentation.

questions.question: True or false: A spoken talk to an audience is a verbal presentation.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A talk uses spoken words, so it is a verbal presentation.

questions.question: Which of these is a visual aid used to support a presentation?
questions.expected: A slide or poster
questions.memo: Slides, posters, charts and handouts are visual aids that support and reinforce a presentation.

questions.question: True or false: A presenter should put the most important information first.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Leading with the most important information makes sure the audience gets the key message even if time runs short.

questions.question: When answering a question about your presentation, you should NOT _________.
questions.expected: argue
questions.memo: You should answer questions calmly and professionally — not argue with the person asking.

questions.question: Sort each format into verbal or non-verbal presentation.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Spoken formats (talk, reading aloud, answering) are verbal; visual formats (charts, diagrams, tables) are non-verbal.

questions.question: An audience member challenges a figure in your presentation. What is the most professional response?
options: Answer calmly, make a note of it, and check the figure if unsure
Argue loudly that you are right
questions.expected: Answer calmly, make a note of it, and check the figure if unsure
questions.memo: Responding professionally means staying calm, noting the point, and checking facts rather than arguing.

questions.question: Put the steps of preparing a presentation in a sensible order.

items.text: Identify the audience and the key message
Design clear visual aids to support it

questions.expected: audience, content, aids, rehearse
questions.memo: Know your audience and message, organise the content, design the visuals, then rehearse — that order builds a strong presentation.

questions.question: A written summary handed to the audience to support a talk is called a _________.
questions.expected: handout
questions.memo: A handout is a printed summary given to the audience to reinforce the spoken message.

questions.question: Why should visual aids be kept clear and simple?
options: So the audience can understand the message quickly
So the slides take longer to read
So less information is ever shared
questions.expected: So the audience can understand the message quickly
questions.memo: Clear, simple visuals help the audience grasp the message fast, rather than struggling with clutter.

questions.question: True or false: If you realise you made an error in your presentation, you should apologise and correct it.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Professionals acknowledge mistakes, apologise and put them right, which keeps the audience's trust.

questions.question: Sort each response to audience feedback into professional or unprofessional.

items.text: Mocking someone for asking a question
Apologising for and fixing an error

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Professional: answer politely, note feedback, fix errors. Unprofessional: arguing, mocking, or refusing to respond.

questions.question: What is the purpose of support materials such as slides and handouts?
options: To reinforce and clarify the spoken message
To make the talk longer for no reason
questions.expected: To reinforce and clarify the spoken message
questions.memo: Support materials back up the spoken presentation, helping the audience follow and remember the message.

questions.question: A good business report should include _________.
options: clear headings and supporting tables or graphs
questions.expected: clear headings and supporting tables or graphs
questions.memo: A clear report uses headings and visual support (tables, graphs) so readers can follow the information easily.

questions.question: Put the steps of writing a business report in a sensible order.

items.text: Decide the purpose and reader of the report
Draft the report with clear headings

questions.expected: purpose, gather, draft, review
questions.memo: Decide the purpose and reader, gather information, draft with clear headings, then review and finalise.

questions.question: A questioner is hostile and tries to provoke you during a presentation. What is the best response?
options: Stay calm, answer the point factually, and keep your composure
Shout back to show you are in charge
questions.expected: Stay calm, answer the point factually, and keep your composure
questions.memo: Staying calm and answering factually keeps you professional and credible, even when a questioner is difficult.

questions.question: A presenter argues with every audience member who gives feedback. Why does this harm the presentation?
options: It looks unprofessional and discourages useful feedback
It makes the presenter more credible
It improves the quality of the slides
It shortens the question time helpfully
questions.expected: It looks unprofessional and discourages useful feedback
questions.memo: Arguing with feedback appears defensive and unprofessional, and it stops people offering the useful comments that could improve the work.

questions.question: Why can a well-chosen graph communicate some information better than words alone?
options: It shows patterns and comparisons at a glance
It hides the data from the audience
It removes the need for any explanation ever
questions.expected: It shows patterns and comparisons at a glance
questions.memo: A graph makes trends and comparisons visible instantly, which words alone often cannot do as quickly.

questions.question: After a presentation, several people point out the same weakness. What should the presenter do?
options: Take the feedback on board and amend the presentation for next time
Ignore it because the presentation is finished
Delete the presentation and give up
questions.expected: Take the feedback on board and amend the presentation for next time
questions.memo: Consistent feedback signals a real weakness; a professional uses it to amend and improve future presentations.

BUS.G11.T3.ENTRE.A1.title: Entrepreneurial qualities & success factors
BUS.G11.T3.ENTRE.A1.description: Assessing the degree to which a business embraces entrepreneurial qualities (risk-taking, perseverance, good management) and critically reflecting on a venture to identify its key success factors (sustainability, profitability, customer base) and areas for improvement.
BUS.G11.T3.ENTRE.A1.strand: T3 — Entrepreneurial success, citizenship, marketing & production functions
BUS.G11.T3.ENTRE.A1.recovery_strategy: Entrepreneurial qualities are personal characteristics (risk-taking, perseverance, good management, vision). Key success factors are what makes a business work: a loyal customer base, profitability and sustainability. Judge a venture against these, then name areas to improve.

questions.question: Which of these is an entrepreneurial quality?
options: Giving up at the first problem
questions.expected: Risk-taking
questions.memo: Risk-taking is a key entrepreneurial quality — the willingness to take calculated chances to pursue an opportunity.

questions.question: A key success factor for a business is a loyal _________ base.
questions.expected: customer
questions.memo: A loyal customer base brings repeat sales and is one of the main factors behind a successful business.

questions.question: True or false: Profitability is one of the key success factors of a business.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A business must make a profit to survive and grow, so profitability is a key success factor.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an entrepreneurial quality?
options: Giving up easily when things get hard
questions.expected: Giving up easily when things get hard
questions.memo: Giving up easily is the opposite of perseverance. The others — perseverance, confidence and vision — are entrepreneurial qualities.

questions.question: _________ means the business is able to keep operating successfully into the future.
questions.expected: Sustainability
questions.memo: Sustainability is the ability of a business to keep going and remain viable over the long term.

questions.question: True or false: Perseverance means continuing to work towards a goal despite setbacks.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Perseverance is pushing on towards a goal even when problems and setbacks arise — a core entrepreneurial quality.

questions.question: Sort each item into whether it is an entrepreneurial quality or not.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Perseverance, vision, good management and confidence are entrepreneurial qualities; fearing all risk and refusing to adapt are not.

questions.question: How do you assess whether a business embraces entrepreneurial qualities?
options: Check whether it shows risk-taking, perseverance, good management and vision
Count how many staff it has only
Look only at the colour of its logo
Check whether the owner is tall
questions.expected: Check whether it shows risk-taking, perseverance, good management and vision
questions.memo: You judge a business against the entrepreneurial qualities — does it take sensible risks, persevere, manage well and have a clear vision?

questions.question: Which of these is a key success factor of a business?
questions.expected: A growing, loyal customer base
questions.memo: A loyal, growing customer base is a key success factor; the other options are problems, not strengths.

questions.question: Thesis: 'A business should regularly identify its areas for improvement.' Choose the THREE strongest supporting reasons.
questions.thesis: A business should regularly identify its areas for improvement.

pool.text: It helps the business fix weaknesses before they become serious
It keeps the business competitive as the market changes
It guides where to focus effort and resources
Identifying weaknesses always bankrupts a business
The owner enjoys filling in forms
A business is already perfect and never needs to improve

questions.memo: The strong reasons are fixing weaknesses early, staying competitive, and focusing effort. The others are false or irrelevant.

questions.question: An area for _________ is a weakness the business should work on.
questions.expected: improvement
questions.memo: An area for improvement is a weak point that, if addressed, would make the business stronger.

questions.question: True or false: A business with no customers at all can still be considered successful.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Without customers there are no sales and no income, so a business cannot be successful without a customer base.

questions.question: Sort each item into whether it is a success factor or an area for improvement for a struggling shop.

items.text: Weak marketing that few people see

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Loyal customers, healthy profit and a trusted brand are success factors; poor stock control, slow service and weak marketing are areas to improve.

questions.question: Why is it useful for a business to identify its areas for improvement?
options: So it can fix weaknesses, grow and stay competitive
So it can ignore all its problems
So it can stop serving customers
So it can avoid making any changes
questions.expected: So it can fix weaknesses, grow and stay competitive
questions.memo: Identifying weak points lets a business improve, grow and keep up with competitors.

questions.question: A business changes its products quickly when customer tastes shift. Which entrepreneurial quality does this show?
questions.expected: Flexibility (the ability to adapt)
questions.memo: Adapting quickly to change shows flexibility, an important entrepreneurial quality.

questions.question: Good _________ and leadership is one of the entrepreneurial qualities.
questions.expected: management
questions.memo: Good management and leadership — planning, organising and guiding others — is a recognised entrepreneurial quality.

questions.question: A café makes a profit but its only chef is overworked and about to quit. Which area for improvement is most urgent for its sustainability?
options: Reducing reliance on one person by training or hiring more staff
Changing the colour of the menus
Ignoring the problem because it is profitable now
questions.expected: Reducing reliance on one person by training or hiring more staff
questions.memo: Depending on a single overworked chef threatens future operations, so spreading that capacity is the key improvement for sustainability.

questions.question: Which situation most threatens a business's long-term sustainability?
options: Losing customers steadily with no plan to win new ones
Earning a small but steady profit
questions.expected: Losing customers steadily with no plan to win new ones
questions.memo: A shrinking customer base with no plan to replace it undermines future income and threatens the business's survival.

questions.question: Why is a loyal customer base so valuable as a success factor?
options: Repeat customers provide steady income and often recommend the business
Loyal customers never need to be served
It means the business can ignore quality
It removes the need to make a profit
questions.expected: Repeat customers provide steady income and often recommend the business
questions.memo: Loyal customers buy again and refer others, giving the business reliable income and free word-of-mouth marketing.

questions.question: An entrepreneur reflects on her venture. Which approach best combines assessing qualities with finding improvements?
options: Judge the business against entrepreneurial qualities and success factors, then list specific things to improve
Assume everything is fine and change nothing
Only count the cash and ignore everything else
questions.expected: Judge the business against entrepreneurial qualities and success factors, then list specific things to improve
questions.memo: A useful reflection measures the venture against the qualities and success factors, then turns the gaps into concrete areas for improvement.

BUS.G11.T3.CITIZEN.A1.title: Citizenship roles & responsibilities
BUS.G11.T3.CITIZEN.A1.description: The citizenship roles and responsibilities business practitioners perform: how citizens, through business, contribute to the social and economic development of their communities, the concept of the business community, and the role of business, civil society, NGOs and CBOs.
BUS.G11.T3.CITIZEN.A1.strand: T3 — Entrepreneurial success, citizenship, marketing & production functions
BUS.G11.T3.CITIZEN.A1.recovery_strategy: NGO = non-governmental organisation (independent, often national). CBO = community-based organisation (local). Business practitioners are citizens who can give time, effort and resources to develop their communities.

questions.question: The letters 'NGO' stand for a _________ organisation.
questions.expected: non-governmental
questions.memo: An NGO is a non-governmental organisation — an independent body, not run by the government, that works for a public cause.

questions.question: A CBO is a _________ organisation.
questions.expected: community-based
questions.memo: A CBO is a community-based organisation that works to meet the needs of a specific local community.

questions.question: True or false: Business practitioners are also citizens who can help their communities.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Business people are citizens too, and through their businesses they can contribute to community development.

questions.question: Which is a way a business person can contribute to their community?
options: Volunteering time and skills to a local cause
questions.expected: Volunteering time and skills to a local cause
questions.memo: Giving time, skills or resources to a community cause is a clear example of a business person fulfilling a citizenship role.

questions.question: Giving _________ and effort to a community cause is part of a business person's citizenship role.
questions.expected: time
questions.memo: Contributing time and effort to help others is a key way business practitioners act as good citizens.

questions.question: True or false: An NGO is simply a government department.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: An NGO is non-governmental — independent of the government — even though it often works alongside it for public benefit.

questions.question: Sort each organisation into the correct type.

items.text: A national charity independent of government
A local soup kitchen run by neighbourhood volunteers
A street committee fixing a local park

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: NGOs are independent (often national/international) bodies; CBOs serve a specific local community; government bodies are run by the state.

questions.question: How can a business contribute to the social and economic development of its community?
options: By creating jobs, training people and supporting community projects
By keeping all its profit hidden offshore
questions.expected: By creating jobs, training people and supporting community projects
questions.memo: Creating jobs, building skills and backing local projects all develop the community both socially and economically.

questions.question: Build a 3-part explanation of why a business practitioner should contribute to their community.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-part explanation of why a business practitioner should contribute to their community.

options.text: Business practitioners should contribute because they are citizens with a role in their community
Business practitioners should contribute only if forced by law
Business practitioners should never get involved in their community
Their skills, resources and influence can address real local needs
Businesses have no resources that could ever help anyone
Communities never benefit from local businesses
A stronger community provides customers, workers and goodwill, benefiting the business too
Helping the community always destroys the business
Community development has no link to business at all

questions.memo: Claim: practitioners are citizens with a community role. Evidence: their skills and resources can meet real needs. Explanation: a stronger community also benefits the business through customers, workers and goodwill.

questions.question: The people connected to and served by a business make up its business _________.
questions.expected: community
questions.memo: The business community is the network of people — customers, staff, neighbours — connected to and affected by the business.

questions.question: What is the main role of a community-based organisation (CBO)?
options: To address the needs of a specific local community
questions.expected: To address the needs of a specific local community
questions.memo: CBOs focus on meeting the needs of their own local community, such as feeding schemes or local clean-ups.

questions.question: True or false: Contributing to the community can also improve a business's reputation.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: When a business gives back, the community and customers see it positively, which strengthens its reputation.

questions.question: Sort each action into whether it is a citizenship contribution or not.

items.text: Sponsoring a local youth sports team
Dumping waste illegally to save money

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Sponsoring, volunteering and mentoring are contributions; dumping waste, overcharging and ignoring needs are not.

questions.question: Which is an example of an individual giving back to the community through business?
options: An owner mentoring local youth and offering work experience
An owner refusing to speak to anyone local
An owner hiding all business activity
An owner blocking a community project
questions.expected: An owner mentoring local youth and offering work experience
questions.memo: Mentoring young people and offering experience uses the owner's position to develop the community.

questions.question: Why can individual business practitioners make a real difference in community development?
options: They have skills, resources and influence they can direct towards local needs
They have no ability to affect anything
Only the government can ever help communities
Businesses are always separate from communities
questions.expected: They have skills, resources and influence they can direct towards local needs
questions.memo: Business practitioners control resources, skills and networks they can put to work solving community problems.

questions.question: Civil society includes _________ and CBOs that work for the public good.
questions.expected: NGOs
questions.memo: Civil society is made up of independent groups such as NGOs and CBOs that act for the public good alongside business and government.

questions.question: A business owner gives staff paid time off each month to volunteer at a local clinic. How is this best evaluated?
options: It fulfils a citizenship role and can build goodwill, though it has a cost
It is pointless because only government should help
It has no possible benefit to the business
questions.expected: It fulfils a citizenship role and can build goodwill, though it has a cost
questions.memo: Releasing staff to volunteer supports the community and builds the business's goodwill, even though it costs some working time.

questions.question: Why is contributing to the community described as a responsibility, not just optional charity?
options: Because businesses use community resources and people, so they have a duty to give back
Because the law requires every business to donate half its profit
Because charity and responsibility are unrelated
Because communities owe businesses their support
questions.expected: Because businesses use community resources and people, so they have a duty to give back
questions.memo: Businesses depend on the community for customers, workers and infrastructure, which is why giving back is seen as a citizenship responsibility.

questions.question: How do business, NGOs and CBOs ideally work together for community development?
options: Each contributes resources and reach to tackle social and economic needs together
They compete to avoid helping anyone
Only one of them is allowed to act at a time
questions.expected: Each contributes resources and reach to tackle social and economic needs together
questions.memo: Business brings resources, NGOs bring reach and expertise, and CBOs bring local knowledge — together they can address community needs more effectively.

questions.question: A successful local manufacturer wants to act as a responsible corporate citizen. Which plan fits best?
options: Partner with a CBO to run a skills programme for unemployed local youth
Quietly cut all ties with the surrounding area
