Stop paying wages to fund a billboard
Move profits offshore and ignore local needs
questions.expected: Partner with a CBO to run a skills programme for unemployed local youth
questions.memo: Partnering with a local CBO to build skills directly develops the community and reflects responsible corporate citizenship.

BUS.G11.T3.MARKETING.A1.title: The marketing function
BUS.G11.T3.MARKETING.A1.description: Aspects of the marketing function: marketing activities, product policy (development, design, packaging, trademarks), pricing policy, distribution policy (channels, intermediaries, direct/indirect), communication policy (advertising, sales promotion, publicity, personal selling) and foreign marketing (imports and exports).
BUS.G11.T3.MARKETING.A1.strand: T3 — Entrepreneurial success, citizenship, marketing & production functions
BUS.G11.T3.MARKETING.A1.recovery_strategy: Tie each activity to its marketing policy: product = design, packaging and brand; pricing = setting the price; distribution = getting it to the customer (channels, intermediaries); communication = telling customers about it (advertising, selling). Foreign marketing = imports and exports.

questions.question: The four Ps of the marketing mix are product, price, place and _________.
questions.expected: promotion
questions.memo: The four Ps are product, price, place (distribution) and promotion (marketing communication).

questions.question: Which marketing policy covers a product's design, packaging and branding?
questions.expected: Product policy
questions.memo: Product policy deals with the product itself — its development, design, packaging and trademark.

questions.question: True or false: Advertising is part of marketing communication.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Advertising is one form of marketing communication, used to tell customers about a product.

questions.question: Distribution (place) is mainly about:
options: Getting the product to the customer
questions.expected: Getting the product to the customer
questions.memo: Distribution is about the channels and intermediaries that move the product from the producer to the customer.

questions.question: Selling goods to customers in other countries is called _________.
questions.expected: exporting
questions.memo: Exporting is selling goods to other countries; importing is buying goods from other countries.

questions.question: True or false: Pricing policy decides how much to charge for a product.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Pricing policy sets the price, using factors such as cost, demand and competition.

questions.question: Sort each activity under the marketing policy it belongs to.

items.text: Setting a discount for bulk buyers
Choosing wholesalers to carry the product

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Packaging and design = product; discounts and price = pricing; wholesalers = distribution; adverts = communication.

questions.question: What is an intermediary in distribution?
options: A middleman, such as a wholesaler or retailer, between producer and consumer
The factory that makes the product
The final customer who uses the product
questions.expected: A middleman, such as a wholesaler or retailer, between producer and consumer
questions.memo: Intermediaries — wholesalers and retailers — sit between the producer and the consumer and help move the product along.

questions.question: Read the case and select the marketing COMMUNICATION (promotion) activities.
questions.source_text: To launch its new juice, a company redesigned the bottle and lowered the price for the first month. It also ran television adverts and offered free samples in supermarkets, while signing a deal with a national chain of stores to stock it.
questions.task: Tap the parts that are marketing communication (promotion) activities.

targets.phrase: ran television adverts
targets.reason: Advertising is a communication activity.

targets.phrase: offered free samples in supermarkets
targets.reason: Free samples are a sales-promotion (communication) activity.

questions.expected: ran television adverts; offered free samples in supermarkets
questions.memo: TV adverts and free samples are communication/promotion. Redesigning the bottle is product, lowering the price is pricing, and the store deal is distribution.

questions.question: _________ marketing involves selling to and buying from other countries through exports and imports.
questions.expected: Foreign
questions.memo: Foreign marketing deals with trade across borders — exporting goods abroad and importing goods from abroad.

questions.question: What is the difference between direct and indirect distribution?
options: Direct sells straight to the customer; indirect uses intermediaries like wholesalers
Direct uses many middlemen; indirect uses none
Direct is always cheaper for the customer
There is no difference between them
questions.expected: Direct sells straight to the customer; indirect uses intermediaries like wholesalers
questions.memo: Direct distribution goes straight from producer to customer; indirect distribution passes through intermediaries such as wholesalers and retailers.

questions.question: True or false: Packaging both protects the product and helps to market it.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Good packaging protects the product and also attracts customers and carries the brand, so it is part of product policy.

questions.question: Sort each example into direct or indirect distribution.

items.text: A farmer selling vegetables at their own farm stall
A factory selling through wholesalers and shops
A baker selling directly from their shopfront
A producer using a chain of retailers
An online store shipping straight to the buyer
A manufacturer supplying a supermarket group

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Selling straight to the customer is direct; using wholesalers or retailers in between is indirect.

questions.question: Which of these is a factor that influences a product's price?
options: The cost of making it, demand, and competitors' prices
The colour of the owner's car
The day of the week the owner was born
The number of letters in the brand name
questions.expected: The cost of making it, demand, and competitors' prices
questions.memo: Pricing is influenced by production cost, customer demand and what competitors charge.

questions.question: What is personal selling?
options: A salesperson dealing directly with a customer to make a sale
Printing posters with no human contact
questions.expected: A salesperson dealing directly with a customer to make a sale
questions.memo: Personal selling is face-to-face (or direct) contact between a salesperson and a customer, a form of marketing communication.

questions.question: Read the case and select the DISTRIBUTION (place) decisions.
questions.source_text: A shoe brand improved its leather quality and set a premium price. It then appointed regional wholesalers and opened branded outlets in three cities, while filming a glossy advert for social media.
questions.task: Tap the parts that are distribution (place) decisions.

targets.phrase: appointed regional wholesalers
targets.reason: Using wholesalers is a distribution decision.

targets.phrase: opened branded outlets in three cities
targets.reason: Opening outlets is about getting the product to customers — distribution.

questions.expected: appointed regional wholesalers; opened branded outlets in three cities
questions.memo: Wholesalers and outlets are distribution. Improving leather is product, the premium price is pricing, and the advert is communication.

questions.question: Sales of a good product are slow because few people know it exists. Which marketing policy most needs attention?
options: Communication (promotion) — to make customers aware of it
Product — the product is the problem
questions.expected: Communication (promotion) — to make customers aware of it
questions.memo: If a good product is simply not known, the gap is in communication/promotion, which builds awareness.

questions.question: How does effective marketing help a business achieve its objectives?
options: It attracts and keeps customers, driving sales and income towards the business's goals
It only adds costs with no benefit
It replaces the need to make a good product
It guarantees the business never competes
questions.expected: It attracts and keeps customers, driving sales and income towards the business's goals
questions.memo: Marketing brings in and retains customers, generating the sales and income a business needs to meet its objectives.

questions.question: Why must foreign marketing be aligned with the production function?
options: Production must be able to meet export demand with the right quantity and quality
Foreign marketing has nothing to do with production
Exports never affect how much is produced
questions.expected: Production must be able to meet export demand with the right quantity and quality
questions.memo: Winning export orders is pointless if production cannot supply the right quantity and quality on time, so the two functions must align.

questions.question: A new premium snack is well-made but priced the same as cheap rivals and sold only at a remote farm stall. Which combination of fixes fits the marketing mix?
options: Set a price that reflects its quality and widen distribution to reach more customers
Lower the quality to match the price
questions.expected: Set a price that reflects its quality and widen distribution to reach more customers
questions.memo: A premium product needs a matching price (pricing) and broader distribution (place) so the right customers can find and buy it.

BUS.G11.T3.PRODUCTION.A1.title: The production function
BUS.G11.T3.PRODUCTION.A1.description: Aspects of the production function: production systems (mass, batch, job), production planning and control, safety management (the Occupational Health and Safety Act), quality control (SABS), and production cost calculations (total cost, unit cost, selling price, profit, break-even).
BUS.G11.T3.PRODUCTION.A1.strand: T3 — Entrepreneurial success, citizenship, marketing & production functions
BUS.G11.T3.PRODUCTION.A1.recovery_strategy: Job = one custom item; batch = a group of identical items at a time; mass = continuous large-scale identical output. Total cost = fixed + variable costs. Break-even = where total income equals total cost (no profit, no loss).

questions.question: Making a single, one-off custom item is an example of _________ production.
questions.expected: job
questions.memo: Job production makes one custom item at a time, such as a tailor-made suit or a single wedding cake.

questions.question: Producing large quantities of identical items continuously is _________ production.
questions.expected: mass
questions.memo: Mass production turns out large volumes of identical products continuously, like bottled drinks on a production line.

questions.question: Producing a set group of identical items at a time, then switching to another group, is _________ production.
questions.expected: batch
questions.memo: Batch production makes a group of identical items together (a 'batch'), such as a tray of one bread type, before moving to the next.

questions.question: True or false: The break-even point is where total income equals total cost.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: At break-even, income exactly covers cost — the business makes neither a profit nor a loss.

questions.question: The Act that governs health and safety in the workplace is the Occupational Health and _________ Act.
questions.expected: Safety
questions.memo: The Occupational Health and Safety Act sets the rules for keeping workers safe in the workplace.

questions.question: True or false: Quality control checks that products meet the required standards.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Quality control inspects products against set standards (such as SABS) to catch and prevent defects.

questions.question: Sort each example into the production system it best fits.

items.text: A tailor making one custom suit
A bakery baking 50 loaves of one bread type, then switching
A bottling plant filling thousands of identical cans non-stop
An architect designing one unique house
A factory producing a run of one shirt size, then another
A car plant assembling identical cars continuously

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: One custom item = job; a group at a time = batch; continuous large-scale identical output = mass.

questions.question: Production planning includes which set of activities?
questions.expected: Planning, routing, scheduling and loading
questions.memo: Production planning decides what to make and how — planning, routing, scheduling and loading the work.

questions.question: Put the production control steps in a sensible order.

items.text: Dispatch the work to start production
Take corrective action on any problems

questions.expected: dispatch, follow, inspect, correct
questions.memo: Production control runs: dispatch the work, follow up on progress, inspect the output, then correct any problems found.

questions.question: The SABS sets _________ standards that products can be tested against.
questions.expected: quality
questions.memo: The South African Bureau of Standards (SABS) sets quality standards used in quality control.

questions.question: Total cost of production is best calculated as:
questions.expected: Fixed costs plus variable costs
questions.memo: Total cost = fixed costs (which stay the same) + variable costs (which change with output).

questions.question: True or false: Unit cost is the total cost divided by the number of units produced.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Unit cost = total cost ÷ number of units, showing how much each item costs to make.

questions.question: Sort each task into production planning or production control.

items.text: Scheduling when each job will run
Following up on a delayed order

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Planning sets up the work (scheduling, routing, loading); control monitors and fixes it (inspecting, following up, correcting).

questions.question: A workshop has fixed costs of R1 000 and variable costs of R2 per unit. If it makes 500 units, what is the total cost?
questions.memo: Total cost = fixed + variable = R1 000 + (R2 × 500) = R1 000 + R1 000 = R2 000.

questions.question: A product sells for R10 and costs R6 in variable cost per unit. The business has R2 000 in fixed costs. How many units must it sell to break even?
questions.expected: 500 units
questions.memo: Each unit contributes R10 − R6 = R4 towards fixed costs. Break-even = R2 000 ÷ R4 = 500 units.

questions.question: What is the main aim of safety management in production?
options: To prevent workplace injuries and protect workers
To raise the price of the product
questions.expected: To prevent workplace injuries and protect workers
questions.memo: Safety management — guided by the Occupational Health and Safety Act — aims to keep workers safe and prevent accidents.

questions.question: A business has fixed costs of R3 000, sells each unit for R20 and has a variable cost of R12 per unit. What is its break-even quantity?
questions.expected: 375 units
questions.memo: Contribution per unit = R20 − R12 = R8. Break-even = R3 000 ÷ R8 = 375 units.

questions.question: Which production system best suits a business making one-of-a-kind custom furniture to order?
questions.expected: Job production
questions.memo: Custom, made-to-order pieces are produced one at a time, which is job production.

questions.question: Why is strong quality control important to a producer's costs and reputation?
options: It reduces waste and returns and protects the brand's reputation
It only adds cost with no benefit
It makes products fail more often
It has no link to customer trust
questions.expected: It reduces waste and returns and protects the brand's reputation
questions.memo: Catching defects early cuts the cost of waste and returns and keeps customers trusting the brand.

questions.question: How do production planning and production control work together?
options: Planning sets up what to make and when; control monitors and corrects the work as it happens
They are unrelated and never interact
Planning replaces the need for control entirely
questions.expected: Planning sets up what to make and when; control monitors and corrects the work as it happens
questions.memo: Planning organises the production in advance; control then tracks progress and fixes problems so the plan is met.

BUS.G11.T4.TEAM.A1.title: Team dynamics & conflict management
BUS.G11.T4.TEAM.A1.description: Team development stages (forming, storming, norming, performing), team dynamics theories (Belbin roles, Jungian insights, group consensus), and conflict management — causes of conflict, conflict-management theories and skills, and the function of workplace forums.
BUS.G11.T4.TEAM.A1.strand: T4 — Team dynamics, conflict & Human Resources
BUS.G11.T4.TEAM.A1.recovery_strategy: Team stages in order: forming (getting to know each other) → storming (conflict) → norming (settling) → performing (working well). Conflict managed well can strengthen a team; a workplace forum is where workers and management consult.

questions.question: The four stages of team development are forming, storming, norming and _________.
questions.expected: performing
questions.memo: The stages run forming → storming → norming → performing, ending with the team working effectively together.

questions.question: At which stage do team members first get to know one another?
questions.expected: Forming
questions.memo: Forming is the first stage, where members meet and get to know each other and the task.

questions.question: True or false: The storming stage often involves conflict as members' true characters show.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Storming is the stage where disagreements and clashes often surface as people assert themselves.

questions.question: What does conflict management aim to do?
options: Force one person to always win
questions.expected: Resolve differences constructively
questions.memo: Conflict management seeks to settle differences in a constructive way so the team can move forward.

questions.question: A workplace _________ is a body where workers and management discuss and consult on issues.
questions.expected: forum
questions.memo: A workplace forum is a structure for consultation between workers and management on workplace matters.

questions.question: True or false: Belbin's theory describes the different roles people play in a team.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Belbin's role theory groups team contributions into roles such as action-oriented, people-oriented and thinking (cerebral) roles.

questions.question: Put the stages of team development in the correct order.

items.text: Forming — members get to know each other
Norming — the team settles and agrees how to work
Performing — the team works well towards the goal

questions.expected: forming, storming, norming, performing
questions.memo: Teams typically move through forming, storming, norming and performing as they develop.

questions.question: What happens at the norming stage of a team?
options: The team settles, agrees how to work, and cooperation improves
The team meets for the very first time
The team breaks into open conflict
The team is performing at its peak
questions.expected: The team settles, agrees how to work, and cooperation improves
questions.memo: At norming the team resolves its early conflicts, agrees on norms and starts working together more smoothly.

questions.question: Match each description to the team stage by sorting them.

items.text: Members are polite and unsure of each other
Members clash over roles and ideas
The team delivers results smoothly together
People are still learning who does what
The team is confident and highly productive

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Forming = polite and unsure; storming = clashes and tension; performing = smooth, productive teamwork.

questions.question: Which of these is a common cause of conflict in a team?
questions.expected: Poor communication and competing goals
questions.memo: Conflict often arises from poor communication, unclear roles and competing goals; the other options reduce conflict.

questions.question: At the _________ stage, the team works well together towards its goal.
questions.expected: performing
questions.memo: Performing is the stage where the team is effective and focused on achieving its goal.

questions.question: True or false: Conflict, when managed well, can lead to better solutions for a team.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Handled well, conflict surfaces different views and can produce stronger, better-considered solutions.

questions.question: Sort each approach into a healthy or an unhealthy way of handling team conflict.

items.text: Focusing on the problem, not the person
Refusing to speak to the other party

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Healthy: listen, compromise, focus on the problem. Unhealthy: shouting, rumours and refusing to engage.

questions.question: What is the function of a workplace forum?
options: To allow workers and management to consult on workplace issues
To set the company's product prices
questions.expected: To allow workers and management to consult on workplace issues
questions.memo: A workplace forum is a consultation structure where workers and management discuss matters affecting the workplace.

questions.question: Belbin's team roles are often grouped into action-oriented, people-oriented and _________ roles.
questions.expected: thinking (cerebral)
questions.memo: Belbin groups roles as action-oriented, people-oriented and thinking (cerebral) — a balanced team needs all three.

questions.question: _________ resolution skills help a team settle disputes and move forward.
questions.expected: Conflict
questions.memo: Conflict-resolution skills — listening, negotiating, finding common ground — help teams settle disputes.

questions.question: Put the steps of resolving a team conflict in a sensible order.

items.text: Identify the real cause of the conflict
Let each side explain their view
Agree on a fair way forward
Follow up to check the solution holds

questions.expected: identify, discuss, agree, follow
questions.memo: Find the real cause, hear both sides, agree a fair solution, then follow up to make sure it works.

questions.question: A team is stuck in the storming stage with constant arguments. What best helps it move forward?
options: Agreeing clear roles and team norms so cooperation can begin
Letting the arguments continue with no structure
Cancelling the project at the first disagreement
questions.expected: Agreeing clear roles and team norms so cooperation can begin
questions.memo: Setting clear roles and norms helps a team move from storming into norming, where it can start working together.

questions.question: Why does understanding team dynamics help a manager?
options: It helps the manager guide the team through its stages and use members' strengths
It lets the manager ignore the team entirely
It guarantees there will never be any conflict
It removes the need for any leadership
questions.expected: It helps the manager guide the team through its stages and use members' strengths
questions.memo: Knowing the stages and roles lets a manager support the team through difficulties and place people where they add most value.

questions.question: Two colleagues clash because each thinks they should lead. What is the best conflict-management response?
options: Discuss the cause openly and agree clear, separate responsibilities
Let them keep fighting until one quits
Pretend the conflict is not happening
Side with the louder colleague immediately
questions.expected: Discuss the cause openly and agree clear, separate responsibilities
questions.memo: Addressing the cause and agreeing clear, distinct roles resolves the clash constructively and lets the team perform.

BUS.G11.T4.HR.A1.title: Introduction to Human Resources
BUS.G11.T4.HR.A1.description: An introduction to the human resources function: recruitment, selection and interviewing; the legalities of employment contracts; induction and placement; salary determination (piecemeal and time-related, including personal tax); and employee benefits. Relevant Acts: LRA, BCEA, EEA, COIDA.
BUS.G11.T4.HR.A1.strand: T4 — Team dynamics, conflict & Human Resources
BUS.G11.T4.HR.A1.recovery_strategy: Recruitment = attracting applicants; selection = choosing the best; induction = settling the new employee in. BCEA sets basic conditions, EEA promotes equity, LRA governs labour relations, COIDA covers workplace injuries.

questions.question: _________ means attracting suitable applicants to apply for a job.
questions.expected: Recruitment
questions.memo: Recruitment is the process of attracting suitable people to apply for a vacant post, for example by advertising it.

questions.question: What does selection involve?
options: Choosing the best candidate from the applicants
questions.expected: Choosing the best candidate from the applicants
questions.memo: Selection is choosing the most suitable applicant, using tools like screening and interviews.

questions.question: True or false: An employment contract sets out the terms agreed between employer and employee.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: An employment contract is a legal agreement stating the duties, pay and conditions agreed between employer and employee.

questions.question: _________ helps a new employee settle into the job and the workplace.
questions.expected: Induction
questions.memo: Induction introduces a new employee to the workplace, the team and their role so they can settle in.

questions.question: Which Act sets the basic conditions of employment, such as working hours and leave?
options: The Basic Conditions of Employment Act (BCEA)
questions.expected: The Basic Conditions of Employment Act (BCEA)
questions.memo: The BCEA sets minimum employment conditions such as working hours, leave and notice periods.

questions.question: True or false: A pension is an example of an employee benefit.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Benefits such as a pension, medical aid and leave are rewards beyond the basic salary.

questions.question: Put the steps of hiring a new employee in the correct order.

items.text: Advertise the post to attract applicants
Appoint and induct the chosen person

questions.expected: advertise, shortlist, interview, induct
questions.memo: Recruitment then selection: advertise, shortlist, interview, then appoint and induct the chosen candidate.

questions.question: Sort each task into recruitment, selection or induction.

items.text: Showing a new hire around the workplace
Posting the vacancy on a job site
Checking references and choosing the best applicant
Explaining the new employee's duties on day one

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Recruitment attracts applicants (adverts); selection chooses the best (interviews, references); induction settles them in (orientation).

questions.question: What is the difference between time-related and piecemeal salary determination?
options: Time-related pays for time worked; piecemeal pays per unit produced
Time-related pays per unit; piecemeal pays per hour
questions.expected: Time-related pays for time worked; piecemeal pays per unit produced
questions.memo: Time-related pay is based on hours or a monthly period; piecemeal pay is based on the number of items produced.

questions.question: _________ pay is calculated according to the number of units a worker produces.
questions.expected: Piecemeal
questions.memo: Piecemeal (piece-rate) pay rewards output — the more units produced, the higher the pay.

questions.question: Which Act promotes equity and protects employees from unfair discrimination at work?
questions.expected: The Employment Equity Act (EEA)
questions.memo: The Employment Equity Act promotes fair treatment and equal opportunity, prohibiting unfair discrimination in the workplace.

questions.question: True or false: COIDA covers compensation for employees injured or made ill at work.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act (COIDA) compensates workers injured or made ill on the job.

questions.question: Sort each Act under what it mainly deals with.

items.text: Rules on working hours and leave
Paying out for a workplace injury

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: BCEA = basic conditions (hours, leave); EEA = equity and fair treatment; COIDA = compensation for workplace injury.

questions.question: Which of these are examples of employee benefits?
questions.expected: Pension and medical aid
questions.memo: Benefits are rewards beyond the basic salary, such as pension contributions and medical aid.

questions.question: What does induction of a new employee involve?
options: Introducing them to the workplace, the team and their role
questions.expected: Introducing them to the workplace, the team and their role
questions.memo: Induction helps a new hire settle in by introducing the workplace, colleagues and their responsibilities.

questions.question: A legal agreement that sets out an employee's duties, pay and conditions is an _________ contract.
questions.expected: employment
questions.memo: An employment contract is the legal agreement governing the relationship between employer and employee.

questions.question: An employee is unfairly dismissed and believes labour rights were ignored. Which Act mainly governs this dispute?
questions.expected: The Labour Relations Act (LRA)
questions.memo: The Labour Relations Act governs fair labour practices, including unfair dismissals and disputes between employers and employees.

questions.question: Why should a business follow proper recruitment and selection procedures?
options: To choose the best candidate fairly and comply with the law
To make hiring as slow as possible
To avoid ever filling the post
questions.expected: To choose the best candidate fairly and comply with the law
questions.memo: Proper procedures help find the most suitable person fairly and keep the business within labour law, avoiding disputes.

questions.question: A factory pays workers for each garment they sew, while the office pays staff a fixed monthly salary. How are these pay methods best described?
options: The factory uses piecemeal pay; the office uses time-related pay
The factory uses time-related pay; the office uses piecemeal pay
Neither is a real pay method
questions.expected: The factory uses piecemeal pay; the office uses time-related pay
questions.memo: Paying per garment is piecemeal (per unit); a fixed monthly salary is time-related (per period).

questions.question: Why must an employer understand the relevant labour Acts when employing staff?
options: To meet legal duties on conditions, equity, safety and injury compensation, avoiding penalties
Because the Acts have no effect on business
To avoid ever paying any salary
questions.expected: To meet legal duties on conditions, equity, safety and injury compensation, avoiding penalties
questions.memo: The BCEA, EEA, LRA and COIDA place legal duties on employers; understanding them keeps the business compliant and protects both staff and the business.

BUS.G12.T1.LEGISLATION.A1.title: Impact of recent legislation on business
BUS.G12.T1.LEGISLATION.A1.description: The impact of recent legislation, developed for redress and equity, on small and large business: the Skills Development Act, Labour Relations Act, Employment Equity Act, Basic Conditions of Employment Act, COIDA, BEE and BBBEE, National Credit Act and Consumer Protection Act, plus human rights, inclusivity and environmental issues.
BUS.G12.T1.LEGISLATION.A1.strand: T1 — Legislation, Human Resources, ethics, creative thinking & business strategies
BUS.G12.T1.LEGISLATION.A1.recovery_strategy: Tie each Act to its purpose: EEA = fair, equal workplaces; BCEA = minimum working conditions; LRA = fair labour relations and unions; SDA = skills and SETAs; CPA = consumer rights; NCA = fair credit; BBBEE = economic redress; COIDA = injury compensation.

questions.question: What does the Employment Equity Act (EEA) mainly promote?
options: Equity and protection from unfair discrimination at work
questions.expected: Equity and protection from unfair discrimination at work
questions.memo: The EEA promotes equal opportunity and fair treatment, prohibiting unfair discrimination in the workplace.

questions.question: The Basic Conditions of Employment Act (BCEA) mainly sets:
options: Minimum working conditions such as hours and leave
questions.expected: Minimum working conditions such as hours and leave
questions.memo: The BCEA sets minimum employment conditions — working hours, leave, notice and similar protections.

questions.question: Which Act compensates employees who are injured or fall ill at work?
questions.expected: COIDA
questions.memo: COIDA — the Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act — pays compensation to workers injured or made ill on the job.

questions.question: True or false: Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment (BBBEE) aims to redress past economic inequality.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: BBBEE seeks to redress the economic imbalances of the past by broadening participation in the economy.

questions.question: The _________ Protection Act protects the rights of consumers.
questions.expected: Consumer
questions.memo: The Consumer Protection Act (CPA) protects consumers' rights to fair, safe and honest treatment.

questions.question: True or false: The Skills Development Act supports training, funded through a skills levy and SETAs.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The Skills Development Act funds and coordinates training through the skills levy and Sector Education and Training Authorities (SETAs).

questions.question: Sort each Act under the area it mainly deals with.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: BCEA and LRA govern the workplace; NCA and CPA protect consumers and credit users; EEA and SDA address equity and skills.

questions.question: What does the Labour Relations Act (LRA) mainly govern?
options: Fair labour relations, including unions and disputes
The interest rate on home loans
questions.expected: Fair labour relations, including unions and disputes
questions.memo: The LRA governs the relationship between employers, employees and unions, covering bargaining, strikes and dispute resolution.

questions.question: Read the case and select the parts that show legislation affecting the business.
questions.source_text: A manufacturer reviews its obligations. It must register staff for injury compensation under COIDA and pay the skills levy that funds SETA training. Its head office was recently repainted, and it has set fair, non-discriminatory hiring rules to meet the Employment Equity Act.
questions.task: Tap the parts that show legislation affecting the business.

targets.phrase: register staff for injury compensation under COIDA
targets.reason: COIDA is legislation requiring injury cover.

targets.phrase: pay the skills levy that funds SETA training
targets.reason: The skills levy comes from the Skills Development Act.

targets.phrase: set fair, non-discriminatory hiring rules to meet the Employment Equity Act
targets.reason: The EEA requires fair, non-discriminatory employment.

questions.expected: register staff for injury compensation under COIDA; pay the skills levy that funds SETA training; set fair, non-discriminatory hiring rules to meet the Employment Equity Act
questions.memo: COIDA, the skills levy (SDA) and the EEA are all legislation shaping the business. Repainting the office is not a legal obligation.

questions.question: BBBEE stands for Broad-Based Black _________ Empowerment.
questions.expected: Economic
questions.memo: BBBEE is Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment, aimed at broadening economic participation.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the National Credit Act (NCA)?
options: To protect consumers in credit agreements and promote responsible lending
questions.expected: To protect consumers in credit agreements and promote responsible lending
questions.memo: The NCA protects consumers who buy on credit and requires lenders to lend responsibly.

questions.question: True or false: The Consumer Protection Act gives consumers the right to fair, safe and honest treatment.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The CPA protects consumers' rights to safe products, honest information and fair business practice.

questions.question: Sort each item into whether it is mainly a cost of compliance or a benefit of the legislation.

items.text: A better-skilled workforce from SETA training
Extra admin to meet equity reporting

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Legislation brings compliance costs (levies, admin, contributions) but also real benefits (skills, fairness, worker protection).

questions.question: How does the Skills Development Act, through SETAs, benefit business?
options: It funds and coordinates training to build a more skilled workforce
It lowers the price of raw materials
It removes the need to pay any tax
questions.expected: It funds and coordinates training to build a more skilled workforce
questions.memo: The SDA uses the skills levy and SETAs to fund training, helping businesses access better-skilled workers.

questions.question: Human rights in the Constitution include the rights to:
questions.expected: Equality, dignity and fair treatment
questions.memo: Constitutional human rights include equality, human dignity and fair treatment, which businesses must respect.

questions.question: Read the case and select the examples of INCLUSIVITY and human-rights measures.
questions.source_text: A company updates its policies. It makes its building wheelchair-accessible for staff with disabilities and adopts a hiring policy that welcomes people of all races and genders. It also buys a new delivery van and repaints the canteen.
questions.task: Tap the parts that show inclusivity or human-rights measures.

targets.phrase: makes its building wheelchair-accessible for staff with disabilities
targets.reason: Accessibility for disabled staff is an inclusivity/human-rights measure.

targets.phrase: adopts a hiring policy that welcomes people of all races and genders
targets.reason: Inclusive, non-discriminatory hiring reflects equity and human rights.

questions.expected: makes its building wheelchair-accessible for staff with disabilities; adopts a hiring policy that welcomes people of all races and genders
questions.memo: Accessibility and inclusive hiring are inclusivity and human-rights measures. Buying a van and repainting the canteen are not.

questions.question: An employee is dismissed without a fair hearing. Which Act most directly applies?
questions.expected: The Labour Relations Act (LRA)
questions.memo: Unfair dismissal is a labour-relations matter governed by the LRA, which requires fair procedures.

questions.question: How does redress-and-equity legislation typically affect small versus large businesses?
options: It adds compliance costs and admin, which can weigh more heavily on small businesses, while promoting fairer workplaces overall
It has no effect on any business
It only ever benefits businesses with no costs
It applies only to large businesses and never to small ones
questions.expected: It adds compliance costs and admin, which can weigh more heavily on small businesses, while promoting fairer workplaces overall
questions.memo: Compliance has real costs that can press harder on small firms, even as the legislation makes workplaces fairer and more inclusive for everyone.

questions.question: Why was legislation such as the EEA and BBBEE introduced?
options: To redress past inequality and create fairer access to the economy
To raise the price of consumer goods
questions.expected: To redress past inequality and create fairer access to the economy
questions.memo: These Acts respond to demands for redress and equity, broadening fair participation in the workplace and economy.

questions.question: A retailer sells a customer a dangerous, faulty appliance and refuses a refund. Which Act protects the customer, and how?
options: The Consumer Protection Act — it gives the right to safe goods and fair redress
The Skills Development Act — it trains the customer
The Labour Relations Act — it governs the sale
questions.expected: The Consumer Protection Act — it gives the right to safe goods and fair redress
questions.memo: The CPA protects consumers' rights to safe products and fair treatment, including remedies such as refunds for defective goods.

BUS.G12.T1.HR.A1.title: The Human Resources function
BUS.G12.T1.HR.A1.description: Relevant legislation and the aspects of the human resources function: recruitment and selection; employee contracts; induction and placement; salary administration (including personal tax); employee benefits; and skills development (the Skills Development Act, SETAs, learnerships, the NQF and SAQA).
BUS.G12.T1.HR.A1.strand: T1 — Legislation, Human Resources, ethics, creative thinking & business strategies
BUS.G12.T1.HR.A1.recovery_strategy: Recruitment attracts applicants, selection chooses, induction settles them in, and skills development grows them. Salary administration includes deducting personal tax (PAYE). SETAs and learnerships develop skills under the Skills Development Act.

questions.question: _________ is the process of attracting suitable applicants, while selection chooses the best of them.
questions.expected: Recruitment
questions.memo: Recruitment attracts applicants (e.g. by advertising); selection then chooses the most suitable one.

questions.question: What do induction and placement involve?
options: Settling a new employee in and assigning them to the right role
questions.expected: Settling a new employee in and assigning them to the right role
questions.memo: Induction settles the new employee into the workplace, and placement assigns them to the job that best fits them.

questions.question: True or false: Skills development includes learnerships and is supported by SETAs.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Skills development uses tools like learnerships, coordinated by SETAs under the Skills Development Act.

questions.question: Salary _________ covers paying staff and deducting tax correctly.
questions.expected: administration
questions.memo: Salary administration manages how staff are paid, including deductions such as personal income tax.

questions.question: Which of these is a deduction from an employee's salary that goes to the government?
questions.expected: Personal income tax (PAYE)
questions.memo: Pay-As-You-Earn (PAYE) is personal income tax deducted from an employee's salary and paid to the government.

questions.question: True or false: Pension and medical aid are examples of employee benefits.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Benefits such as pension and medical aid are rewards beyond the basic salary that help attract and keep staff.

questions.question: Put the stages of the HR employment cycle in a sensible order.

items.text: Induct and place the new employee

questions.expected: recruit, select, contract, induct
questions.memo: Attract applicants, choose the best, sign the contract, then induct and place the new employee.

questions.question: Sort each task into the HR activity it belongs to.

items.text: Sending workers on a SETA training course

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Interviewing and advertising = recruitment/selection; PAYE and net pay = salary administration; learnerships and SETA courses = skills development.

questions.question: What do the NQF and SAQA relate to?
options: A national framework that records and recognises qualifications
questions.expected: A national framework that records and recognises qualifications
questions.memo: The National Qualifications Framework (NQF) and the South African Qualifications Authority (SAQA) organise and recognise qualifications.

questions.question: A structured programme that combines workplace experience with formal study is called a _________.
questions.expected: learnership
questions.memo: A learnership combines on-the-job experience with study, leading to a recognised qualification.

questions.question: Why is good induction of new employees important?
options: It helps them become productive sooner and reduces staff turnover
It increases the company's tax bill
It replaces the need for any training
It slows the new employee down on purpose
questions.expected: It helps them become productive sooner and reduces staff turnover
questions.memo: A good induction settles new staff quickly, so they reach productivity sooner and are more likely to stay.

questions.question: True or false: An employment contract should comply with the Basic Conditions of Employment Act.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Employment contracts must meet the minimum standards set by the BCEA, such as hours and leave.

questions.question: Sort each item into recruitment, selection or induction.

items.text: Giving the new hire a tour and a mentor
Explaining policies on the first day

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Adverts attract (recruit); interviews and tests choose (select); tours and policy briefings settle people in (induct).

questions.question: A worker is paid R50 for every chair they assemble, with no fixed monthly amount. How is this pay best described?
questions.expected: Piecemeal (per-unit) pay
questions.memo: Paying a set amount per item produced is piecemeal (piece-rate) pay, based on output rather than time.

questions.question: What is the role of a SETA?
options: To fund and coordinate skills training within an industry sector
To set the price of consumer goods
questions.expected: To fund and coordinate skills training within an industry sector
questions.memo: Sector Education and Training Authorities (SETAs) use the skills levy to fund and organise training in their sector.

questions.question: Personal income tax deducted directly from an employee's salary is commonly called _________.
questions.expected: PAYE
questions.memo: PAYE (Pay-As-You-Earn) is the personal income tax deducted from salaries and paid over to the tax authority.

questions.question: A business struggles to find skilled workers. Which HR action best addresses this in the long term?
options: Using learnerships and SETA training to develop its own skilled staff
questions.expected: Using learnerships and SETA training to develop its own skilled staff
questions.memo: Skills development through learnerships and SETA-funded training builds the skilled workforce the business needs over time.

questions.question: Why must an employer handle employee contracts and salaries within the relevant labour laws?
options: To stay compliant, treat staff fairly and avoid disputes or penalties
Because the laws have no effect on business
questions.expected: To stay compliant, treat staff fairly and avoid disputes or penalties
questions.memo: Following labour law on contracts and pay keeps the business compliant, protects employees and prevents costly disputes.

questions.question: How can a strong benefits package (pension, medical aid, leave) help a business?
options: It helps attract and retain good employees
It guarantees the business never pays tax
It removes the need to pay any salary
It lowers the quality of staff
questions.expected: It helps attract and retain good employees
questions.memo: Good benefits make a business more attractive to work for, helping it recruit and keep skilled staff.

questions.question: How do the HR activities and the relevant Acts fit together?
options: HR carries out recruitment, contracts, pay and development within the limits set by labour legislation
HR and the Acts are completely unrelated
The Acts apply only to marketing
HR can ignore the law when convenient
questions.expected: HR carries out recruitment, contracts, pay and development within the limits set by labour legislation
questions.memo: The HR function operates inside the framework of the BCEA, EEA, LRA, COIDA and SDA, which shape how staff are hired, paid, protected and developed.

BUS.G12.T1.ETHICS.A1.title: Ethics & professionalism
BUS.G12.T1.ETHICS.A1.description: How professional, responsible, ethical and effective business practice should be conducted in changing and challenging environments: the meaning of ethical behaviour, ethical vs unethical and professional vs unprofessional practice, the link between them, and strategies to address issues such as taxation, sexual harassment, unfair advertising and abuse of work time.
BUS.G12.T1.ETHICS.A1.strand: T1 — Legislation, Human Resources, ethics, creative thinking & business strategies
BUS.G12.T1.ETHICS.A1.recovery_strategy: Ethical practice is honest and fair (pay fair wages, pay tax, advertise truthfully). Unethical practice harms others for gain (corruption, unfair ads, abusing work time). Professional behaviour supports ethical behaviour, especially under pressure.

questions.question: What does ethical behaviour in business mean?
options: Doing what is morally right, even when it is difficult
Doing whatever makes the most money
Following the crowd no matter what
questions.expected: Doing what is morally right, even when it is difficult
questions.memo: Ethical behaviour is acting in a morally right and fair way, even when an unethical choice might be easier or more profitable.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of UNETHICAL business practice?
questions.expected: Misleading customers with false advertising
questions.memo: False, misleading advertising deceives customers, which is unethical. The other options are ethical practices.

questions.question: Spending most of the work day on personal social media is an example of abusing work _________.
questions.expected: time
questions.memo: Using paid work hours for personal activities is abusing work time — an unprofessional and unethical practice.

questions.question: True or false: Paying the tax that is due is an ethical and responsible business practice.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Paying tax honestly is a legal and ethical duty that supports society and reflects responsible business practice.

questions.question: Sexual harassment in the workplace is:
questions.expected: Unethical and unlawful
questions.memo: Sexual harassment harms people and breaks the law, making it both unethical and unlawful.

questions.question: _________ behaviour and professionalism are closely linked at work.
questions.expected: Ethical
questions.memo: Ethical behaviour and professionalism reinforce each other — professional standards make ethical conduct part of daily work.

questions.question: Sort each practice into ethical or unethical.

items.text: Overcharging rural customers who have no alternative
Using company funds for personal expenses
Hiding a known safety defect from customers

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Honest advertising, fair wages and paying tax are ethical; overcharging, misusing funds and hiding defects are unethical.

questions.question: What is the relationship between ethical and professional behaviour?
options: They reinforce each other — professional standards support ethical conduct
They are opposites that cannot exist together
Professionalism replaces the need for ethics
questions.expected: They reinforce each other — professional standards support ethical conduct
questions.memo: A professional standard of honesty, respect and accountability naturally supports ethical behaviour, and ethics underpins professionalism.

questions.question: Build a 3-part explanation of why ethical practice matters even in a tough, changing business environment.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-part explanation of why ethical practice matters even in a tough, changing business environment.

options.text: Ethical practice matters under pressure because shortcuts damage trust and reputation
Ethics should be dropped whenever times get hard
Ethics only matters when the business is doing well
Customers, staff and partners avoid businesses caught acting dishonestly
Dishonesty has no effect on a business's reputation
People prefer to deal with businesses that cheat them
Keeping standards under pressure protects long-term trust and survival, which short-term gains cannot replace
A ruined reputation can be rebuilt instantly at no cost
Long-term trust has no value to a business

questions.memo: Claim: shortcuts under pressure damage trust. Evidence: people avoid dishonest businesses. Explanation: protecting long-term trust matters more than short-term gain.

questions.question: A document that guides how staff should behave ethically and professionally is a code of _________.
questions.expected: conduct
questions.memo: A code of conduct sets out the ethical and professional standards expected of everyone in the business.

questions.question: Which strategy best addresses the problem of unfair advertising in a business?
options: Adopt and enforce honest advertising standards
Advertise even more aggressively with false claims
questions.expected: Adopt and enforce honest advertising standards
questions.memo: Setting and enforcing honest advertising standards prevents misleading claims and protects customers and the brand.

questions.question: True or false: Maintaining good ethics under pressure builds long-term trust in a business.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A business that stays ethical even when it is hard earns lasting trust from customers, staff and partners.

questions.question: Sort each action into professional or unprofessional conduct under pressure.

items.text: Keeping promises to customers despite a busy period
Cutting safety checks to meet a deadline
Blaming junior staff for management's mistakes
Staying calm and respectful with an angry client
Taking credit for a colleague's work

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Keeping promises, honest communication and respect are professional; cutting safety, shifting blame and stealing credit are unprofessional.

questions.question: How can a business address the problem of staff abusing work time?
options: Set clear policies and monitor fairly, with consequences for abuse
Reward those who waste the most time
questions.expected: Set clear policies and monitor fairly, with consequences for abuse
questions.memo: Clear, fair policies and reasonable monitoring discourage the abuse of work time while respecting staff.

questions.question: A competitor wins business by bribing buyers. What is the ethical response?
options: Keep to your own honest standards and compete fairly
Spread false rumours about the competitor
questions.expected: Keep to your own honest standards and compete fairly
questions.memo: Ethical practice means holding to your standards and competing fairly, even when a rival behaves unethically.

questions.question: Charging far higher prices in a remote rural area only because customers have no alternative is generally regarded as _________.
questions.expected: unethical
questions.memo: Exploiting people's lack of choice to overcharge them is unfair to those customers, which is unethical.

questions.question: During a downturn, a manager is tempted to delay paying suppliers indefinitely and hide it from them. How is this best evaluated?
options: Unethical — it deceives suppliers and damages trust; honest negotiation is better
Ethical, because survival justifies any action
Irrelevant, because suppliers do not matter
questions.expected: Unethical — it deceives suppliers and damages trust; honest negotiation is better
questions.memo: Hiding non-payment deceives suppliers and breaks trust; the ethical path is to communicate honestly and negotiate terms.

questions.question: Why is cutting ethical corners to survive a tough period usually a poor long-term strategy?
options: It risks lasting damage to trust and reputation that outweighs the short-term gain
It always guarantees survival with no downside
Ethics has no effect on customers
questions.expected: It risks lasting damage to trust and reputation that outweighs the short-term gain
questions.memo: Unethical shortcuts can destroy the trust and reputation a business depends on, causing harm that outlasts any short-term benefit.

questions.question: Why does professionalism matter most in changing and challenging business environments?
options: Pressure makes shortcuts tempting, so professional standards keep conduct ethical and reliable
Professionalism only applies when business is easy
Challenges remove all need for standards
questions.expected: Pressure makes shortcuts tempting, so professional standards keep conduct ethical and reliable
questions.memo: It is under pressure that standards are tested; professionalism keeps behaviour ethical and dependable when it matters most.

questions.question: Which combination best embeds ethical, professional practice across a business?
options: A clear code of conduct, leadership that models it, and fair consequences for breaches
A poster in the lobby and nothing else
Hoping staff behave well with no guidance
questions.expected: A clear code of conduct, leadership that models it, and fair consequences for breaches
questions.memo: Ethics is embedded when there is a clear code, leaders who live it, and consistent, fair consequences — not slogans alone.

BUS.G12.T1.CREATIVE.A1.title: Creative thinking in complex contexts
BUS.G12.T1.CREATIVE.A1.description: Applying creative thinking and advanced problem-solving skills to respond to challenges in dynamic and complex business contexts and case studies, building on the problem-solving cycle and techniques from earlier grades.
BUS.G12.T1.CREATIVE.A1.strand: T1 — Legislation, Human Resources, ethics, creative thinking & business strategies
BUS.G12.T1.CREATIVE.A1.recovery_strategy: Complex problems need creative thinking: generate several options, weigh them against the real business situation, and choose the best. Advanced problem-solving combines techniques rather than relying on one fixed answer.

questions.question: A complex business problem usually has:
options: Several possible solutions to weigh up
Only the answer in a textbook
questions.expected: Several possible solutions to weigh up
questions.memo: Complex problems rarely have a single right answer; they call for generating and weighing several possible solutions.

questions.question: Creative thinking helps a business respond to _________ and changing situations.
questions.expected: complex
questions.memo: Creative thinking is especially valuable when situations are complex and constantly changing.

questions.question: True or false: Advanced problem-solving may combine several creative-thinking techniques.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Tough problems often need more than one technique, combined, to generate and test good solutions.

questions.question: Which of these is a creative-thinking technique?
questions.expected: Brainstorming
questions.memo: Brainstorming generates many ideas freely, making it a creative-thinking technique.

questions.question: A real business situation presented for analysis and solving is called a case _________.
questions.expected: study
questions.memo: A case study presents a real or realistic business situation to analyse and solve, testing applied thinking.

questions.question: True or false: In complex business contexts there is rarely a single 'correct' answer.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Complex contexts usually allow several reasonable responses, so judgement is needed rather than one fixed answer.

questions.question: Sort each approach into helpful or unhelpful for solving a complex problem.

items.text: Insisting there is only one possible answer
Testing ideas against the real situation
Refusing to consider any new idea
Copying last year's plan without thought

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Helpful: generate options, test against reality, combine techniques. Unhelpful: assuming one answer, refusing new ideas, copying blindly.

questions.question: What is a sensible first step when facing a complex business problem?
options: Understand and define the problem fully before solving it
Pick the first idea and act immediately
questions.expected: Understand and define the problem fully before solving it
questions.memo: Defining the problem properly first prevents solving the wrong problem and guides the search for good solutions.

questions.question: Thesis: 'Creative thinking is essential in a dynamic, fast-changing business environment.' Choose the THREE strongest supporting reasons.
questions.thesis: Creative thinking is essential in a dynamic, fast-changing business environment.

pool.text: New problems have no ready-made answers, so fresh ideas are needed
It helps a business adapt faster than competitors
It opens up new opportunities as conditions change
Creative thinking guarantees a business never fails
Brainstorming meetings often have nice biscuits
A changing environment never affects a business

questions.memo: The strong reasons are that new problems need fresh ideas, faster adaptation, and new opportunities. The others overclaim, are irrelevant, or are false.

questions.question: _________ thinking generates fresh options that go beyond the obvious answer.
questions.expected: Creative
questions.memo: Creative thinking deliberately moves beyond the obvious to produce new, useful options.

questions.question: Why might combining several techniques help solve a complex problem?
options: Different techniques surface different ideas and angles
Using more techniques always wastes time
One technique can never produce ideas
questions.expected: Different techniques surface different ideas and angles
questions.memo: Each technique looks at the problem differently, so combining them produces a richer set of possible solutions.

questions.question: True or false: Even for complex problems, ideas should still be evaluated against the real business situation.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: However creative an idea, it must be checked against the business's resources, costs and conditions before being used.

questions.question: Sort each problem into whether routine thinking can solve it or it needs creative thinking.

items.text: Re-ordering stock that has run low
Finding a new market after the main one collapses
Reinventing a product customers no longer want
Responding to a sudden disruptive new technology

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Familiar, repeatable tasks suit routine thinking; new, unfamiliar challenges need creative thinking.

questions.question: What does it mean that a business environment is 'dynamic'?
options: Its conditions change quickly and often
questions.expected: Its conditions change quickly and often
questions.memo: A dynamic environment is one that changes rapidly, so businesses must keep adapting.

questions.question: How does creative thinking help a business cope with rapid change?
options: It finds new ways to adapt, compete and seize opportunities
It freezes the business in place
It removes the need to make decisions
questions.expected: It finds new ways to adapt, compete and seize opportunities
questions.memo: Creative thinking generates the new responses a business needs to adapt and find opportunity when conditions shift.

questions.question: Solving a problem presented in a case _________ tests a learner's ability to apply creative thinking.
questions.expected: study
questions.memo: A case study gives a realistic situation in which to apply problem-solving and creative thinking.

questions.question: A delivery business is hit at once by fuel hikes, a driver shortage and a new rival. What is the best creative-thinking response?
options: Generate and test several combined options (e.g. route software, training, new services) against the real situation
Pick the first idea that comes to mind and ignore the rest
Copy a competitor's plan without checking if it fits
questions.expected: Generate and test several combined options (e.g. route software, training, new services) against the real situation
questions.memo: A complex, multi-part problem calls for generating several ideas, combining them, and testing them against the business's reality.

questions.question: Why is applying a single fixed answer often wrong for a complex business problem?
options: Complex problems have many factors, so one rigid answer usually misses important parts
Fixed answers are always the most creative
Complex problems never have any solution
questions.expected: Complex problems have many factors, so one rigid answer usually misses important parts
questions.memo: Because complex problems involve many interacting factors, a single rigid answer typically overlooks key aspects.

questions.question: Why are advanced problem-solving skills emphasised at Grade 12 level?
options: Real business challenges are complex and changing, so deeper, combined thinking is needed
Because simple recall is all business ever requires
Because problems disappear on their own
Because creativity is banned in business
questions.expected: Real business challenges are complex and changing, so deeper, combined thinking is needed
questions.memo: Grade 12 builds advanced problem-solving because real business problems are complex and dynamic, needing deeper, combined creative thinking.

questions.question: Which process best reflects creative problem-solving in a complex situation?
options: Define the problem, generate many options, test them against reality, then choose and act
Act first and only think if it fails
Choose the cheapest option without thought
Refuse to consider more than one idea
questions.expected: Define the problem, generate many options, test them against reality, then choose and act
questions.memo: Strong creative problem-solving defines the problem, generates options, evaluates them against the real situation, and then implements the best.

BUS.G12.T1.STRATEGY.A1.title: Macro-environment business strategies
BUS.G12.T1.STRATEGY.A1.description: Devising strategies for how a business can respond to challenges of the macro environment, then evaluating them: SWOT-based formulation, implementation and evaluation; integration strategies (forward, backward, horizontal), intensive strategies (market penetration, market and product development), diversification strategies, and defensive strategies (retrenchment, divestiture, liquidation).
BUS.G12.T1.STRATEGY.A1.strand: T1 — Legislation, Human Resources, ethics, creative thinking & business strategies
BUS.G12.T1.STRATEGY.A1.recovery_strategy: Integration = take over another level (supplier = backward, distributor = forward, competitor = horizontal). Intensive = grow current/new products and markets. Diversification = move into new areas. Defensive = cut back (retrench, divest, liquidate).

questions.question: A business taking over its own supplier is using _________ integration.
questions.expected: backward
questions.memo: Backward integration is taking control of a supplier — moving 'back' up the supply chain.

questions.question: A business taking over a distributor or retailer that sells its products is using _________ integration.
questions.expected: forward
questions.memo: Forward integration is taking control of a distributor or retailer — moving 'forward' down the supply chain towards the customer.

questions.question: A business taking over a competitor at the same level is using _________ integration.
questions.expected: horizontal
questions.memo: Horizontal integration is taking over a competitor operating at the same level of the market.

questions.question: True or false: Market penetration means selling more of existing products in existing markets.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Market penetration grows sales of current products in current markets, for example through more advertising or lower prices.

questions.question: Closing a business down completely and selling off all its assets is called _________.
questions.expected: liquidation
questions.memo: Liquidation is a defensive strategy where the business is closed and its assets sold off.

questions.question: A _________ analysis of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats helps a business formulate strategy.
questions.expected: SWOT
questions.memo: A SWOT analysis identifies internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats, guiding strategy.

questions.question: Sort each strategy into its category.

items.text: Selling more of the current product through heavy advertising
Launching a completely new product in a new industry
Buying a competitor at the same level
Entering a new geographic market with the existing product

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Integration takes over suppliers/distributors/competitors; intensive grows current and new products/markets; diversification enters new areas; defensive cuts back.

questions.question: What does market development mean?
options: Selling existing products in new markets
questions.expected: Selling existing products in new markets
questions.memo: Market development takes existing products into new markets — for example new regions or new customer groups.

questions.question: What does product development mean?
options: Creating new or improved products for existing markets
Selling old products in old markets unchanged
questions.expected: Creating new or improved products for existing markets
questions.memo: Product development creates new or improved products aimed at the markets the business already serves.

questions.question: _________ strategies include retrenchment, divestiture and liquidation.
questions.expected: Defensive
questions.memo: Defensive strategies cut a business back — retrenching staff, selling off parts (divestiture) or closing entirely (liquidation).

questions.question: True or false: Diversification means moving into new products and new markets.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Diversification spreads the business into new products and often new markets or industries, reducing reliance on one area.

questions.question: Read both firms' strategies, then decide which each statement matches.

source_a.text: Sales of our existing drinks are flat, so we are advertising harder and cutting prices to sell more of them in the markets we already serve.

source_b.text: Demand has collapsed and we are losing money, so we are retrenching staff and selling off a loss-making division to survive.

statements.text: Is using an intensive (market penetration) strategy
Is using a defensive strategy
Is responding to a challenge in its environment
Is taking over a supplier

questions.expected: s1=a_only, s2=b_only, s3=both, s4=neither
questions.memo: Firm A pushes existing products harder (intensive/penetration); Firm B cuts back to survive (defensive). Both respond to their environment; neither integrates a supplier.

questions.question: Sort each situation by the type of strategy it most calls for.

items.text: A profitable firm wants to expand into new regions
A loss-making firm must cut costs to survive
A firm launches an improved product to win more sales
A firm closes an unprofitable division
A firm enters a new industry to spread risk
A failing firm sells all its assets and shuts down

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Expanding, improving products and entering new industries are growth strategies; cutting costs, closing divisions and liquidating are defensive.

questions.question: A bakery buys the wheat farm that supplies its flour. Which strategy is this?
questions.expected: Backward integration
questions.memo: Taking over a supplier (the farm) is backward integration, securing the bakery's raw materials.

questions.question: When is a defensive strategy most appropriate?
options: When the business is struggling or declining and must cut back to survive
When the business is growing strongly
When demand for its products is rising fast
When it has more orders than it can fill
questions.expected: When the business is struggling or declining and must cut back to survive
questions.memo: Defensive strategies suit a business under pressure that needs to retrench, divest or liquidate to survive.

questions.question: Selling off a part or division of the business is called _________.
questions.expected: divestiture
questions.memo: Divestiture is a defensive strategy where the business sells off a part or division, often to focus or raise cash.

questions.question: Read both struggling firms' plans, then decide which each statement matches.

source_a.text: We will keep the whole business but sell off one loss-making division to raise cash and refocus.

source_b.text: The business cannot be saved, so we will close it entirely and sell all the assets to repay debts.

statements.text: Is using divestiture
Is using liquidation
Is using a defensive strategy
Is expanding into a new market

questions.expected: s1=a_only, s2=b_only, s3=both, s4=neither
questions.memo: Selling one division is divestiture; closing entirely and selling all assets is liquidation. Both are defensive; neither is expansion.

questions.question: A firm's main product is dying and it has cash to invest. Which strategy most directly reduces its reliance on that one product?
options: Diversification into new products or industries
questions.expected: Diversification into new products or industries
questions.memo: Diversifying into new products or industries spreads risk so the firm no longer depends on its declining product.

questions.question: In a market where almost everyone already owns the product, why might market penetration alone be a weak strategy?
options: There is little room left to grow sales in a saturated market, so new markets or products may be needed
Penetration always works in every market
Saturated markets have unlimited new customers
Penetration is illegal in saturated markets
questions.expected: There is little room left to grow sales in a saturated market, so new markets or products may be needed
questions.memo: When a market is saturated, pushing existing products harder yields little; market development or product development may work better.

questions.question: Why should a business evaluate its strategies after implementing them?
options: To compare actual results with what was expected and take corrective action
questions.expected: To compare actual results with what was expected and take corrective action
questions.memo: Strategy evaluation checks whether results match expectations and prompts corrective action where they fall short.

BUS.G12.T2.CSR.A1.title: Social responsibility, CSR & CSI
BUS.G12.T2.CSR.A1.description: Critically examining social responsibility and its implications for business and communities: Corporate Social Responsibility (nature, process, benefits, challenges, components) and Corporate Social Investment (nature, projects, responsible business practice), and meaningfully contributing time and effort to others' well-being.
BUS.G12.T2.CSR.A1.strand: T2 — CSR, human rights, teams, sector & environment, leadership & quality
BUS.G12.T2.CSR.A1.recovery_strategy: CSR = the whole responsible way a business operates (ethics, environment, health and safety). CSI = the specific projects and money a business invests in communities (a part of CSR). Both go beyond what the law requires.

questions.question: What do the letters 'CSR' stand for?
questions.expected: Corporate Social Responsibility
questions.memo: CSR is Corporate Social Responsibility — a business operating responsibly towards society and the environment.

questions.question: What do the letters 'CSI' stand for?
questions.expected: Corporate Social Investment
questions.memo: CSI is Corporate Social Investment — the specific projects and resources a business invests in communities.

questions.question: True or false: Corporate Social Responsibility goes beyond what the law strictly requires.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: CSR is voluntary responsibility beyond the legal minimum — giving back to society and protecting the environment.

questions.question: Funding and running a community school project is an example of corporate social _________.
questions.expected: investment
questions.memo: Specific community projects a business funds, like a school, are Corporate Social Investment (CSI).

questions.question: True or false: CSR can benefit both the business and the community.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Done well, CSR helps the community and also builds the business's reputation, staff morale and customer goodwill.

questions.question: CSR includes caring for the _________, for example by reducing pollution.
questions.expected: environment
questions.memo: Protecting the environment — reducing pollution and waste — is one component of CSR.

questions.question: Sort each example into CSR (broad responsible practice) or CSI (a specific community project).

items.text: Building a clinic for a township
Treating all staff and suppliers fairly
Operating safely and ethically as standard

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: CSR is the overall responsible way of operating; CSI is the specific projects and investments in communities.

questions.question: What is the difference between CSR and CSI?
options: CSR is the overall responsible way a business operates; CSI is the specific community projects it invests in
CSR is illegal; CSI is legal
CSR is only about profit; CSI is only about tax
They are exactly the same thing
questions.expected: CSR is the overall responsible way a business operates; CSI is the specific community projects it invests in
questions.memo: CSR is the broad responsibility; CSI is the concrete investment in projects — CSI is one part of CSR.

questions.question: Thesis: 'A profitable business should invest some of its resources in its community.' Choose the THREE strongest supporting reasons.
questions.thesis: A profitable business should invest some of its resources in its community.

pool.text: It helps address real social needs like education and health
It builds goodwill and a strong reputation
A healthier, more skilled community provides better customers and workers
Investing in the community always bankrupts a business
The CEO enjoys cutting ribbons at events
It is only worth doing if it is legally forced

questions.memo: The strong reasons are meeting real needs, building goodwill, and a stronger community of customers and workers. The others are false, irrelevant or miss the voluntary nature of CSR.

questions.question: A key benefit of CSR to a business is an improved _________.
questions.expected: reputation
questions.memo: Visible responsibility improves a business's reputation, which helps attract customers, staff and partners.
