questions.question: What is a challenge of CSR for a business?
options: It costs money and time that must be balanced against other needs
It always makes an instant profit with no cost
It is completely free to run
questions.expected: It costs money and time that must be balanced against other needs
questions.memo: CSR requires real resources — money, time and effort — which the business must balance against its other priorities.

questions.question: True or false: CSI projects can help address human-rights issues in a community.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: CSI projects — such as supporting education, health or access for people with disabilities — can advance human rights in a community.

questions.question: Sort each outcome into whether it mainly benefits the business or the community.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Reputation, loyalty and morale mainly benefit the business; schooling, a cleaner environment and jobs mainly benefit the community — though the two often overlap.

questions.question: Which of these is a component of CSR?
options: Caring for the environment, health and safety, and acting ethically
questions.expected: Caring for the environment, health and safety, and acting ethically
questions.memo: CSR components include environmental care, health and safety, and ethical conduct.

questions.question: What does responsible business practice involve over the longer term?
options: Meeting the longer-term needs of the society in which the business operates
Focusing only on this month's profit
questions.expected: Meeting the longer-term needs of the society in which the business operates
questions.memo: Responsible business practice considers the long-term well-being of society, not just immediate profit.

questions.question: Meaningfully contributing _________ and effort helps advance the well-being of others.
questions.expected: time
questions.memo: Giving time and effort — not only money — is part of contributing meaningfully to others' well-being.

questions.question: A company wants its CSI to make a real, lasting difference. Which project fits best?
options: A skills-training centre that helps locals find lasting employment
A one-off photo opportunity with no follow-up
A donation announced loudly but never paid
A project that benefits only the executives
questions.expected: A skills-training centre that helps locals find lasting employment
questions.memo: Lasting CSI builds capacity — like a skills centre — rather than one-off gestures that fade quickly.

questions.question: How should one critically evaluate CSR that is used mainly for publicity?
options: Genuine CSR creates real, lasting benefit; CSR used only for image risks being seen as 'window-dressing'
Publicity is the only purpose of CSR
questions.expected: Genuine CSR creates real, lasting benefit; CSR used only for image risks being seen as 'window-dressing'
questions.memo: CSR should be judged by real impact; doing it only for publicity, without lasting benefit, can backfire as hollow 'window-dressing'.

questions.question: Why can CSR support a business's long-term success, not just its image?
options: A healthier, more skilled, more stable community provides better customers, workers and operating conditions
Because CSR removes the need to make any profit
Because society has no link to business
questions.expected: A healthier, more skilled, more stable community provides better customers, workers and operating conditions
questions.memo: Investing in the community strengthens the very base of customers, workers and conditions the business depends on for long-term success.

questions.question: How are CSR and CSI best understood together?
options: CSI (specific community projects) is one way a business puts its broader CSR into practice
CSR and CSI have nothing in common
CSR is only for charities and CSI only for governments
questions.expected: CSI (specific community projects) is one way a business puts its broader CSR into practice
questions.memo: CSR is the broad responsibility; CSI is a concrete part of it — the projects through which a business acts on that responsibility.

BUS.G12.T2.HUMANRIGHTS.A1.title: Human rights, inclusivity & environment
BUS.G12.T2.HUMANRIGHTS.A1.description: Evaluating the extent to which a business venture addresses human rights (as defined in the Constitution), inclusivity (diversity of poverty, inequality, race, gender, language, age, disability) and environmental issues (protecting the environment and human health), and assessing a venture against these criteria.
BUS.G12.T2.HUMANRIGHTS.A1.strand: T2 — CSR, human rights, teams, sector & environment, leadership & quality
BUS.G12.T2.HUMANRIGHTS.A1.caps_topic: Human rights, inclusivity and environmental issues
BUS.G12.T2.HUMANRIGHTS.A1.recovery_strategy: Human rights = equality, dignity, fair treatment of people. Inclusivity = welcoming diversity (gender, race, disability, age, language). Environmental issues = protecting nature and human health. Judge a venture against all three.

questions.question: Which of these are human rights protected by the Constitution?
questions.expected: Equality, dignity and fair treatment
questions.memo: The Constitution protects rights such as equality, human dignity and fair treatment, which businesses must respect.

questions.question: _________ means welcoming and accommodating diversity such as race, gender, age and disability.
questions.expected: Inclusivity
questions.memo: Inclusivity means valuing and accommodating people of all backgrounds and abilities in the workplace.

questions.question: True or false: Protecting the environment and human health is an issue businesses are expected to address.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Businesses are expected to protect the environment and human health, for example by limiting pollution and waste.

questions.question: Which of these is an inclusivity issue a business should consider?
options: The colour of the company car
The wording of a price tag
questions.expected: Access for people with disabilities
questions.memo: Ensuring access for people with disabilities is part of building an inclusive, diverse workplace.

questions.question: Treating every person fairly and with _________ upholds their human dignity.
questions.expected: respect
questions.memo: Respecting people — treating them fairly and valuing them — upholds the human right to dignity.

questions.question: True or false: A business venture can be assessed against human-rights, inclusivity and environmental criteria.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A venture can and should be judged on how well it respects human rights, includes diverse people and protects the environment.

questions.question: Sort each issue into human rights, inclusivity or environment.

items.text: Treating all employees with equal dignity
Making the workplace accessible to disabled staff
Hiring across all races, genders and ages

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Dignity and non-discrimination are human rights; accessibility and diverse hiring are inclusivity; reducing pollution and recycling are environmental.

questions.question: How does a business respect human rights in the workplace?
options: By treating staff fairly, avoiding discrimination and providing safe conditions
By paying staff as little as possible
By ignoring safety to cut costs
By favouring only one group of people
questions.expected: By treating staff fairly, avoiding discrimination and providing safe conditions
questions.memo: Respecting human rights means fair treatment, no unfair discrimination and safe working conditions for everyone.

questions.question: Build a 3-part explanation of why a business should address human rights and inclusivity.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-part explanation of why a business should address human rights and inclusivity.

options.text: A business should address human rights and inclusivity because every person deserves fair, dignified treatment
A business should address them only when it is sued
A business should ignore human rights to save money
An inclusive, fair workplace draws on a wider pool of talent and ideas
Discrimination has no effect on staff or customers
Excluding people improves a business's reputation
Respecting rights and including everyone builds trust, talent and a stronger reputation, while meeting legal and moral duties
Respecting rights has no benefit and only costs money
Inclusivity drives all customers away

questions.memo: Claim: everyone deserves fair, dignified treatment. Evidence: inclusivity widens talent and ideas. Explanation: it builds trust, talent and reputation while meeting legal and moral duties.

questions.question: _________ is the variety of people — by race, gender, age, language and ability — in a workplace.
questions.expected: Diversity
questions.memo: Diversity is the range of different people in a workplace; inclusivity is about welcoming and accommodating that diversity.

questions.question: Which is an environmental measure a business can take?
options: Reducing pollution and managing waste to protect health
Dumping waste into a river to save money
Wasting as much water as possible
questions.expected: Reducing pollution and managing waste to protect health
questions.memo: Reducing pollution and properly managing waste protects both the environment and human health.

questions.question: True or false: Inclusivity can benefit a business by widening its talent pool and its markets.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: An inclusive business attracts talent from everywhere and connects with a broader range of customers.

questions.question: Sort each business action into whether it supports or violates human rights and inclusivity.

items.text: Refusing to hire people of a certain race
Harassing staff who speak a different language
Promoting on merit regardless of gender
Paying women less for the same job

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Equal pay, accessibility and merit-based promotion support rights and inclusivity; discrimination, harassment and unequal pay violate them.

questions.question: How can a business make its workplace more inclusive?
options: Accommodate diversity and give everyone equal opportunity
Hire only one type of person
Make the building hard to access
questions.expected: Accommodate diversity and give everyone equal opportunity
questions.memo: Inclusive workplaces accommodate diverse needs and offer equal opportunity to all.

questions.question: Equality and dignity in business mean that:
options: All people are treated fairly and with respect
Some groups may be treated unfairly
questions.expected: All people are treated fairly and with respect
questions.memo: Equality and dignity require that everyone — staff, customers and the community — is treated fairly and respectfully.

questions.question: Installing a wheelchair ramp improves _________ for staff and customers with disabilities.
questions.expected: access
questions.memo: A ramp improves physical access, helping make the business inclusive for people with disabilities.

questions.question: A new venture hires diversely and treats staff fairly, but dumps untreated waste into a local stream. How should it be assessed?
options: Strong on rights and inclusivity, but failing on the environmental criterion
It cannot be assessed at all
questions.expected: Strong on rights and inclusivity, but failing on the environmental criterion
questions.memo: Assessing against all three criteria shows it does well on rights and inclusivity but fails on the environment, which it must fix.

questions.question: Why is it not enough for a venture to create jobs if it also seriously harms the environment?
options: A full assessment weighs all criteria, and serious environmental harm damages health and the community the business depends on
Jobs cancel out any amount of pollution
The environment is never relevant to business
Only profit should ever be measured
questions.expected: A full assessment weighs all criteria, and serious environmental harm damages health and the community the business depends on
questions.memo: Creating jobs is positive, but a venture must also protect the environment and health; serious harm undermines the community and fails a key criterion.

questions.question: Why is inclusivity often described as good for business, not just the right thing to do?
options: Diverse teams bring more ideas and reach more customers, strengthening the business
Inclusivity always reduces a business's customers
questions.expected: Diverse teams bring more ideas and reach more customers, strengthening the business
questions.memo: Beyond being right, inclusivity brings varied perspectives and connects the business to a wider market, which strengthens it.

questions.question: Which plan best addresses human rights, inclusivity and the environment together?
options: Fair, non-discriminatory employment; accessible facilities; and cleaner, less wasteful operations
Hire one group only and ignore pollution
Maximise waste but treat staff well
Focus on profit and ignore all three
questions.expected: Fair, non-discriminatory employment; accessible facilities; and cleaner, less wasteful operations
questions.memo: A strong plan covers all three: fair employment (rights), accessible and diverse workplaces (inclusivity), and cleaner operations (environment).

BUS.G12.T2.TEAM.A1.title: Team performance & conflict management
BUS.G12.T2.TEAM.A1.description: Collaborating to achieve objectives: criteria for successful team performance, self- and team-assessment against those criteria, performing a specific role in a team, problem-solving when working with others, correct procedures to deal with grievances, and ways of dealing with difficult people.
BUS.G12.T2.TEAM.A1.strand: T2 — CSR, human rights, teams, sector & environment, leadership & quality
BUS.G12.T2.TEAM.A1.recovery_strategy: Successful teams share clear goals, trust, communication and commitment. Handle grievances through the correct steps (raise it, discuss, escalate if unresolved). Deal with difficult people calmly and professionally.

questions.question: Which of these is a criterion for successful team performance?
questions.expected: Clear, shared goals
questions.memo: Successful teams share clear goals, along with trust, open communication and commitment.

questions.question: A formal complaint raised by an employee about a workplace problem is called a _________.
questions.expected: grievance
questions.memo: A grievance is an employee's formal complaint, which should be handled through the correct procedure.

questions.question: True or false: Collaboration means working together towards shared objectives.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Collaboration is people working together, combining effort and skills to achieve common objectives.

questions.question: What is the best way to deal with a difficult colleague?
options: Stay calm, professional and address the issue respectfully
Shout at them in front of others
Refuse to ever speak to them
questions.expected: Stay calm, professional and address the issue respectfully
questions.memo: Difficult people are best handled by staying calm and professional and addressing the real issue respectfully.

questions.question: _________-assessment means judging your own performance against the team's criteria.
questions.expected: Self
questions.memo: Self-assessment is honestly judging your own contribution and performance against agreed criteria.

questions.question: True or false: Good teams share trust and open communication.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Trust and open communication are essential criteria for a team to perform well together.

questions.question: Put the steps of a fair grievance procedure in order.

items.text: The employee raises the grievance formally
The grievance is discussed with the supervisor
If unresolved, it is escalated to higher management
A decision is made and recorded

questions.expected: raise, discuss, escalate, resolve
questions.memo: A grievance is raised, discussed with the supervisor, escalated if unresolved, then decided and recorded.

questions.question: Sort each item into a criterion for good teamwork or a barrier to it.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Trust, shared goals and commitment are criteria for good teamwork; poor communication, prejudice and unresolved conflict are barriers.

questions.question: How does a member perform their specific role well in a team?
options: Understand the role and deliver their part reliably and on time
Do whatever they feel like ignoring the team
Leave their tasks for others to finish
questions.expected: Understand the role and deliver their part reliably and on time
questions.memo: Performing a role well means knowing what is expected and reliably delivering it so the team can succeed.

questions.question: Team _________ assessment judges the team's work against the agreed criteria.
questions.expected: performance
questions.memo: Team performance assessment measures how well the team meets criteria such as goals, communication and trust.

questions.question: What is a constructive way to handle conflict within a team?
options: Address the issue calmly through the correct procedure and seek a fair solution
Let it fester until the team breaks up
Pick sides and ignore the facts
questions.expected: Address the issue calmly through the correct procedure and seek a fair solution
questions.memo: Conflict is best handled by addressing it calmly and fairly through proper procedures, aiming for a workable solution.

questions.question: True or false: Ignoring an employee's grievance is the best way to handle it.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Ignoring a grievance lets the problem grow and breaks trust; it should be addressed through the correct procedure.

questions.question: Sort each approach into helpful or unhelpful when dealing with a difficult team member.

items.text: Focusing on the behaviour, not the person

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Listening, focusing on behaviour and agreeing expectations help; humiliating, excluding and retaliating make things worse.

questions.question: Why is it useful to assess a team's performance against criteria?
options: It identifies the team's strengths and where it must improve
It guarantees the team never changes
It hides problems from the manager
It removes the need for any goals
questions.expected: It identifies the team's strengths and where it must improve
questions.memo: Assessment against criteria highlights what the team does well and where it needs to improve.

questions.question: What is a good approach to solving a problem that arises from working in a team?
options: Involve the members, discuss openly and agree a shared solution
Have one person decide secretly and tell no one
Ignore the problem and hope it disappears
questions.expected: Involve the members, discuss openly and agree a shared solution
questions.memo: Team problems are best solved by involving members, discussing openly and agreeing a solution everyone supports.

questions.question: Clear _________ help every team member know what the team is trying to achieve.
questions.expected: goals
questions.memo: Clear, shared goals give the team direction and a common purpose to work towards.

questions.question: Put the steps of solving a problem that arises in a team in a sensible order.

items.text: Identify the problem affecting the team
Discuss it openly with the members
Act, then review whether it worked

questions.expected: identify, discuss, agree, review
questions.memo: Identify the problem, discuss it with the team, agree a shared solution, then act and review the outcome.

questions.question: A skilled team member constantly criticises others and misses deadlines, hurting team morale. What is the best response?
options: Speak to them privately, set clear expectations and follow up
Ignore it because they are skilled
Criticise them loudly in the next meeting
Quietly remove all their work without telling them
questions.expected: Speak to them privately, set clear expectations and follow up
questions.memo: A private, respectful conversation that sets clear expectations and is followed up addresses the behaviour without damaging the team further.

questions.question: Why does effective collaboration help a team achieve its objectives?
options: Members combine their strengths and cover each other's gaps towards a shared goal
Working alone is always faster than any team
Collaboration removes the need for any goals
Sharing work guarantees no one is accountable
questions.expected: Members combine their strengths and cover each other's gaps towards a shared goal
questions.memo: Collaboration lets members pool their different strengths and support one another, which helps the team meet objectives it could not reach alone.

questions.question: Two team members have a serious disagreement that is blocking the project. Which response best combines conflict management and problem-solving?
options: Bring them together, identify the real cause, agree a fair way forward and follow up
Tell them to sort it out alone with no support
Side immediately with the more senior person
Reassign the whole project to avoid the issue
questions.expected: Bring them together, identify the real cause, agree a fair way forward and follow up
questions.memo: Combining conflict management and problem-solving means surfacing the real cause, agreeing a fair solution together, and checking it holds.

BUS.G12.T2.SECTORENV.A1.title: Business sector and its environment
BUS.G12.T2.SECTORENV.A1.description: Selecting a business from each economic sector and describing the three business environments related to those sectors and the extent to which a business can control each environment.
BUS.G12.T2.SECTORENV.A1.strand: T2 — CSR, human rights, teams, sector & environment, leadership & quality
BUS.G12.T2.SECTORENV.A1.recovery_strategy: Whatever the sector (primary, secondary, tertiary), the rule holds: full control of the micro environment, influence over the market, no control over the macro environment.

questions.question: A gold mine belongs to which sector?
questions.expected: Primary
questions.memo: A mine extracts raw materials, so it is a primary-sector business.

questions.question: How much control does a business have over its micro environment?
questions.expected: Full control
questions.memo: The micro environment is inside the business — its mission, structure, resources and culture — so the business controls it fully, in any sector.

questions.question: True or false: A business has no control over its macro environment, whatever its sector.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The macro environment is beyond any business's control, regardless of whether it is primary, secondary or tertiary.

questions.question: A bank belongs to the _________ sector.
questions.expected: tertiary
questions.memo: A bank provides a service, so it is a tertiary-sector business.

questions.question: A car-assembly factory belongs to the _________ sector.
questions.expected: secondary
questions.memo: A factory processes materials into products, making it a secondary-sector business.

questions.question: True or false: In every sector, a business can influence but not control its market environment.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Across all sectors, the market environment can only be influenced (e.g. by advertising or negotiating), not controlled.

questions.question: Sort each business into the correct sector.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Farms and fishing extract (primary); factories and mills process (secondary); travel agencies and brokers serve (tertiary).

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes a business's control across the three environments?
options: Full control of the micro, influence over the market, no control of the macro
Full control of all three environments
Control of the macro but not the micro
questions.expected: Full control of the micro, influence over the market, no control of the macro
questions.memo: Control decreases outward: full (micro), influence (market), none (macro) — the same in every sector.

questions.question: Read both businesses, then decide which each statement matches.

source_a.text: We are a wheat farm in the primary sector. We control how we run the farm, but we cannot control rainfall or world grain prices.

source_b.text: We are a logistics company in the tertiary sector. We control our own operations, but we cannot control the fuel price or new transport laws.

statements.text: Operates in the primary sector
Operates in the tertiary sector
Cannot control its macro environment
Can control the national economy

questions.expected: s1=a_only, s2=b_only, s3=both, s4=neither
questions.memo: The farm is primary, the logistics firm tertiary; both control their micro environment but not the macro, and neither controls the economy.

questions.question: A business can _________ its market environment but not control it.
questions.expected: influence
questions.memo: The market environment can be influenced through actions like advertising and negotiation, but not controlled.

questions.question: Why does the same control rule apply to businesses in all three sectors?
options: The three environments work the same way no matter what a business produces or sells
Sectors change the laws of the macro environment
questions.expected: The three environments work the same way no matter what a business produces or sells
questions.memo: Whatever a business makes or sells, its micro is controllable, its market influenceable and its macro uncontrollable.

questions.question: True or false: A primary-sector mine can control global commodity prices.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Global commodity prices are a macro force; even a large mine cannot control them — it can only adapt.

questions.question: Sort each factor by how much control a tertiary retailer has over it.

items.text: Its own store layout and staff

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Store layout and pricing are micro; suppliers and competitors are market; interest rates and laws are macro.

questions.question: Which is a macro-environment factor that could affect a tertiary tourism business?
options: A change in the exchange rate affecting foreign visitors
Its own choice of staff uniforms
The layout of its reception desk
questions.expected: A change in the exchange rate affecting foreign visitors
questions.memo: The exchange rate is a macro force the tourism business cannot control but must adapt to; the others are internal (micro).

questions.question: How does a business in any sector respond to its macro environment?
options: By adapting, since it cannot control macro forces
By controlling the macro forces directly
By passing laws to change them
questions.expected: By adapting, since it cannot control macro forces
questions.memo: Because macro forces are beyond control, a business in any sector responds by adapting its own plans.

questions.question: The _________ environment is the one inside the business that it controls fully.
questions.expected: micro
questions.memo: The micro environment — vision, structure, resources, culture — is internal and fully controlled by the business.

questions.question: Read both businesses, then decide which each statement matches.

source_a.text: Our steel mill (secondary sector) can decide how we run our plant, and we negotiate hard with suppliers, but new import tariffs are out of our hands.

source_b.text: Our accounting firm (tertiary sector) controls how we serve clients and which software we use, but we cannot control new tax legislation.

statements.text: Negotiates with suppliers (a market-environment action)
Provides a professional service to clients
Controls its own internal operations
Can control national legislation

questions.expected: s1=a_only, s2=b_only, s3=both, s4=neither
questions.memo: The mill influences suppliers (market); the firm serves clients; both control their micro operations; neither controls legislation (macro).

questions.question: A learner claims, 'A big enough company in any sector can eventually control its macro environment.' How is this best evaluated?
options: Incorrect — no business, however large, controls the macro environment; it can only influence and adapt
Correct — size grants full macro control
Correct, but only in the primary sector
questions.expected: Incorrect — no business, however large, controls the macro environment; it can only influence and adapt
questions.memo: Size may give influence (e.g. lobbying), but the macro environment remains beyond control for every business and sector.

questions.question: Why is it useful to compare a primary, a secondary and a tertiary business when studying the environments?
options: It shows the control rule holds across sectors, even though the specific factors differ
It proves each sector controls a different environment fully
It shows only one sector has a macro environment
It removes the need to study the environments
questions.expected: It shows the control rule holds across sectors, even though the specific factors differ
questions.memo: Comparing sectors demonstrates that the micro/market/macro control pattern is universal, while the particular factors vary by business.

questions.question: A tertiary delivery firm faces rising fuel prices, tough competitors and outdated vehicles. How should it map these to the environments?
options: Fuel prices = macro (adapt), competitors = market (influence), vehicles = micro (control)
All three are macro and uncontrollable
All three are micro and fully controlled
questions.expected: Fuel prices = macro (adapt), competitors = market (influence), vehicles = micro (control)
questions.memo: Fuel prices are macro (adapt), competitors are market (influence), and its own vehicles are micro (control) — the standard pattern.

BUS.G12.T2.MGMTLEAD.A1.title: Management & leadership
BUS.G12.T2.MGMTLEAD.A1.description: Differentiating between management and leadership styles and approaches: the difference between leadership and management, leadership styles (democratic, autocratic, laissez-faire), theories of management and leadership (situational, transactional, transformational), and the role of personal attitude in success and leadership.
BUS.G12.T2.MGMTLEAD.A1.strand: T2 — CSR, human rights, teams, sector & environment, leadership & quality
BUS.G12.T2.MGMTLEAD.A1.recovery_strategy: Management = planning, organising and controlling the work. Leadership = inspiring and influencing people toward a vision. Autocratic leaders decide alone; democratic leaders involve the team; laissez-faire leaders are hands-off.

questions.question: What is the main difference between management and leadership?
options: Management organises the work; leadership inspires and guides people
They are exactly the same thing
questions.expected: Management organises the work; leadership inspires and guides people
questions.memo: Management is about planning, organising and controlling tasks; leadership is about inspiring and influencing people toward a vision.

questions.question: An autocratic leader mainly:
options: Makes decisions alone and tells the team what to do
questions.expected: Makes decisions alone and tells the team what to do
questions.memo: An autocratic leader keeps decision-making to themselves and directs the team.

questions.question: A _________ leader involves the team in making decisions.
questions.expected: democratic
questions.memo: A democratic leader consults the team and involves them in decisions.

questions.question: True or false: Leadership is about inspiring and influencing people towards a vision.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Leadership focuses on inspiring, motivating and influencing people to pursue a shared vision.

questions.question: A laissez-faire leadership style is best described as:
options: Hands-off, leaving staff to make their own decisions
questions.expected: Hands-off, leaving staff to make their own decisions
questions.memo: Laissez-faire leaders take a hands-off approach, giving staff freedom to decide how to do their work.

questions.question: _________ leadership inspires major change and motivates people beyond their normal expectations.
questions.expected: Transformational
questions.memo: Transformational leadership inspires people with a vision and motivates them to achieve more than expected.

questions.question: Sort each activity into management or leadership.

items.text: Inspiring the team with a vision
Motivating staff to give their best

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Scheduling, budgeting and organising are management tasks; inspiring, motivating and influencing are leadership.

questions.question: In which situation is an autocratic style often most useful?
options: An urgent crisis where fast, clear decisions are needed
questions.expected: An urgent crisis where fast, clear decisions are needed
questions.memo: Autocratic leadership suits crises where quick, decisive direction matters more than wide consultation.

questions.question: Read both leaders, then decide which each statement matches.

source_a.text: I make the decisions and expect my team to carry them out without debate. It is faster this way.

source_b.text: I gather my team's views and we decide together. People are more committed when they have a say.

statements.text: Uses an autocratic style
Uses a democratic style
Is in a leadership position
Refuses to make any decision ever

questions.expected: s1=a_only, s2=b_only, s3=both, s4=neither
questions.memo: Leader A decides alone (autocratic); Leader B involves the team (democratic). Both lead; neither refuses all decisions.

questions.question: _________ leadership adapts its style to fit the situation and the people involved.
questions.expected: Situational
questions.memo: Situational leadership changes its approach depending on the task, the team and the circumstances.

questions.question: Transactional leadership mainly motivates people through:
options: Rewards for good performance and consequences for poor performance
questions.expected: Rewards for good performance and consequences for poor performance
questions.memo: Transactional leadership works through exchanges — rewarding good performance and correcting poor performance.

questions.question: True or false: A positive personal attitude supports good leadership.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A leader's positive attitude influences the team's morale and is linked to success in leadership.

questions.question: Sort each description under the leadership style it fits.

items.text: The leader decides alone and directs the team
The leader consults the team before deciding
The leader lets staff decide for themselves
Strict control with little input from staff

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Deciding alone = autocratic; consulting the team = democratic; hands-off = laissez-faire.

questions.question: What is the difference between transactional and transformational leadership?
options: Transactional uses rewards and rules; transformational inspires change through a vision
Transactional avoids all targets; transformational sets none
questions.expected: Transactional uses rewards and rules; transformational inspires change through a vision
questions.memo: Transactional leadership runs on rewards and consequences; transformational leadership inspires people to embrace change and a shared vision.

questions.question: In which situation does a democratic style usually work well?
options: When team input is valuable and there is time to consult
When a decision is needed in seconds during a crisis
When no one in the team has any knowledge
When the leader wants to avoid all input
questions.expected: When team input is valuable and there is time to consult
questions.memo: Democratic leadership suits situations where the team's knowledge adds value and there is time to involve them.

questions.question: Management mainly focuses on planning, organising and _________.
questions.expected: controlling
questions.memo: The management tasks are planning, organising, leading/activating and controlling the work.

questions.question: Read two managers handling a sudden safety emergency, then decide which each statement matches.

source_a.text: During the gas leak I gave clear, direct orders immediately and everyone followed them. There was no time for discussion.

source_b.text: For our new product strategy I held workshops, gathered ideas from the whole team and we shaped the plan together.

statements.text: Used an autocratic style suited to a crisis
Used a democratic style suited to a creative task
Chose a style to fit the situation
Failed to make any decision

questions.expected: s1=a_only, s2=b_only, s3=both, s4=neither
questions.memo: Manager A was autocratic in a crisis; Manager B democratic for a creative task. Both matched their style to the situation; neither failed to decide.

questions.question: A manager keeps every decision to themselves even for creative, long-term projects, and staff feel unmotivated. How is this best evaluated?
options: The autocratic style is poorly matched here; a more democratic style would likely raise motivation
Autocratic is always the best style for everything
The staff are simply wrong to feel demotivated
questions.expected: The autocratic style is poorly matched here; a more democratic style would likely raise motivation
questions.memo: Style should fit the situation; for creative, long-term work, involving the team (democratic) usually lifts motivation more than strict autocratic control.

questions.question: Why is matching leadership style to the situation important?
options: Different situations call for different approaches, and the right style improves results and morale
One fixed style is always best in every case
Style has no effect on a team
Leaders should change style at random
questions.expected: Different situations call for different approaches, and the right style improves results and morale
questions.memo: Situational leadership recognises that the best style depends on the task and people; matching them improves both results and morale.

questions.question: How do strong management and strong leadership together benefit a business?
options: Management keeps work organised and controlled, while leadership inspires people towards the vision
Only one is ever needed at a time
questions.expected: Management keeps work organised and controlled, while leadership inspires people towards the vision
questions.memo: A business needs both: management to organise and control the work, and leadership to inspire and guide people towards its goals.

BUS.G12.T2.QUALITY.A1.title: Quality of performance & TQM
BUS.G12.T2.QUALITY.A1.description: How the quality of performance within the business functions influences the success or failure of a business: the concept of quality, its relation to the various functions, and the elements of Total Quality Management (TQM) — continuous skills development, total client satisfaction and continuous improvement of processes and systems.
BUS.G12.T2.QUALITY.A1.strand: T2 — CSR, human rights, teams, sector & environment, leadership & quality
BUS.G12.T2.QUALITY.A1.recovery_strategy: TQM means everyone in every function continuously improves quality: total client satisfaction, ongoing skills development and constant improvement of processes and systems. Poor quality in any function can sink the business.

questions.question: What does 'quality' mean in business?
options: Meeting or exceeding the standards customers expect
Producing as much as possible regardless of standards
questions.expected: Meeting or exceeding the standards customers expect
questions.memo: Quality is about meeting or exceeding the standards and expectations of customers.

questions.question: TQM stands for Total _________ Management.
questions.expected: Quality
questions.memo: TQM is Total Quality Management — a whole-business approach to continuously improving quality.

questions.question: True or false: Quality applies to every business function, not just production.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Quality matters in every function — finance, HR, marketing, admin — not only in making the product.

questions.question: Which of these is an element of Total Quality Management?
questions.expected: Continuous improvement of processes
questions.memo: Continuous improvement of processes and systems is a core element of TQM.

questions.question: Total client _________ is one of the elements of TQM.
questions.expected: satisfaction
questions.memo: Total client satisfaction — fully meeting customers' needs — is a key element of TQM.

questions.question: True or false: Poor quality can contribute to the failure of a business.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Poor quality drives away customers, raises costs through returns and damages reputation, which can lead to failure.

questions.question: Sort each item into whether it is a TQM element or not.

items.text: Continuous improvement of processes and systems
Doing a task right once and never reviewing it

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: TQM elements include continuous skills development, total client satisfaction and continuous improvement. Ignoring complaints or cutting quality are not.

questions.question: How does high quality of performance support business success?
options: It satisfies customers, reduces returns and builds a strong reputation
It guarantees the business pays no tax
It removes the need for any customers
questions.expected: It satisfies customers, reduces returns and builds a strong reputation
questions.memo: Good quality keeps customers happy, cuts the cost of returns and rework, and builds the reputation that drives future sales.

questions.question: Thesis: 'Quality must be managed across all business functions, not just production.' Choose the THREE strongest supporting reasons.
questions.thesis: Quality must be managed across all business functions, not just production.

pool.text: Poor quality in finance, admin or service also loses customers and money
Customers judge the whole experience, not only the product
Weakness in one function can drag down the whole business
Only the production line ever affects customers
Quality posters look nice on the wall
Quality is a one-time task that never needs reviewing

questions.memo: The strong reasons are that poor quality anywhere loses money, customers judge the whole experience, and one weak function harms the whole. The others are false or irrelevant.

questions.question: Continuous _________ development keeps staff skilled and is part of TQM.
questions.expected: skills
questions.memo: Continuous skills development keeps the workforce capable of delivering and improving quality — a TQM element.

questions.question: What does quality look like in the finance function?
questions.expected: Accurate, reliable financial records
questions.memo: Quality in finance means accurate, reliable records and reporting — errors here harm the whole business.

questions.question: True or false: TQM is a once-off project that is finished and then forgotten.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: TQM is ongoing — it is about continuous improvement, not a single completed task.

questions.question: Sort each example of quality under the business function it belongs to.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Defect-free, consistent goods = production quality; accurate, timely records and payments = finance quality; skilled staff and fair recruitment = HR quality.

questions.question: What is a likely impact of consistently poor quality?
options: Returns, lost customers and higher costs
questions.expected: Returns, lost customers and higher costs
questions.memo: Poor quality causes returns, drives customers away and raises costs through rework — the opposite of what a business needs.

questions.question: How does the need for quality differ between a sole trader and a large business?
options: Both need quality, but a large business needs formal systems to maintain it across many staff
Neither needs to worry about quality
questions.expected: Both need quality, but a large business needs formal systems to maintain it across many staff
questions.memo: Every business needs quality; a large business relies on formal quality systems to keep standards consistent across many people and sites.

questions.question: Continuous _________ of processes and systems is a key TQM element.
questions.expected: improvement
questions.memo: TQM relies on continuously improving processes and systems so quality keeps rising over time.

questions.question: A well-made product is ruined by slow, rude service and billing errors. How does this affect the business?
options: Quality failures in service and finance can still drive customers away despite the good product
Nothing changes, because the product is good
questions.expected: Quality failures in service and finance can still drive customers away despite the good product
questions.memo: Because customers judge the whole experience, poor service and billing can lose them even when the product itself is excellent.

questions.question: A manager wants to cut quality checks to save money. How should this be evaluated?
options: Risky — short-term savings can be outweighed by returns, lost customers and reputational damage
Always a good idea with no downside
questions.expected: Risky — short-term savings can be outweighed by returns, lost customers and reputational damage
questions.memo: Cutting quality control may save a little now but often costs far more later through defects, returns and lost trust.

questions.question: Why does TQM treat quality as everyone's responsibility?
options: Because quality depends on every function and person, so all must continuously improve
Because quality is fixed and cannot change
Because customers do not notice quality
questions.expected: Because quality depends on every function and person, so all must continuously improve
questions.memo: TQM recognises that quality is created across every function, so it makes continuous improvement everyone's job.

questions.question: How does consistent quality of performance influence whether a business succeeds or fails?
options: High quality builds loyalty and reputation that drive success; poor quality erodes them towards failure
Quality has no link to success or failure
questions.expected: High quality builds loyalty and reputation that drive success; poor quality erodes them towards failure
questions.memo: Quality is a major driver of success: it builds the loyalty and reputation a business depends on, while poor quality steadily undermines them.

BUS.G12.T3.SECURITIES.A1.title: Investment: securities
BUS.G12.T3.SECURITIES.A1.description: A range of business investment opportunities: business investments and the JSE, types of shares, unit trusts and government retail bonds; returns such as dividends and interest; and calculations including the difference between simple and compound interest.
BUS.G12.T3.SECURITIES.A1.recovery_strategy: Simple interest is on the original amount only; compound interest is on the amount plus past interest, so it grows faster. Shares pay dividends (a share of profit); savings and bonds pay interest. Unit trusts spread money across many investments.

questions.question: The JSE is the Johannesburg _________ Exchange, where shares are bought and sold.
questions.expected: Stock
questions.memo: The JSE (Johannesburg Stock Exchange) is the market where shares in listed companies are traded.

questions.question: What does owning a share in a company give you?
questions.expected: Part-ownership of the company
questions.memo: A share represents part-ownership of a company, entitling the holder to a share of profits (dividends).

questions.question: True or false: Shares can pay their owners dividends.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Companies may pay dividends — a share of their profit — to shareholders.

questions.question: _________ interest is calculated only on the original amount invested.
questions.expected: Simple
questions.memo: Simple interest is worked out only on the original principal, the same amount each period.

questions.question: Compound interest is calculated on:
options: The original amount plus the interest already earned
questions.expected: The original amount plus the interest already earned
questions.memo: Compound interest is calculated on the principal plus accumulated interest, so it grows faster than simple interest.

questions.question: True or false: A government retail bond is a form of investment.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A government retail bond is a relatively safe investment in which you lend money to the government and earn interest.

questions.question: Sort each item into the type of investment it describes.

items.text: Part-ownership of a single listed company
A pooled fund spread across many investments
Lending money to the government for interest
Earns dividends when the company profits
Managed by a fund manager on investors' behalf

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Shares = part-ownership earning dividends; unit trusts = pooled, managed funds; government retail bonds = lending to the state for interest.

questions.question: What is the difference between dividends and interest?
options: Dividends are a share of a company's profit; interest is a reward for lending or saving money
Dividends are paid on savings; interest is paid on shares
Neither is a form of return
questions.expected: Dividends are a share of a company's profit; interest is a reward for lending or saving money
questions.memo: Shares earn dividends (a portion of profit); savings and bonds earn interest (a reward for lending money).

questions.question: What is the simple interest on R5 000 invested at 10% per year for 2 years?
questions.memo: Simple interest = R5 000 × 10% × 2 = R500 × 2 = R1 000.

questions.question: A _________ trust pools many investors' money to buy a spread of shares and other assets.
questions.expected: unit
questions.memo: A unit trust pools investors' money, which a fund manager spreads across many investments to reduce risk.

questions.question: Why does compound interest grow an investment faster than simple interest?
options: Because the interest itself earns further interest over time
Because it ignores the original amount
Because it is calculated only once
Because it removes interest each year
questions.expected: Because the interest itself earns further interest over time
questions.memo: With compounding, each period's interest is added to the balance and then earns interest too, so growth accelerates.

questions.question: True or false: Investing in shares carries the risk that their value can fall.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Share prices rise and fall, so there is a real risk that an investment in shares can lose value.

questions.question: Sort each return into whether it comes from shares or from lending/saving.

items.text: A dividend paid out of company profit
A rise in a share's market value
Interest from a fixed savings account
A share of profits distributed to owners
Interest earned on a retail bond

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Dividends and share-value growth come from shares; interest comes from lending or saving money (bonds, savings accounts).

questions.question: What is the simple interest on R2 000 invested at 8% per year for 3 years?
questions.memo: Simple interest = R2 000 × 8% × 3 = R160 × 3 = R480.

questions.question: What is a key benefit of a unit trust for a small investor?
options: It spreads money across many investments, reducing risk
It guarantees the investor will never lose money
It gives full control of a single company
It avoids all fees and charges
questions.expected: It spreads money across many investments, reducing risk
questions.memo: A unit trust diversifies across many assets, so a small investor is less exposed to any single investment failing.

questions.question: A _________ is a portion of a company that an investor can buy on the stock exchange.
questions.expected: share
questions.memo: A share is a unit of ownership in a company that can be bought and sold, for example on the JSE.

questions.question: R1 000 is invested for 2 years at 10% per year. Which earns more — simple or compound interest — and roughly by how much?
questions.expected: Compound earns more (R210 vs R200)
questions.memo: Simple = R1 000 × 10% × 2 = R200. Compound = R1 000 × 1.1² − R1 000 = R1 210 − R1 000 = R210. Compound earns R10 more.

questions.question: An investor wants low risk and a predictable return. Which option fits best?
options: Shares in a single small start-up
Borrowing to bet on one volatile share
Putting everything into one speculative company
questions.expected: A government retail bond
questions.memo: A government retail bond is relatively low-risk with predictable interest, suiting a cautious investor; single shares carry more risk.

questions.question: Why do many investors spread their money across different types of investments?
options: Diversifying reduces the impact if any single investment performs badly
It guarantees the highest possible return
questions.expected: Diversifying reduces the impact if any single investment performs badly
questions.memo: Spreading investments (diversification) means a loss in one is cushioned by others, lowering overall risk.

questions.question: A young investor saving for retirement in 30 years asks why compound interest matters so much over a long period.
options: Over many years, interest earning interest causes the investment to grow dramatically
Compound interest only matters for one year
Time makes no difference to compound growth
Compound interest shrinks an investment over time
questions.expected: Over many years, interest earning interest causes the investment to grow dramatically
questions.memo: Compounding builds on itself, so over decades the growth becomes very large — time is a powerful ally for long-term investors.

BUS.G12.T3.INSURANCE.A1.title: Investment: insurance & assurance
BUS.G12.T3.INSURANCE.A1.description: Distinguishing assurance from insurance, compulsory and non-compulsory insurance, life insurance and retirement annuities, insurance of goods, the principle of average with over- and under-insurance calculations, and the compulsory funds — the Unemployment Insurance Fund (UIF) and Road Accident Fund (RAF).
BUS.G12.T3.INSURANCE.A1.recovery_strategy: Assurance covers an event that WILL happen (death) — e.g. life cover. Insurance covers an event that MIGHT happen (fire, theft). UIF and RAF are compulsory. Under the principle of average, under-insuring means you are paid out proportionally less.

questions.question: Assurance covers an event that:
options: Will definitely happen, such as death
Might or might not happen, such as a fire
questions.expected: Will definitely happen, such as death
questions.memo: Assurance covers a certain event (such as death); the question is only when it happens, not if.

questions.question: Insurance covers an event that:
options: Might happen, such as fire or theft
Is certain to happen, such as death
questions.expected: Might happen, such as fire or theft
questions.memo: Insurance covers an uncertain event that may or may not happen, such as fire, theft or an accident.

questions.question: The _________ is the compulsory fund that helps workers who lose their jobs.
questions.expected: UIF
questions.memo: The Unemployment Insurance Fund (UIF) is a compulsory fund that provides short-term relief to workers who become unemployed.

questions.question: True or false: The Road Accident Fund (RAF) compensates victims of road accidents.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The RAF is a compulsory fund that compensates people injured or affected by road accidents.

questions.question: Life _________ pays out a sum when the insured person dies.
questions.expected: assurance
questions.memo: Life assurance pays out on death — a certain event — which is why it is 'assurance' rather than 'insurance'.

questions.question: True or false: Over-insurance means insuring an item for more than it is worth.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Over-insurance is insuring for more than an item's actual value — but a payout is still limited to the real loss, so you cannot profit.

questions.question: Sort each example into assurance or insurance.

items.text: Life cover that pays out on death
Cover against the shop burning down
A retirement annuity that matures at a set age
Cover against a delivery van being stolen
A funeral policy paying out on death
Cover against flood damage to stock

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Cover for certain events (death, reaching a set age) is assurance; cover for uncertain events (fire, theft, flood) is insurance.

questions.question: Which of these is COMPULSORY insurance in South Africa?
questions.expected: UIF contributions for employees
questions.memo: UIF (and the RAF levy on fuel) is compulsory; insuring possessions like a TV or pet is voluntary (non-compulsory).

questions.question: An asset worth R100 000 is insured for only R50 000. Under the principle of average, what is paid for a R20 000 loss?
questions.memo: Payout = (insured ÷ value) × loss = (R50 000 ÷ R100 000) × R20 000 = ½ × R20 000 = R10 000.

questions.question: A retirement _________ is a long-term plan that helps a person save for retirement.
questions.expected: annuity
questions.memo: A retirement annuity is a long-term savings plan designed to provide income after retirement.

questions.question: What does under-insurance mean for a claim?
options: The item is insured for less than its value, so the payout is reduced proportionally
The insurer pays double the loss
The item is insured for more than its value
No claim can ever be made
questions.expected: The item is insured for less than its value, so the payout is reduced proportionally
questions.memo: Under-insurance means cover below the item's value, so under the principle of average the payout is scaled down.

questions.question: True or false: Both the UIF and the RAF are compulsory.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The UIF (employee contributions) and the RAF (funded by a fuel levy) are both compulsory.

questions.question: Sort each item into compulsory or non-compulsory insurance.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: UIF and the RAF levy are compulsory; insuring household goods, a cellphone or taking a voluntary life policy is non-compulsory.

questions.question: If a business over-insures stock worth R30 000 for R45 000 and the stock is destroyed, how much can it claim?
options: R30 000 — the actual value, since you cannot profit from insurance
questions.expected: R30 000 — the actual value, since you cannot profit from insurance
questions.memo: Insurance compensates the actual loss, not more — over-insuring does not let you claim above the item's real value.

questions.question: Why does a business insure its goods and premises?
options: To protect against losses from events like fire, theft or flood
To increase the chance of a fire
To raise the price of its products
questions.expected: To protect against losses from events like fire, theft or flood
questions.memo: Insuring goods and premises protects the business financially if an uncertain event like fire or theft occurs.

questions.question: The principle of _________ reduces a payout when an item is under-insured.
questions.expected: average
questions.memo: The principle of average scales the payout down in proportion to how much the item was under-insured.

questions.question: Equipment worth R200 000 is insured for R150 000. Under the principle of average, what is paid for a R40 000 loss?
A young breadwinner wants to make sure their family is provided for if they die. Which product fits best?
options: Life assurance, which pays out on death
questions.expected: Life assurance, which pays out on death
questions.memo: Because death is certain, life assurance is the product designed to provide for dependants when the breadwinner dies.

questions.question: Why is under-insuring assets a risky decision for a business?
options: The principle of average means a claim will be paid out only in proportion, leaving a shortfall
Under-insurance always pays out the full value
questions.expected: The principle of average means a claim will be paid out only in proportion, leaving a shortfall
questions.memo: If an under-insured asset is damaged, the payout is scaled down, so the business must cover the rest of the loss itself.

questions.question: What is the key difference that decides whether a product is 'assurance' or 'insurance'?
options: Whether the event covered is certain to happen (assurance) or only possible (insurance)
The price of the monthly premium
Whether the company is large or small
The colour of the policy document
questions.expected: Whether the event covered is certain to happen (assurance) or only possible (insurance)
questions.memo: Assurance covers a certain event (like death); insurance covers an uncertain one (like fire or theft) — that certainty is the deciding difference.

BUS.G12.T3.OWNERSHIP.A1.title: Forms of ownership & business success
BUS.G12.T3.OWNERSHIP.A1.description: Determining the extent to which a particular form of ownership contributes to the success or failure of a business, recapping the characteristics, advantages, disadvantages and comparison of forms of ownership with a focus on capacity, taxation, management, capital, division of profits and legislation.
BUS.G12.T3.OWNERSHIP.A1.recovery_strategy: Judge a form of ownership by how it affects success: limited liability and continuity help a company raise capital and survive; unlimited liability and limited capital can hold a sole trader back. Match capital, tax, management and risk to the venture.

questions.question: A sole trader has _________ liability.
questions.expected: unlimited
questions.memo: A sole trader is personally liable for all the business's debts — unlimited liability.

questions.question: A company offers its shareholders _________ liability.
questions.expected: limited
questions.memo: Shareholders of a company have limited liability — they can lose only what they invested.

questions.question: True or false: A company has continuity, while a sole trader's business may end when the owner dies.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A company carries on regardless of changes in ownership; a sole trader's business is tied to the owner.

questions.question: A _________ company may not sell its shares to the public.
questions.expected: private
questions.memo: A private company (Pty) Ltd cannot offer shares to the public, unlike a public company.

questions.question: True or false: A partnership shares its profits among the partners.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: In a partnership, profits are divided among the partners according to their agreement.

questions.question: Which form of ownership can usually raise the most capital?
questions.expected: A public company
questions.memo: A public company can sell shares to the public, giving it access to the largest pool of capital.

questions.question: Sort each feature under the form of ownership it best describes.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Sole trader: unlimited liability, full control, simple start. Company: limited liability, separate legal person, continuity.

questions.question: How can limited liability help a business succeed?
options: It protects owners' personal assets and encourages people to invest
It forces owners to risk their homes
It removes the need for any capital
It guarantees the business cannot fail
questions.expected: It protects owners' personal assets and encourages people to invest
questions.memo: Limited liability lowers the risk to owners and investors, making it easier to attract the capital a business needs to grow.

questions.question: Read both owners, then decide which each statement matches.

source_a.text: As a sole trader I keep full control and all the profit, but I am personally liable for every debt and I struggle to raise much capital.

source_b.text: As a company we have limited liability and can raise large capital by issuing shares, but we face more regulation and share control.

statements.text: Bears unlimited personal liability
Can raise large capital by issuing shares
Is a recognised form of business ownership
Pays no tax of any kind

questions.expected: s1=a_only, s2=b_only, s3=both, s4=neither
questions.memo: The sole trader has unlimited liability; the company can raise share capital. Both are forms of ownership; neither escapes tax.

questions.question: A form of ownership with _________ liability puts the owner's personal assets at risk.
questions.expected: unlimited
questions.memo: Unlimited liability means the owner's personal possessions can be used to pay the business's debts.

questions.question: How does taxation differ between a company and a sole trader?
options: A company is taxed at the company rate; a sole trader's profit is taxed as personal income
Companies pay no tax; sole traders pay double
questions.expected: A company is taxed at the company rate; a sole trader's profit is taxed as personal income
questions.memo: A company pays tax in its own name; a sole trader's profit is part of the owner's personal income for tax.

questions.question: True or false: The form of ownership a business chooses can affect its chances of success.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The form of ownership shapes capital, liability, tax, management and continuity — all of which affect success.

questions.question: Sort each factor by which form of ownership it tends to favour for a fast-growing venture.

items.text: Needs to raise large amounts of capital
Wants the simplest, cheapest possible start
Wants one person to keep full control
Has a very small, low-risk operation

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Large capital, limited liability and continuity favour a company; simplicity, full control and a small low-risk scale favour a sole trader.

questions.question: Why might a venture that needs large capital choose to be a company?
options: A company can raise capital by issuing shares and offers limited liability to investors
A company cannot raise any capital
A company always pays less tax than any other form
A company has no legal requirements
questions.expected: A company can raise capital by issuing shares and offers limited liability to investors
questions.memo: Companies can sell shares and limit investor risk, making it easier to attract the large capital a big venture needs.

questions.question: In a partnership, how are profits usually handled?
options: Divided among the partners according to their agreement
questions.expected: Divided among the partners according to their agreement
questions.memo: Partners share the profits as set out in their partnership agreement, often according to their contributions.

questions.question: _________ means a business continues to exist despite changes in its ownership.
questions.expected: Continuity
questions.memo: Continuity is the ability of a business — especially a company — to keep operating even as owners change.

questions.question: Read two ventures, then decide which each statement matches.

source_a.text: Our small craft business stayed a sole trader. When the owner fell ill, the business stopped and creditors came after her personal savings.

source_b.text: We registered as a company. When a director left, the business carried on, and investors only risked the money they had put in.

statements.text: Suffered because of unlimited liability and no continuity
Benefited from limited liability and continuity
Shows how the form of ownership affected the outcome
Operated with no owners at all

questions.expected: s1=a_only, s2=b_only, s3=both, s4=neither
questions.memo: Venture A was hurt by unlimited liability and lack of continuity; Venture B gained from limited liability and continuity. Both show ownership shaping the outcome; neither lacks owners.

questions.question: A high-risk venture needing major investment is set up as a sole trader. Why might the form of ownership threaten its success?
options: Unlimited liability and limited capital expose the owner and constrain growth
Sole traders always raise the most capital
Unlimited liability protects the owner's assets
The form of ownership cannot affect a high-risk venture
questions.expected: Unlimited liability and limited capital expose the owner and constrain growth
questions.memo: For a high-risk, capital-hungry venture, a sole trader's unlimited liability and limited capital are poorly matched and can hold it back or ruin the owner.

questions.question: To what extent does the form of ownership determine a business's success?
options: It strongly shapes capital, liability, tax and continuity, but success also depends on management and the market
It is the only thing that determines success
It has no effect on success at all
questions.expected: It strongly shapes capital, liability, tax and continuity, but success also depends on management and the market
questions.memo: The form of ownership powerfully influences key factors, but success ultimately also depends on good management and market conditions.

questions.question: Three friends want to start a growing tech venture, attract investors and protect their personal assets. Which form best supports success?
options: A company, for limited liability, shared capital and continuity
A sole trader, so one friend controls everything
A form with unlimited liability for all three
questions.expected: A company, for limited liability, shared capital and continuity
questions.memo: A company suits a growing venture seeking investors and asset protection, offering limited liability, easier capital and continuity.

BUS.G12.T3.PRESENT.A1.title: Presentation & data response
BUS.G12.T3.PRESENT.A1.description: Accurate, succinct verbal and non-verbal presentation of business information, including the criteria for a logical and effective presentation, the process and style of using visual aids, responding professionally to questions and feedback, and amending plans and documents as necessary.
BUS.G12.T3.PRESENT.A1.recovery_strategy: An effective presentation knows its audience, puts the most important information first, and uses clear visuals. After feedback, amend the plan and documents and carry the improvements into future work.

questions.question: An effective presentation should be designed around:
options: The needs and level of its audience
questions.expected: The needs and level of its audience
questions.memo: Knowing the audience lets you pitch the content and language at the right level so the message lands.

questions.question: True or false: The most important information should be presented first.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Leading with the key information ensures the audience gets the main message, even if attention or time fades.

questions.question: Answering questions about figures and business information presented is called a _________ response.
questions.expected: data
questions.memo: A data response involves reading, interpreting and answering questions on presented business information and figures.

questions.question: Which of these is a visual aid for presenting data clearly?
questions.expected: A graph
questions.memo: A graph is a visual (non-verbal) aid that shows data and trends clearly.

questions.question: True or false: After receiving feedback, a presenter should amend the work where needed.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Acting on feedback by amending plans and documents improves the work and future presentations.

questions.question: When responding to questions, a presenter should not _________.
questions.expected: argue
questions.memo: A professional presenter answers and clarifies calmly rather than arguing with the questioner.

questions.question: Sort each feature into effective or ineffective presentation.

items.text: Clear headings and key points first
Simple charts that show the data

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Effective: clear structure, simple charts, suitable language. Ineffective: cluttered slides, reading dense text, ignoring questions.

questions.question: Which is a criterion for a logical, effective presentation of information?
options: Know your audience and use clear headings, charts and the most important points first
Use as many long words as possible
Hide the key message at the very end
questions.expected: Know your audience and use clear headings, charts and the most important points first
questions.memo: Effective presentations are audience-aware, well-structured, and lead with the key points supported by clear visuals.

questions.question: Put the stages of delivering and improving a presentation in order.

items.text: Prepare the content and visuals for the audience
Respond professionally to questions and feedback
Amend the work based on the feedback

questions.expected: prepare, present, questions, amend
questions.memo: Prepare, present, handle questions and feedback, then amend the work — that order improves both the message and future versions.

questions.question: Knowing your _________ lets you pitch a presentation at the right level.
questions.expected: audience
questions.memo: Understanding the audience shapes the content, depth and language so the message is understood.

questions.question: How should a presenter handle critical but fair feedback?
options: Listen, thank the person, and use it to improve the work
Take it personally and refuse to continue
questions.expected: Listen, thank the person, and use it to improve the work
questions.memo: Fair feedback is valuable; a professional listens, acknowledges it and amends the work accordingly.

questions.question: True or false: Amending plans and documents after feedback can improve future presentations.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Carrying improvements from feedback into the documents and future plans makes later work stronger.

questions.question: Sort each response to questions and feedback into professional or unprofessional.

items.text: Blaming the audience for not understanding
Offering to follow up on an unknown answer

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Professional: answer calmly, correct errors, offer to follow up. Unprofessional: aggression, blaming the audience, refusing feedback.

questions.question: Why are charts and graphs useful in a data-response presentation?
options: They show figures, patterns and comparisons quickly and clearly
They hide the data from the audience
They always replace the need for any explanation
They make the data impossible to read
questions.expected: They show figures, patterns and comparisons quickly and clearly
questions.memo: Charts and graphs turn raw figures into clear visual patterns, helping the audience grasp the data fast.

questions.question: A presenter is asked a question they genuinely cannot answer. What is the professional response?
options: Admit it honestly and offer to find out and follow up
Make up a confident but false answer
questions.expected: Admit it honestly and offer to find out and follow up
questions.memo: Honesty plus a commitment to follow up keeps the presenter credible; bluffing risks giving wrong information.

questions.question: Clear _________ help organise information so the audience can follow it.
questions.expected: headings
questions.memo: Clear headings (and subheadings) structure the information so the audience can follow the flow.

questions.question: Put the steps of an effective data-response presentation in order.

items.text: Read and understand the data provided
Organise the key figures and points
Present them clearly with suitable visuals
Respond to questions and amend if needed

questions.expected: read, organise, present, respond
questions.memo: Understand the data, organise the key points, present them with clear visuals, then respond to questions and amend.

questions.question: After a presentation, the audience raises several valid concerns. What is the best response?
options: Note the concerns, amend the plan and documents, and apply the lessons next time
Argue that the audience misunderstood everything
questions.expected: Note the concerns, amend the plan and documents, and apply the lessons next time
questions.memo: Valid feedback should be recorded and acted on by amending the work and improving future presentations.

questions.question: Why is the ability to amend information after feedback an important business skill?
options: It keeps plans and documents accurate and shows responsiveness, building trust
It is unnecessary because first drafts are always perfect
It wastes time with no benefit
It signals weakness and should be avoided
questions.expected: It keeps plans and documents accurate and shows responsiveness, building trust
questions.memo: Updating work in response to feedback keeps it accurate and relevant and shows stakeholders the business listens and improves.

questions.question: Which presenter is most likely to communicate business data effectively?
options: One who knows the audience, leads with key points, uses clear visuals and handles questions calmly
One who reads dense text aloud and argues with questioners
One who hides the main message and uses cluttered slides
One who ignores the audience entirely
questions.expected: One who knows the audience, leads with key points, uses clear visuals and handles questions calmly
questions.memo: Effective communication combines audience awareness, a clear structure, good visuals and a calm, professional handling of questions.
